questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God is the only Redeemer, who made a way in the past and will make a new way now, so we can trust Him.

en.reflection: Today, in what area do you most need to experience God's redemptive power and trust that He will make a new way for you?
en.prayer: Only Redeemer, thank You that You are the God who does new things and makes a way. Please remove my fears and unbelief, and help me let go of the past, fixing my eyes on the new path You have prepared for me. Pour out Your Spirit upon me, filling me with strength and hope. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to meditate on “I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King.” (Isaiah 43:15) and express your trust in God.

en.theme: The One True God, Our Only Redeemer
en.focus: God declares Himself to be the only true God, the only Saviour, and invites His people to trust in Him alone.

questions.question: How does God refer to Himself in Isaiah 44:6?
options: The Creator
The King and Redeemer of Israel
The LORD of hosts
The Holy One of Israel
questions.explanation: God declares through the prophet Isaiah that He is the King and Redeemer of Israel, the First and the Last, and there is no God besides Him.

questions.question: How does the passage describe those who make idols?
options: They are wise and can create beautiful gods
Their eyes are covered, so they cannot think or understand
They are devout people seeking God
They are wealthy people who can afford expensive materials
questions.explanation: The passage states that those who make idols have their eyes covered so they cannot see, and their minds closed so they cannot understand. They have no knowledge or discernment.

questions.question: Why does God say He has “blotted out your transgressions like a cloud”?
options: Because the people of Israel had never sinned
Because God was indifferent to the sins of His people
Because God graciously forgave their sins and invited them to return
Because the people of Israel had already paid the price for their sins
questions.explanation: God actively declares His forgiveness of Israel’s sins, like a cloud being blotted out, and calls them to return to Him.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us to trust in God?
options: It teaches us how to make our own gods
It shows that God is weak and needs human help
It reveals God as the one true God, capable of forgiving sin and saving
It tells us that good works alone will bring blessings
questions.explanation: This passage strongly asserts God's uniqueness, omnipotence, and His grace in forgiving and redeeming, encouraging us to trust Him completely.

en.reflection: Have you ever, perhaps unknowingly, placed certain people, things, or achievements above God in your life? How can you more intentionally trust in the one true God today?
reflectionOptions: Let go of a pursuit of worldly success
Stop relying on someone else's help
en.prayer: O one true God, King and Redeemer of Israel, I thank You that You are the First and the Last, and there is no God besides You. Help me to trust You alone in every aspect of my life, and not to rely on false idols. Thank You for blotting out my transgressions and calling me back to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a few minutes to consider anything in your life that might be taking God's place, and pray to Him, asking for help to put Him first.

en.focus: God is the Creator and Sustainer of all things, who foretells the future and accomplishes His purposes through chosen instruments.

questions.question: How does God identify Himself at the beginning of today's passage?
options: King of Israel
Your Maker and Redeemer
Lord of Hosts
The Supreme Judge
questions.explanation: God explicitly states, 'Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb...' and 'your Maker'.

questions.question: How does God demonstrate His uniqueness in this passage?
options: By performing miracles and wonders
By raising the dead
By thwarting false prophets and fulfilling His servants' words
By giving laws and commandments
questions.explanation: God declares that He 'frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners; who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish; who confirms the word of His servant and performs the counsel of His messengers.'

questions.question: What was God's primary purpose in raising up King Cyrus?
options: To enable him to build a mighty empire
To teach him about the faith of Israel
To use him to rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple for the LORD
To conquer Egypt
questions.explanation: God prophesies that Cyrus will be His shepherd who will accomplish all His pleasure, including saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'

questions.question: How does today's passage encourage your trust in God?
options: It reminds me that God controls history, and my future is in His hands
It motivates me to work harder, knowing God will help me succeed
It makes me believe God is only with the people of Israel
It encourages me to seek wealth and power
questions.explanation: God is the Creator and Redeemer; He controls all things, even prophesying about and using a king who doesn't know Him to achieve His purposes. This assures us that He also governs our lives and future.

en.reflection: Knowing that God is in control of everything, how does this help you with a current worry or plan in your life?
reflectionOptions: Entrust a difficult situation with greater faith
Seek God's guidance in a decision
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for being the one true God who created heaven and earth. You govern history and You govern my life. Please help me to trust more deeply in Your sovereignty and wisdom, and to surrender all my worries and plans into Your hands. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to list one thing you are most concerned about, then pray to God, acknowledging His sovereignty and control over it.

en.focus: God is the Creator with absolute sovereignty and wisdom, and as His creation, we are to trust and submit to His plans.

questions.question: What metaphor does the prophet use here to describe the relationship between man and the Creator?
options: Worker and employer
Sheep and shepherd
Clay and potter
Servant and master
questions.explanation: The passage directly uses the metaphor of 'clay saying to the potter,' emphasizing the relationship between Creator and creation.

questions.question: How does God respond to those who question His actions in the passage?
options: He will show them His mighty power
He emphasizes that He is the unique Creator with absolute authority
He will explain His plans to them
He will punish all who question Him
questions.explanation: God responds to human questioning by emphasizing that He is the one true God who created everything and humanity.

questions.question: What main truth about the relationship between God and humanity does this passage teach us?
options: Humans have the right to question every one of God's decisions
God will change His plans based on human demands
God is the supreme sovereign, and humans should submit to and trust His will
People can control their own destiny if they try hard enough
questions.explanation: The core message of this passage is God's absolute sovereignty and wisdom as Creator, and the humility and trust due from humanity as His creation.

questions.question: In what area of your life do you most need to trust God's sovereignty and wisdom more deeply?
options: Future plans
Unjust circumstances
Health of loved ones
Other personal response
questions.explanation: (This is a personal application question, without a standard answer, intended to guide reflection.)

en.reflection: When you feel confused or have questions about God's plans, how does this passage help you to reframe your perspective on His sovereignty and your role?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me that God is all-powerful
It helps me release my need for control
It makes me more willing to trust God's wisdom
en.prayer: Dear Lord, You are the Potter, and I am the clay. Help me, in both good times and challenging circumstances, to fix my eyes on Your wisdom and sovereignty. When I do not understand Your ways, may I humbly submit and trust in Your goodness. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, when something doesn't go your way, try to pause and silently say to God, “Lord, You are the Potter, and You know everything.”

en.theme: The One True God and His Salvation
en.focus: The LORD is the one and only true God, and His salvation is real and available to all who believe in Him.

questions.question: In Isaiah 45:14-17, which nations or peoples are mentioned as coming to Israel and the LORD?
options: Egypt and Cush
Assyria and Babylon
Tyre and Sidon
Moab and Edom
questions.explanation: The passage states that the wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush will come to Israel, and they will acknowledge the LORD as God.

questions.question: What attribute of the LORD is repeatedly emphasized in the passage?
options: He is the Creator and controller of the universe
He is a hidden God, the Savior of Israel
He is a righteous judge who punishes the wicked
He is a generous giver of wealth
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that the LORD is “a God who conceals himself, the God and Savior of Israel” (v. 15), and declares, “I am the LORD, and there is no other” (v. 18).

questions.question: What is God's purpose in calling the 'ends of the earth' to turn to Him?
options: To increase His glory and power
To punish all who do not know Him
So that they may be saved, for He is the only Savior
So that they may serve Israel
questions.explanation: God explicitly declares, “Turn to me and be saved, all you ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.”

questions.question: How does recognizing the LORD as the only Savior impact your life today?
options: I should try harder to prove His existence
I should focus only on my own salvation and not care about others
I should trust Him wholeheartedly and share this hope of salvation with others
I should feel fear, as He will judge all who do not believe
questions.explanation: Since God is the only Savior, we should trust Him completely and be eager to share this good news with everyone who needs salvation.

en.reflection: When facing difficulties and confusion in life, do you still believe that the LORD is the one true God and your Savior?
reflectionOptions: Yes, He is my strong refuge
Sometimes I waver, but I'm willing to seek Him again
I often find myself forgetting His uniqueness
en.prayer: O one true God, my Savior, thank You for revealing Yourself to me. Help me to trust You firmly in all circumstances, for You alone can give true salvation. May my life glorify Your name and bear witness to Your truth to those around me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, intentionally find an opportunity to share your faith in God with a friend or family member, even if it's just a brief testimony.

en.focus: Only God is eternally unchanging, sovereign from beginning to end, and able to save His people.

questions.question: What is described as happening to the two Babylonian idols mentioned by the prophet?
options: They are being carried on beasts, a heavy burden
They are speaking to the people, promising salvation
They are being newly adorned for a festival
They are being cast into fire and completely burned
questions.explanation: The passage describes the Babylonian idols, Bel and Nebo, being carried on beasts of burden, becoming a heavy load.

questions.question: How does God describe His difference from these idols?
options: God lives in heaven, while idols reside on earth
God is the Creator, while idols are man-made
God has carried His people from birth to old age
God has many names, while idols have only one name
questions.explanation: God emphasizes that He has carried His people from birth, and will continue to sustain and deliver them even in their old age, in stark contrast to idols that need to be carried.

questions.question: How does God demonstrate that He acts alone and declares the end from the beginning?
options: He gathers all the nation's leaders for counsel
He prophesies that King Cyrus will fulfill His purpose
He challenges all the gods of the idols
He displays His power to create heaven and earth
questions.explanation: God states that He calls a man from the east (referring to King Cyrus) to accomplish His purpose, thus demonstrating His foreknowledge and control over future events.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us when facing life's challenges and uncertainties?
options: We need to rely more on our own wisdom and strength
We should imitate idols and seek external help
We can trust God as the consistent, sovereign Saviour
We should avoid difficulties and focus only on immediate pleasures
questions.explanation: The passage highlights that God is sovereign from beginning to end, and He will sustain, carry, and deliver His people. Therefore, we can fully trust in Him.

en.reflection: In your life, have you ever treated anything as an “idol,” allowing it to bear a burden that only God can carry?
en.prayer: Eternal Father, thank You for being the God who has carried me from birth, and who will sustain and save me even in my old age. Help me to lay down all false burdens in my life and to trust solely in Your power and love. May my heart cherish You above all else. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a minute today to reflect on what feels like a heavy burden in your life and commit it to God, trusting that He will carry it.

en.focus: God will judge all arrogance and self-reliance; only those who humbly depend on Him will find true peace.

questions.question: Babylon (the 'daughter of the Chaldeans') is called a 'virgin'. What does this imply?
options: She had been conquered by many nations
She was known for her purity
She had never been subdued by invaders
She was about to experience a new beginning
questions.explanation: Calling Babylon a 'virgin' implies that she had never been conquered by foreign powers, priding herself on her security and independence.

questions.question: What does God command Babylon to do, indicating her loss of esteemed status?
options: Put on splendid robes
Sit on a throne and rule
Take off her crown and sit in the dust
Build higher walls
questions.explanation: God commands Babylon to come down from her throne and sit in the dust, removing her crown, symbolizing her fall from honor to humiliation and loss of dominion.

questions.question: What was Babylon's primary sin?
options: She did not have enough wealth
She did not worship God enough
She relied on her own wisdom and knowledge, believing herself to be unrivaled
She did not treat her own people well
questions.explanation: Babylon's core sin was her arrogant self-reliance on her own wisdom and knowledge, saying, 'I am, and there is none besides me.'

questions.question: What main truth about God does this passage teach us?
options: God is not concerned with the rise and fall of earthly nations
God will allow any nation to remain powerful forever
God is the Lord of history, and He will judge all arrogant and self-exalting powers
Human wisdom and power can resist God's will
questions.explanation: This passage clearly demonstrates that God is sovereign over all, and He will judge those powers that are arrogant, self-sufficient, and do not fear Him.

en.reflection: In your life, have you ever been proud or self-reliant due to your abilities, achievements, or wisdom, perhaps overlooking God's grace and sovereignty?
en.prayer: Lord, You are the God who governs all things, and all wisdom and power come from You. Please help me to constantly examine my heart, removing all pride and self-reliance, and humbly depending on You. May my life bring glory to You alone, and not to myself. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute today quietly reflecting on areas where you tend to rely on yourself rather than on God, and confess this to Him.

en.focus: God recounts Israel's rebellious history, yet remains faithful for His own glory, promising salvation.

questions.question: What problem does God highlight about the people of Israel at the beginning of the passage?
options: They did not know God
They were hypocritical and did not genuinely seek God
They had not built the temple
They did not observe the Sabbath
questions.explanation: The passage states that while the people of Israel called themselves citizens of the holy city and invoked the name of the LORD, they did so not in truth or righteousness, but with hypocrisy.

questions.question: What was God's purpose in repeatedly mentioning that He declared things beforehand?
options: To prove His power was greater than idols
To make the people realize their foolishness
To make them admit that the fulfillment of prophecies came from God, not their idols
To make them repent of their sins
questions.explanation: God declared things in advance so that the people could not attribute their fulfillment to idols, but had to acknowledge that the LORD accomplished them.

questions.question: God stated that He did not destroy Israel for His own name's sake and glory. What does this reveal?
options: God valued Israel's strong national power
God could not tolerate His glory being defiled
God needed Israel to demonstrate His love
God feared other nations would mock Him
questions.explanation: God explained that He did not destroy Israel for His own name's sake and glory, not wanting His name to be profaned, showing His high regard for His holy name.

questions.question: What important truths about God can we learn from this passage?
options: God is fickle, and His plans often change
God is faithful to His covenant, and His prophecies and promises will surely be fulfilled
God only saves those who perfectly obey His laws
God is not concerned with human history and future
questions.explanation: Despite Israel's rebellion, God, out of His own faithfulness, fulfilled His prophecies and promised salvation, demonstrating that He is a faithful covenant-keeping God.

en.reflection: In what areas today do you need to acknowledge God's faithfulness and turn back to Him?
reflectionOptions: Admit I have doubted God's promises
Admit I have rebelled against God's Word
Admit I have given glory to other things
en.prayer: Faithful Lord, thank You for not abandoning me despite my rebellion, but for leading and saving me because of Your own glory and faithfulness. Help me to know Your faithfulness more deeply today and to genuinely turn back to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to recall a promise God has fulfilled in your life and give thanks for it.

en.theme: The Mission and Hope of God's Servant
en.focus: God calls His servants, gives them a mission, and promises to sustain and glorify them through all difficulties.

questions.question: How does Isaiah describe the LORD's calling of His servant?
options: Chosen before the nations
Called from the womb
Anointed in the temple
Encountered in the wilderness
questions.explanation: The passage states that God called the servant before birth and named him Israel.

questions.question: What was the servant's initial feeling about his ministry?
options: Full of accomplishment
Feeling inadequate
Feeling that his labor was in vain
Desiring greater authority
questions.explanation: The servant complained, 'I have toiled in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing at all,' indicating a sense of futility in his service.

questions.type: Understand God's broader mission for the servant
questions.question: Beyond bringing Israel back, what greater mission did God give His servant?
options: To be a light for the Gentiles, so that God’s salvation may reach to the ends of the earth
To establish a powerful military empire
To write more laws and commandments
To become a source of wealth for the world
questions.explanation: God says, 'I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.' This shows the servant's mission extends beyond Israel.

questions.question: How does God respond to His servant to address his concerns and doubts?
options: By promising him more wealth and status
By assuring him he would face no difficulties
By promising to sustain him, cause kings to bow, and bring back the captives
By telling him he could succeed through his own efforts
questions.explanation: God promises to uphold the despised servant, cause kings to rise, answer him in a time of favor, and lead out prisoners, bringing freedom to the captives.

en.reflection: Are there times in your life when you feel your efforts in service are in vain? How can you find strength and hope from today's passage?
reflectionOptions: Trust that God is in control and His purposes will prevail
Re-examine my motives, ensuring they are to glorify God
Seek prayer support and share my feelings with a fellow believer
en.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for knowing me from my mother's womb and having a purpose for my life. When I feel weak or that my efforts are fruitless, turn my heart back to Your promises. Help me to understand that my worth is not in my achievements, but in Your calling and sustaining grace. May I be a light in Your hands, bringing Your salvation to those around me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for a fellow believer who is facing challenges or feeling discouraged in their service, asking God to strengthen and encourage them.

en.theme: God Will Never Forget His People
en.focus: Even in seemingly desperate situations, God promises He will never forget or abandon His people.

questions.question: What was Zion’s complaint?
options: God had forgotten her
God had forsaken her
God had not heard her prayers
God had not blessed her
questions.explanation: Zion felt forgotten and forsaken by God, stating, “The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me.”

questions.question: What illustration does God use to emphasize that He will not forget Zion?
options: A mother not forgetting her nursing child
A shepherd not forgetting his flock
A gardener not forgetting his planted trees
A father not forgetting his children
questions.explanation: God uses the powerful imagery of a mother not forgetting her nursing child to illustrate His unfailing remembrance, stating that even if a mother could forget, He never would.

questions.question: How does this passage describe God’s steadfast commitment to His people?
options: God has engraved their names on His hands
God builds strong walls for His people
God provides abundant food for His people
God sends messengers to protect His people
questions.explanation: God says He has engraved Zion on the palms of His hands, and her walls are ever before Him, symbolizing His eternal remembrance and watchfulness.

questions.question: When you feel forgotten by God in difficult times, what comfort can this passage offer you?
options: A reminder of God’s infinite power
Assurance that God has never forgotten you and is determined to save you
Encouragement to seek God more diligently
A message that difficulties are just temporary tests
questions.explanation: The most direct comfort is God's explicit assurance that He will never forget His people and will personally redeem them.

en.reflection: Is there any area in your life where you feel God might have forgotten you?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me that You never forget me. Even when I feel alone or abandoned, Your love and promises stand firm. Help me to cling to Your truth, trusting that You have engraved me on the palms of Your hands and will deliver me in due time. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to meditate on the phrase, 'God has engraved me on the palms of His hands,' and give thanks for it.

en.focus: Even in difficult times, listening to God's word and trusting in His help is the only way out of darkness.

questions.question: What is the reason given in Isaiah 50:1 for the people of Israel being 'divorced'?
options: They committed grave sins
They did not listen to God's word
They were attacked by enemies
They failed to offer sacrifices on time
questions.explanation: The text states that God did not divorce His wife or sell His children; rather, the people were sold because of their iniquities, and their mother was put away because of their transgressions.

questions.question: How does the prophet describe his response to God's call and teaching?
options: He often rejected God's call
He complained that God's will was too difficult
He was not rebellious and did not turn backward
He frequently questioned God's wisdom
questions.explanation: The prophet clearly states that he 'was not rebellious; I turned not backward,' demonstrating his obedience and steadfastness to God.

questions.question: What kind of suffering did the prophet endure for speaking God's word?
options: He was promoted to high office
He received praise from the people
He was beaten, had his beard plucked, and was spat upon
He lived in wealth and was highly respected
questions.explanation: The prophet describes being beaten, having his beard plucked, and being spat upon, yet he did not hide his face because he trusted in God.

questions.question: What guidance does this passage offer to those who walk in darkness and have no light?
options: Rely on their own wisdom and intelligence
Kindle their own fire and walk by its light
Trust in the name of the Lord and rely on their God
Seek help and guidance from other people
questions.explanation: The passage clearly indicates that those who walk in darkness and have no light should trust in the name of the Lord and rely on their God, rather than kindling their own fire.

en.reflection: In your life, have you ever experienced hardship because you obeyed God’s word? How do you continue to trust Him?
reflectionOptions: Share with fellow believers and seek support
Recall God's faithfulness in the past
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your Word is my light and guide. When I face difficulties or feel in darkness, please help me to trust in Your name and rely on Your presence. May I, like the prophet, not be rebellious or turn backward, even in suffering. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, for one area in your life where you are struggling, pray for God to grant you a spirit of obedience and a trusting faith.

en.focus: God reminds His people to remember His past works and to anticipate the salvation and comfort He will surely bring.

questions.question: Who does God call to listen to Him?
options: Those who pursue righteousness and seek the LORD
Those who love strife and reject truth
Those who fear enemies and dare not act
Those who are rich and powerful and need no help
questions.explanation: The passage begins by calling those who pursue righteousness and seek the LORD to listen to God.

questions.question: What example does God use to remind His people of His past grace?
options: He governs the stars in the heavens
He created the mountains and oceans
He called Abraham and made his descendants numerous
He judged the unrighteous nations
questions.explanation: God reminds His people how He called Abraham as one man and made his descendants numerous, demonstrating His grace and power.

questions.question: What does God promise His people they will receive?
options: Greater wealth and power
No more sickness and pain
Everlasting joy and gladness, with sorrow and sighing fleeing away
A mighty army and secure city walls
questions.explanation: God promises comfort for Zion, where there will be gladness and joy, thanksgiving and the sound of singing, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

questions.question: When God calls His people to look to His salvation and righteousness, what does He want them to understand?
options: Human strength and wisdom are enough to solve all problems
God is the Creator, and His salvation and righteousness endure forever
Reliance on foreign allies will bring security
Past experiences are irrelevant to the present situation
questions.explanation: God emphasizes that He is the Creator of heaven and earth, His salvation will never cease, and His righteousness will never be broken, so His people can fully trust Him.

en.reflection: In what difficulty or worry do you need to fix your gaze on God's eternal salvation and comfort today?
en.prayer: Eternal Lord, thank You for being my Creator and Redeemer. When I face difficulties and worries, help me to remember Your past works and to fix my gaze on Your eternal salvation and comfort. May my heart be filled with the joy and hope that You provide. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to recall one act of grace God has performed in your life and thank Him for it.

en.focus: God promises to deliver His people from their distress and bring them back to Zion with shouts of joy.

questions.question: How is Jerusalem described in Isaiah 51:17?
options: A new city loved by God
A strong city being rebuilt
A city that has drunk the cup of staggering
A city full of joy and singing
questions.explanation: The passage describes Jerusalem as having drunk the cup of the LORD’s wrath, suffering greatly.

questions.question: What commands does God give to Jerusalem in 52:1-2?
options: Wake up, put on your beautiful garments, shake off your dust, and loose the bonds from your neck
Build stronger walls and store more provisions
Take revenge on your enemies and defeat them
Show off your wealth and glory to the nations
questions.explanation: God commands Jerusalem to awake, put on strength and beautiful garments, shake off dust, and loose herself from bonds, preparing for new glory.

questions.question: What message does the messenger of good news proclaim?
options: New laws and regulations
Prophecies of war and destruction
Good news of God's salvation and reign
A political declaration for a new nation
questions.explanation: The messenger proclaims peace, good news, salvation, and the message that 'Your God reigns!'

questions.question: How does this passage describe God's deliverance of His people?
options: God will protect them with an army
God will reveal His holy arm and save them in the sight of all nations
God will require His people to strive first before helping them
God will resolve issues through diplomatic means
questions.explanation: God Himself comforts His people and will reveal His holy arm in the sight of all nations to bring salvation, without human assistance.

en.reflection: How does this passage remind you that God is still in control and will bring deliverance, even in the most difficult times?
reflectionOptions: It helps me to release anxiety and trust in God's sovereignty
It motivates me to share God's good news with others
It strengthens my hope for the future
en.prayer: My Heavenly Father, thank You for being my comforting and saving God. When I feel trapped or despairing, please help me to awaken and put on the strength and hope You provide. May I be like the messenger of good news, proclaiming Your peace, blessings, and salvation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, intentionally pray for a friend you know who is going through a difficult time, asking God to comfort and deliver them.

en.theme: The Suffering Servant: His Wounds, Our Healing
en.focus: The suffering and death of Jesus Christ is God's provision for our salvation, bringing us healing and peace through His bearing of our burdens.

questions.question: How does the prophet Isaiah describe the ultimate outcome for 'my servant'?
options: His kingdom will expand, and His power will be unmatched
He will prosper, be raised and lifted up, and highly exalted
He will be despised by nations and unknown to many
He will become a great military leader
questions.explanation: The passage begins by declaring that the servant's ultimate outcome is to “prosper; he will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.”

questions.question: In the eyes of the world, what unattractive characteristics did the servant possess?
options: Handsome in appearance, attracting many
No beauty or majesty to attract us to him, nothing in his appearance that we should desire him
Dressed in splendid robes, showing his dignity
A loud voice, full of authority
questions.explanation: The scripture describes the servant: “He had no beauty or majesty to attract us to him, nothing in his appearance that we should desire him.”

questions.type: Understand the meaning of the servant's suffering
questions.question: According to the passage, for whom did the servant suffer and endure scourging?
options: To punish those who rebelled against God
To prove His own power
To bear our transgressions and diseases
To show the world His endurance
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states, “But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.”

questions.question: Because of this suffering servant, what can we receive today?
options: Earthly wealth and fame
Peace of forgiveness, hope of salvation, and reconciliation with God
Exemption from all suffering in life
Becoming a leader in the world
questions.explanation: Through His suffering, we are reconciled with God, our sins are forgiven, we receive healing and peace, and we have eternal hope.

en.reflection: Today, which burden (guilt, worry, pain) do you most need to entrust to the Savior who suffered for us?
reflectionOptions: Seeking forgiveness for a past transgression
Seeking healing for physical or emotional pain
Seeking peace for a heavy worry
en.prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank You for suffering for me, bearing my iniquities and diseases. Please forgive my transgressions, heal my hurts, and grant me Your peace that transcends all understanding. I cast all my burdens upon You, knowing that You have accomplished salvation for me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take one minute today to silently reflect on Jesus’ suffering for us, and say, “Thank You, Lord Jesus.”

en.theme: God's Everlasting Love and Promise of Restoration
en.focus: Even in seemingly desolate circumstances, God promises His people immeasurable expansion, comfort, and everlasting peace.

questions.question: Who does the prophet Isaiah call to sing at the beginning of chapter 54?
options: The barren woman
The woman with many children
The suffering servant
The foreign king
questions.explanation: The passage begins by calling the barren woman, who has not given birth, to sing, foreshadowing God's unexpected prosperity.

questions.type: Observe God's description of His people
questions.question: How does God describe His people, promising not to be angry with them anymore?
options: My enemies
My people
A forsaken wife
My servants
questions.explanation: God compares His people to a 'forsaken wife' and 'a wife of one's youth,' whom He briefly abandoned but now calls back with great compassion, no longer to be angry with them.

questions.question: What kind of peace does God promise to His people?
options: Temporary peace
Conditional peace
Everlasting peace
Material peace
questions.explanation: God promises His people 'everlasting peace,' which is firm and unchangeable, just as Noah's flood will no longer cover the earth.

questions.type: Understand God's rebuilding of His people
questions.question: How does God promise to rebuild His city and its inhabitants?
options: With stones and wood
With jewels and precious stones
With gold and silver
With human effort and armies
questions.explanation: God promises to rebuild His city with rubies, sapphires, jewels, and precious stones, and all its inhabitants will be taught by the LORD and enjoy great peace.

en.reflection: Have you ever felt 'forsaken' or 'desolate' by God in your life? How does this passage bring you comfort?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me of God's eternal love and promises
It helps me see hope in difficult situations
It encourages me to trust in God's faithfulness
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for being a God who deals with me with everlasting kindness. When I feel abandoned or in distress, please remind me of Your eternal covenant and unchanging promises. Help me open my heart to receive the peace and restoration You offer. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a minute to meditate on 'though the mountains be shaken and the hills be removed, yet my unfailing love for you will not be shaken' (Isaiah 54:10), and apply it to one of your worries today.

en.focus: God freely offers salvation and abundant life to all who seek Him.

questions.question: At the beginning of Isaiah 55, who does God invite to come to Him?
options: All wealthy and powerful people
All who are thirsty and have no money
All priests and Levites of Israel
All who live in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: God invites those who are thirsty and have no money to come and buy wine and milk, to be satisfied freely.

questions.question: What covenant does God promise to make with David?
options: A covenant of wealth and power
A covenant of peace and long life
An everlasting covenant, the sure mercies
A covenant to defeat all enemies
questions.explanation: God promises to make an everlasting covenant with them, the sure mercies shown to David.

questions.question: According to this passage, what is the main reason God invites people to seek Him?
options: Because God needs human worship
Because people cannot satisfy their spiritual hunger on their own
Because God wants to judge the evil in the world
Because God wants to give material wealth
questions.explanation: The passage points out that people toil but are not satisfied because true satisfaction and living water can only be found freely in God.

questions.question: Based on this passage, how should we respond to God's invitation today?
options: Work harder to earn more money
Seek worldly pleasures and success
Forsake wickedness and seek the LORD
Wait for God to actively find us
questions.explanation: The passage encourages the wicked to forsake their way and the unrighteous their thoughts, and to return to the LORD.

en.reflection: What 'toil that does not satisfy' do you need to lay down today to seek God's free grace?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for freely giving salvation and the living water of life. Please help me to lay down all my toils and pursuits that do not satisfy me, and turn to You. May my heart seek You alone and receive Your sure mercies. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to quietly reflect on the phrase 'freely given' in the scripture and offer thanks to God.

en.focus: God's salvation is inclusive, extended to all who keep His covenant, welcoming them into His household.

questions.question: What does God call His people to do at the beginning of the passage?
options: Offer more sacrifices
Maintain justice and do what is right
Build a larger temple
Fight against enemy nations
questions.explanation: God commands His people to maintain justice and do what is right, for His salvation is coming soon.

questions.type: Observe God's promises to different groups
questions.question: Which two groups, often excluded from the Israelite assembly, does God promise blessings if they keep His covenant?
options: Levites and priests
Kings and nobles
Foreigners and eunuchs
Children and the elderly
questions.explanation: The passage specifically mentions foreigners and eunuchs, promising them blessings if they keep God's covenant and enter His house.

questions.question: What does God promise these 'outsiders' if they keep His statutes?
options: To become kings of Israel
A name and a memorial in His house, better than sons and daughters
More land and wealth
Victory in battle
questions.explanation: God promises them 'an everlasting name that will not be cut off' in His house, 'better than sons and daughters'.

questions.question: What is the primary message about God's salvation conveyed in this passage?
options: Salvation is only for the Jews
Salvation is based on ethnicity, not faith
God's salvation is universal and open to all who keep His covenant
Only men can enter God's temple
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God's salvation is not limited by race or status, but is open to all who keep His covenant and seek Him.

en.reflection: Today, do you feel God's acceptance and love for you are universal and unconditional? How does this encourage you?
reflectionOptions: Greater gratitude for God's love for me
More willingness to share the gospel
Reflect on any exclusive attitudes I might have
en.prayer: Loving Heavenly Father, thank You that Your salvation is so broad, welcoming all who seek You. Please help me to love those around me with Your love, and to always live in the grace of Your acceptance. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Think of someone you might not often interact with. Pray for them, asking God to reveal His love and salvation to them.

en.focus: God warns those who are unrighteous and ungodly, but also offers comfort and salvation to those who seek Him and trust in Him.

questions.question: Who does the prophet Isaiah call to devour God's people in Isaiah 56:9?
options: All you beasts of the field, all you beasts in the forest
Armies of the nations
Hungry lions
Evil shepherds
questions.explanation: The passage begins by calling on the beasts of the field and forest to devour, indicating judgment on the derelict leaders of Israel.

questions.question: How are Israel's watchmen (leaders) described in Isaiah 56:10-12?
options: They are alert and constantly watching
They are blind, ignorant, loving to slumber, greedy for gain and drink
They are wise and teach the people
They are humble and sacrifice for the people
questions.explanation: The watchmen (leaders) are severely criticised as blind, ignorant, loving to slumber, and greedy for gain and drink, showing their irresponsibility.

questions.type: Understand God's comfort for the righteous
questions.question: While the wicked are punished, how does God treat the righteous?
options: They will suffer along with the wicked
They are taken away to be at rest in their beds, entering into peace
They will receive wealth and power
They will be asked to intercede for the wicked
questions.explanation: The righteous, though taken away early, enter into peace and rest in their beds, as they walk uprightly and are spared from coming calamity.

questions.question: Despite the people's rebellion, what kind of God is He?
options: A God who completely abandons His people
A God who only cares about punishment
A God who, though angry, is still willing to heal, guide, and comfort His people
A God who only loves those who are completely without sin
questions.explanation: Although God was angry and struck His people for their sin, He still promises to heal, guide, and comfort them, and bring peace to the repentant.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us of God's justice and mercy. Do you feel that you need God's healing and guidance in any specific area of your life?
reflectionOptions: Confess my shortcomings and seek God's forgiveness
Trust in God's mercy and healing
en.prayer: Righteous and loving Heavenly Father, thank You for being not only a Judge but also a Healer and Comforter. Please help me examine my heart, and if there is any unrighteousness or rebellion, I ask for Your forgiveness. May I fully trust in Your mercy and seek Your guidance, finding true peace in You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute today reflecting: How can I better trust God's mercy and seek His guidance today?

en.focus: God desires not outward rituals, but a sincere heart expressed through actions of love towards Him and our neighbours.

questions.question: What does God command the prophet Isaiah to do at the beginning of the passage?
options: Declare Israel's sins
Call the people to repentance
Cry aloud; do not hold back
Encourage the people to continue fasting
questions.explanation: God instructs Isaiah to “cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet” to declare the people’s transgression.

questions.question: Despite their fasting, what problem did the people's actions reveal?
options: They quarreled and exploited others
They secretly worshipped idols
They refused to offer sacrifices to God
They no longer observed the Sabbath
questions.explanation: The passage indicates that on their fast days, they still pursued their own interests, quarreled, and exploited their workers.

questions.question: What actions primarily constitute the fasting and worship that God desires?
options: Wearing sackcloth and eating only vegetables
Praying loudly and kneeling for long periods
Loosening bonds, sharing food, clothing the naked, sheltering the poor
Observing legalistic rules and offering burnt offerings
questions.explanation: God clearly states that the fast He desires involves loosing the bonds of injustice, sharing food with the hungry, and caring for the afflicted and naked.

questions.question: What blessings does God promise if the people live in the way He desires?
options: Becoming the head of nations
Light, healing, guidance, satisfaction, strength
Abundant harvests on the land
The destruction of all their enemies
questions.explanation: God promises that if the people do what is pleasing to Him, their light will break forth, their healing will quickly appear, and God will guide, satisfy, and strengthen them.

en.reflection: In which area of your life can you live out God's desired 'true fast' today?
reflectionOptions: Being more patient with family or colleagues
Actively reaching out to someone in need
en.prayer: Dear Lord, thank You for teaching me what true worship and living mean to You. Please help me not to be content with outward religious rituals, but to let sincere love flow from my heart, serving You and my neighbour with practical actions. May my life bring glory to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, intentionally look for an opportunity to do a small act of kindness or help for someone around you.

en.focus: Human sin separates us from God, but God's arm is not too short; He is still able to save.

questions.question: What does the prophet Isaiah clearly state at the beginning separates people from God?
options: God's lack of power
God's ears being dull of hearing
People's iniquities and sins
Attacks and oppression from other nations
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that it is people's iniquities that separate them from God, not any issue with God's power or willingness.

questions.question: According to the passage, in what specific ways did the people of Israel demonstrate their sin?
options: Focusing on building magnificent temples
Dealing unjustly in the marketplace and lying
Refusing to preach God's law to gentiles
Constantly offering fragrant sacrifices to God
questions.explanation: The passage lists many sins, including hands defiled with blood, fingers stained with guilt, lips speaking lies, tongues uttering evil, practicing injustice, and speaking falsehood, reflecting widespread moral corruption in their daily lives.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the consequences of sin?
options: It makes the nation strong and prosperous
It causes people to stumble, turning light into darkness
It brings more peace and joy
It makes people feel more secure and stable
questions.explanation: The consequence of sin is that people stumble, lack justice, walk in darkness instead of light, grope like the blind, and cannot find peace or walk in upright paths.

questions.question: What truth about sin and salvation does today's passage remind us of?
options: We can atone for our sins by trying harder to do good
God is powerless against human sin
Sin separates us from God, but God's power to save is never diminished
We should focus solely on condemning the sins of others
questions.explanation: The passage clearly points out the separating effect of sin, but more importantly, it emphasizes that God's arm is not too short; He is able and willing to save.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that our sins can separate us from God. Is there any sin you feel is hindering your closeness with God?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of a specific sin
Seek God's forgiveness and restore your relationship with Him
Meditate more deeply on God's power to save
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me that though my iniquities separate me from You, Your arm is not too short; You are still able to save. Please forgive my sins in word and deed, help me to turn back to You, and experience Your forgiveness and peace more deeply. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time today in prayer, confessing a sin you are aware of to God and asking for His forgiveness.

en.focus: Even when human sin abounds and justice is absent, God intervenes with His justice and redemptive action, making a covenant with those who seek Him.

questions.question: What is described as being 'lost' in society?
options: Wealth
Justice
Wisdom
Power
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states, 'Justice is driven back, and righteousness stands at a distance; truth has stumbled in the streets, honesty cannot enter.'

questions.question: What did God do when He saw there was no justice and no one to intercede?
options: Became frustrated and did nothing
Sent angels to punish the people
Clothed Himself with righteousness as armor and brought salvation
Immediately destroyed the whole world
questions.explanation: God saw the situation, 'was appalled that there was no one to intercede,' and therefore 'He put on righteousness as His breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head' to personally intervene.

questions.question: How does God promise to deal with those in Zion who turn to Him?
options: Merely forgive their transgressions
Make a covenant with them, giving His Spirit and His words
Grant them great earthly wealth
Make them rulers over the nations
questions.explanation: God promises, 'As for me, this is my covenant with them,' says the LORD. 'My Spirit, who is on you, and my words that I have put in your mouth will not depart from your mouth, or from the mouths of your children, or from the mouths of their descendants from this time on and forever.'

questions.question: In what situation does this passage most encourage us to trust God?
options: When the world is peaceful and everything is going well
When we feel helpless and justice is lacking around us
When we have enough ability to solve all problems ourselves
When we only need to rely on our own efforts
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that in desperate situations where justice is absent and no one intercedes, God personally intervenes to bring salvation, encouraging us to trust Him when we feel helpless.

en.reflection: Are there situations around you today that make you feel unjust or hopeless? How will you bring these situations before God?
reflectionOptions: Pray for others for God's justice
en.prayer: God of justice and salvation, I confess that I sometimes feel frustrated and helpless by the injustices in the world. Thank You that even in the darkest moments, You personally intervene to bring salvation. Help me to bring all injustice before You and trust in Your promise that Your Spirit and Your words will not depart from me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Pray for one situation you consider unjust, asking God to intervene and demonstrate His justice.

en.focus: When God's glorious light shines upon His people, darkness dissipates, and nations will gather to Him, bringing abundance and joy.

questions.question: What does the prophet call Jerusalem (Zion) to do at the beginning?
options: Arise and observe God's works
Arise, shine
Arise and fight
Arise and repent
questions.explanation: The passage begins by calling Jerusalem to 'Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you.'

questions.question: How will the nations respond after God's light shines on Zion?
options: They will come to wage war
They will bring their wealth and children
They will become even darker
They will mock Zion
questions.explanation: Nations will come to Zion's light, and kings to the brightness of its rising, bringing their sons, daughters, and wealth.

questions.question: What is the primary reason for the future glory described in this passage?
options: Zion's own wealth and power
Strong support from surrounding nations
The glory and presence of the LORD God
The perfect performance of Zion's people
questions.explanation: The core of the passage is the glory of the LORD 'rising upon you,' indicating that God's own action brings about all this restoration and glory.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us when facing darkness and challenges today?
options: We should overcome all difficulties by our own strength
We should wait for God's glory to be fully revealed before acting
We should trust that God's light can penetrate darkness and shine in Him
We should focus on the world's darkness rather than God's promises
questions.explanation: Even when the world is covered in darkness, God's light has come, and we are called to arise and shine in Him, reflecting His glory.

en.reflection: Is there an area in your life where you feel covered by darkness? How can you trust that God's light can shine even there?
reflectionOptions: Trusting God to reveal His presence in difficult times
Sharing with trusted brothers/sisters and seeking prayer
en.prayer: Glorious God, thank You that You are light, and in You there is no darkness. Let Your light illuminate every dark corner of my life, so that I may arise and shine, becoming a witness to Your glory. May my life reflect Your love and hope. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute in quiet prayer today, asking God's light to shine into an area of your life where you feel darkness or confusion.

en.theme: The Anointed One Brings Good News
en.focus: God anoints His servant to bring good news of salvation and joy to the oppressed and brokenhearted.

questions.question: Whose Spirit does the prophet Isaiah declare is upon him?
options: The Spirit of the LORD God
The spirit of many angels
The Spirit of the LORD of hosts
The spirit of a great king
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states, “The Spirit of the Sovereign LORD is on me.”

questions.type: Observe the mission of the Anointed One
questions.question: To whom is the Anointed One sent to proclaim good news?
options: Kings and rulers of nations
The wealthy and comfortable citizens
The poor, the brokenhearted, and captives
All the inhabitants of Jerusalem
questions.explanation: The Anointed One is sent to proclaim good news to the poor, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim freedom for the captives, and release from darkness for the prisoners.

questions.type: Understand the new identity from God
questions.question: In verse 3, how does God transform the identity and destiny of those who grieve?
options: Crowns of beauty instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair
Gold and silver instead of poverty, high positions instead of low, and long life instead of short
Strong walls instead of ruins, abundant food instead of famine, and a powerful army instead of weakness
Wisdom instead of folly, knowledge instead of ignorance, and honor instead of shame
questions.explanation: God promises to bestow on them a crown of beauty instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair.

questions.question: As God's people today, how can we participate in the mission described in this passage?
options: Focus on accumulating personal wealth to glorify God
Wait for God to do everything Himself, without our action
Bring the good news of the gospel to those in need around us and offer them hope
Only serve within the church, without concern for suffering in society
questions.explanation: This passage prophesies Jesus' mission and also calls us, as His followers, to bring the good news of the gospel and God-given hope to those who are spiritually poor, brokenhearted, and captive.

en.reflection: Are there 'ashes,' 'mourning,' or a 'spirit of despair' in your life that you need God to replace with His crown of beauty, oil of joy, and garment of praise?
reflectionOptions: Heartbroken over the suffering of others
en.prayer: Sovereign LORD, thank You for sending the Anointed One to bring good news of salvation and joy. May Your Spirit fill me, enabling me to personally experience Your healing and comfort. Please also use me to bring this good news to those in need around me, so they too can receive Your hope and garment of praise. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, specifically pray for a friend you know who is going through a difficult time, asking God to replace their ashes, mourning, and despair with His crown of beauty, oil of joy, and garment of praise.

en.focus: God delights in His people, bestowing salvation and righteousness, making them blessed witnesses to the nations.

questions.question: In Isaiah 61:10, what does the prophet Isaiah use to describe his joy?
options: A prodigal son returning home
A bridegroom and a bride adorned for a wedding
A poor person who found treasure
A slave released from bondage
questions.explanation: The prophet describes himself as a bridegroom adorned with a garland and a bride with her jewels, because the LORD has clothed him with garments of salvation.

questions.question: How does the LORD declare He will treat His people so they become a glory in the eyes of the nations?
options: He will give them a powerful army
He will make their wealth surpass other nations
He will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all nations
He will grant them authority to conquer the world
questions.explanation: The LORD promises to make righteousness and praise spring forth before all nations, just as the earth brings forth its sprouts and a garden makes what is sown in it spring up.

questions.type: Understand God's heart for His people
questions.question: Why does God not rest until His righteousness and salvation are displayed?
options: Because He needs His people's help
Because He wants to show off His power to the nations
Because of His deep love and steadfast purpose for His people
Because His people keep complaining to Him
questions.explanation: God will not keep silent or be at rest for Zion's sake and for Jerusalem's sake, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness and her salvation as a burning torch, showing His deep love and unwavering will for His people.

questions.question: When God calls His people 'Hephzibah' (meaning 'My delight is in her') and 'Beulah' (meaning 'Married'), how does this impact our identity?
options: It means we no longer need to strive for good deeds
It reminds us that our worth and identity are given by God, and we are His beloved and cherished possession
It suggests that we are superior to others
It encourages us to only seek our own joy, disregarding others
questions.explanation: These names signify God's personal delight in and precious regard for His people, whose identity and worth are entirely based on His love and choice for them.

en.reflection: How can you more deeply experience and live out the 'garments of salvation' and 'robe of righteousness' God has given you today?
reflectionOptions: Seek to manifest righteousness in daily life
Share the hope God has given you with others
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for clothing me with garments of salvation and arraying me with a robe of righteousness. Please help me to live out the joy and glory You have manifested in my life each day. May my life bring forth Your righteousness and praise, becoming a beautiful testimony of You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take one minute to reflect on God's love and delight in you, and offer Him thanks.

en.focus: Recalling God's abundant love and faithfulness in the past can help us refocus on Him and call out to Him in times of distress.

questions.question: How does the prophet Isaiah begin his prayer and reflection in verse 7?
options: He first confesses sin to God
He first proclaims God's judgment
He first praises God's lovingkindness and deeds
He first expresses disappointment in God
questions.explanation: Isaiah begins by recounting God’s great love and deeds, mentioning all the good things He has done for the house of Israel.

questions.type: Observe God's relationship with His people
questions.question: How did God view His people, Israel, in the past?
options: As rebellious enemies
As His children, and became their Savior
As dispensable servants
As troublesome strangers
questions.explanation: God said, “Surely they are my people, children who will not deal falsely.” So He became their Savior and shared in their distress.

questions.question: What was the consequence of the people's rebellion for God's Spirit?
options: It made God's Spirit joyful
It made God's Spirit stronger
It grieved and vexed God's Holy Spirit
It caused God's Spirit to leave them entirely
questions.explanation: The passage states that their rebellion grieved God's Holy Spirit, causing God to turn against them and fight them.

questions.question: After reviewing God's past actions and the people's rebellion, what is Isaiah's main plea to God?
options: For God to utterly destroy the rebellious people
For God to no longer remember His love and mercy
For God to again show concern for His people, displaying His mercy and power
For God to let the people solve all their problems themselves
questions.explanation: After recalling God's past grace and the people's rebellion, the prophet cries out to God to 'look down from heaven and see, from your holy and glorious habitation,' and asks where His zeal and might are, implying a plea for God to act graciously again.

en.reflection: Today, in your life, what past acts of God's grace and faithfulness do you need to remember to help you face current difficulties or challenges?
reflectionOptions: Recalling God helped me through financial hardship
Recalling God healed me or a family member
Recalling God guided me when I was lost
en.prayer: Faithful Lord, thank You for all the goodness and lovingkindness You have shown me in the past. Forgive me for sometimes forgetting Your deeds, and even for rebelling against You. Father, please look down upon me again, and help me with Your mercy and power, so that I may trust You anew today and live in a way that honors You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to recall three specific good things or acts of help God has done for you in the past, and offer thanks.

en.theme: Oh, That You Would Rend the Heavens!
en.focus: When God's people cry out in distress, they believe He will intervene powerfully again and make His name known.

questions.question: In what emotional state does the prophet cry out to God?
options: Gratitude and praise
Repentance and hope
Anger and complaint
Pride and self-confidence
questions.explanation: The prophet acknowledges the people's sinfulness and cries out to God with hope in His mighty acts.

questions.question: What does the prophet pray for God to do to demonstrate His power?
options: Grant the people more wealth
Allow the people to defeat all their enemies
Rend the heavens and make the nations tremble before Him
Harden the people's hearts further
questions.explanation: The prophet calls on God to appear mightily as in ancient times, causing nations to tremble before Him.

questions.question: What image does the prophet use to illustrate the vast difference between God and His people?
options: Potter and clay
Shepherd and sheep
King and subjects
Father and children
questions.explanation: The prophet uses the imagery of 'we are the clay, and You are our potter' to show God as the Creator and His people as His handiwork.

questions.question: What is the main message of this passage about how we should respond when we face difficulties?
options: Blame others and shirk responsibility
Bear the burden alone and stop seeking help
Humbly confess sin and earnestly cry out to God
Wait for things to improve before seeking God
questions.explanation: In the midst of the people's distress, the prophet confesses their sins and earnestly pleads for God to intervene according to His mercy and power.

en.reflection: Is there a 'mountain' or 'difficulty' in your life right now where you desperately need to cry out for God to 'rend the heavens'?
en.prayer: Almighty Father, You are the Redeemer of Israel and my Potter. I confess my weaknesses and shortcomings. I pray that You, in Your abundant mercy, will show me grace again. Rend the heavens, O Lord, and display Your mighty power in my difficulties, for the glory of Your holy name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take one minute today to silently tell God about a specific difficulty where you most need His intervention and ask for His grace.

en.focus: God extends His call to those who do not seek Him, and justly judges the rebellion of His people, yet promises new blessings for the faithful.

questions.question: To whom does God extend His call in Isaiah 65:1?
options: Those who seek Him
Those who did not seek Him
The priests of Israel
The kings of foreign nations
questions.explanation: God says, “I was sought by those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me. I said, ‘Here I am, here I am,’ to a nation that was not called by my name.” This indicates His call to those who did not actively seek Him.

questions.question: How does God describe the rebellious actions of His people?
options: They built magnificent temples
They offered sacrifices in gardens and burned incense on altars of brick
They faithfully observed the Sabbath
They diligently studied the law
questions.explanation: The passage describes their actions: “who offer sacrifices in gardens and burn incense on altars of brick,” which are acts of idolatry.

questions.question: In His judgment, how does God differentiate between the faithful and the unfaithful?
options: Everyone will receive the same punishment
God only saves the wealthy
The unfaithful will be put to shame, while the faithful will rejoice
Everyone will be forsaken
questions.explanation: God states, “My servants will eat, but you will go hungry; my servants will drink, but you will go thirsty; my servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame.” He will treat them differently, rewarding the faithful and punishing the rebellious.

questions.question: What is the primary truth this passage teaches us about God's relationship with humanity?
options: God only has a relationship with the Israelites
God is a just judge and a loving caller who values human response
Human actions have no impact on God
God always punishes sin immediately
questions.explanation: The passage clearly shows God extending a call to those who do not seek Him (love), while also justly judging acts of rebellion and idolatry (justice). He values human response.

en.reflection: In what areas today do you sense God's call to you, or do you need to examine if any 'idols' are replacing God's rightful place in your heart?
reflectionOptions: Respond to God's call and seek Him more deeply
Examine and remove any 'idols' in my heart
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for proactively calling me even when I don't seek You. Please help me to have a sensitive heart to hear Your voice and to bravely examine if there are any 'idols' in my life replacing You. Forgive my rebellion and lead me to turn solely to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some quiet time today to reflect on anything in your life that might be subtly taking God's rightful place. Ask God to reveal it to you.

en.theme: New Heavens and New Earth: Eternal Joy
en.focus: God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, where His people will enjoy eternal joy and peace.

questions.question: What does God promise to create, emphasizing that past things will no longer be remembered or come to mind?
options: A new temple
A new nation
New heavens and a new earth
A new law
questions.explanation: God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, and His people will no longer remember or consider the former things.

questions.type: Observe characteristics of the new earth
questions.question: In the new heavens and new earth, Jerusalem is called a 'city of rejoicing,' and its people 'a joy.' Which of the following conditions is *not* explicitly mentioned as being absent from the new earth?
options: The sound of weeping
The sound of crying
Infants living only a few days
Sickness and death
questions.explanation: The passage states that in the new heavens and new earth, there will be no more weeping or crying, and no infant will live but a few days; people will live to a great age. While life is extended greatly, even to a hundred years, sickness is not explicitly mentioned as being absent, but rather the extension of life suggests a lack of premature death.

questions.type: Understand the relationship between God and His people
questions.question: What special relationship will exist between God and His people in the new heavens and new earth?
options: God will no longer care about their needs
God will answer before they call and hear before they speak
People must first fulfill all laws before God responds
God only responds to those who cry out loudly to Him
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes the intimate relationship God will have with His people, stating that before they call, He will answer; while they are still speaking, He will hear.

questions.type: Understand the application of the passage
questions.question: What significant meaning does this passage hold for our lives today?
options: We should only focus on earthly pleasures and not anticipate the future
This passage is merely a literary metaphor with no practical significance
It gives us hope that God will ultimately remove all suffering and bring complete joy and peace
We should strive to build a perfect society through our own efforts
questions.explanation: This passage offers immense hope to believers, assuring them that God's promised future is one of joy, peace, and righteousness, where all suffering and imperfections will be removed, encouraging us to live in this hope.

en.reflection: What aspect of the new heavens and new earth described in this passage brings you the most comfort and anticipation today?
reflectionOptions: Intimate relationship with God, who hears and answers prayers
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your promise of new heavens and a new earth, where there will be no sorrow, only eternal joy and peace. Please help me to hold fast to this eternal hope as I face today's challenges. May my heart find comfort and strength in Your promises. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment and spend one minute meditating on the vision of the new heavens and new earth, where there is no more pain, sickness, or sorrow, allowing this hope to fill your heart.

en.theme: New Heavens, New Earth, and God's People
en.focus: God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, and He will dwell eternally with those who are humble, contrite, and tremble at His word.

questions.question: According to Isaiah 66:1-2, what kind of person does God value?
options: Those with wealth and power
Those who build magnificent temples
Those who are humble, contrite in spirit, and tremble at His word
Those with large armies and chariots
questions.explanation: God clearly states that He values those who are humble in spirit, grieved over their sins, and who revere His word.

questions.question: How does God describe those who are hypocritical in their religious rituals?
options: They are faithful servants
They are priests pleasing to God
Their sacrifices are like offering a dog, pig's blood, or worshipping idols
They are devout worshippers
questions.explanation: God sternly condemns those who outwardly follow religious rules but inwardly choose their own ways and delight in their abominations, comparing their actions to detestable things.

questions.question: In Isaiah 66, what does God promise to those who are faithful to Him but are hated for His name's sake?
options: They will suffer greater hardship
They will be forgotten by God
They will see God's glory and rejoice, while their enemies will be put to shame
They will be cast out of God's temple forever
questions.explanation: God promises that those who are hated and cast out by their brethren for His name's sake will see God display His glory, rejoice, and their haters will be put to shame.

questions.question: At the end of Isaiah 66, what future does God proclaim?
options: The world will be utterly destroyed without hope
Israel will be forsaken forever
New heavens and a new earth will be established, where all flesh will worship Him, and the rebellious will suffer eternal punishment
Only a few select people will enter heaven
questions.explanation: God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, and all people will come to worship Him. Concurrently, those who are rebellious and do not know God will suffer eternal punishment, where their fire will not be quenched, nor their worm die.

en.reflection: Today, are you approaching God with a humble, contrite spirit, trembling at His word?
reflectionOptions: Yes, I long to draw closer to God
I need to examine my heart more
en.prayer: Lord, Creator of heaven and earth, You are the Most High God, yet You look upon those who are humble, contrite in spirit, and tremble at Your word. Help me to maintain such a heart, not offering sacrifices or living according to my own will, but in complete obedience to You. May I have a part in Your new heavens and new earth, and worship You forever. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Read Isaiah 66:2 again today and meditate on the attitude of heart that God values.

en.focus: God chooses and equips His servants, promising His presence even in challenging circumstances.

questions.question: How is Jeremiah described at the beginning of the book?
options: A wealthy merchant
One of the priests at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin
A renowned scholar
A military leader
questions.explanation: Jeremiah is identified as one of the priests in Anathoth, Benjamin, and his call took place during the reign of King Josiah.

questions.question: When Jeremiah expressed that he was too young and could not speak, how did God respond?
options: God told him to find a more experienced replacement
God commanded him to study more
God promised to be with him and put His words in his mouth
God told him to rely on his own strength to persuade others
questions.explanation: God promised Jeremiah not to be afraid, for He would be with him to rescue him. God also touched Jeremiah's mouth, putting His words in it.

questions.question: What two visions did God show Jeremiah?
options: A burning bush and a split rock
An almond branch and a boiling pot
A golden lampstand and seven stars
A great fish and a grapevine
questions.explanation: God showed Jeremiah a branch of an almond tree and a boiling pot, tilting from the North.

questions.question: According to this passage, what did God's call to Jeremiah entail?
options: He would enjoy fame and an easy life
He would have to bear all responsibilities alone
He was appointed over nations and kingdoms to uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, and plant
His primary task was to persuade kings to change national policies
questions.explanation: God appointed Jeremiah over nations and kingdoms, empowering him to carry out God's mission, which included uprooting, tearing down, destroying, overthrowing, as well as building and planting.

en.reflection: Have you ever felt 'too young' or 'unable to speak' to respond to God's call? How does this passage encourage you today?
reflectionOptions: Trust that God will be with me
Trust that God will give me the words to speak
Let go of my inadequacies and focus on God's promises
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your call on Jeremiah's life, and for Your plans for my life too. When I feel inadequate or afraid, please remind me of Your presence and power. Help me to respond courageously to Your call, whether big or small, and to fulfill it faithfully. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to reflect: Has God ever called you to do something you felt unqualified or unable to do? Recommit that task to God, trusting in His promises.

en.focus: God reminds His people of their initial love and faithfulness, and reveals how they have forsaken the source of life.

questions.question: How does God describe the relationship with Israel at the beginning of Jeremiah chapter 2?
options: His enemy
His bride and young wife
His servant
His judge
questions.explanation: Through Jeremiah, God declares that He remembers Israel's faithfulness to Him in her youth, like a bride's love for her groom.

questions.question: What did the people of Israel pursue after forsaking God?
options: Seeking wisdom
Pursuing power
Worthless idols
Building strong cities
questions.explanation: The passage states that Israel went after 'worthless idols,' which could not benefit them.

questions.question: How does God describe Israel's act of forsaking Him?
options: They became stronger
They dug broken cisterns that cannot hold water
They found new sources of water
They became wiser
questions.explanation: God says His people committed two evils: they forsook Him, the spring of living water, and dug their own broken cisterns that could hold no water.

questions.question: What feelings might we experience when we stray from God, as today's passage reminds us?
options: A sense of satisfaction and joy
An inner emptiness and restlessness
Increased strength and courage
A feeling of closeness to God
questions.explanation: When one forsakes the spring of living water for broken cisterns that can hold no water, feelings of emptiness, thirst, and restlessness are natural.

en.reflection: Are there areas in your life that feel like 'broken cisterns,' consuming your time and energy but failing to truly satisfy your thirst?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me that You are the spring of living water. Please forgive me for straying from You at times, chasing after things that cannot truly satisfy. Help me to return to Your love and find my joy in You alone. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a few moments to quietly reflect on how God has satisfied you in your life and offer Him thanks for His faithfulness.

en.theme: Forsaking the Fountain of Living Water
en.focus: God reminds His people that they have abandoned the source of life and pursued empty idols, and they will face the consequences.

questions.question: In verse 20, how does the LORD describe Israel's past faithfulness to Him?
options: You came from afar to worship Me
You played the harlot on every high hill and under every green tree
You loved Me wholeheartedly and never turned away
You constantly purified yourself and avoided idols
questions.explanation: The text describes Israel's actions on every high hill and under every green tree as playing the harlot, symbolizing their forsaking of the LORD for idol worship.

questions.question: What analogy is used to describe Israel's stubbornness in sin?
options: A lost sheep
A hunted deer
