A wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness
A bird caught in a net
questions.explanation: The text uses the image of a 'wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness' to illustrate Israel's persistent devotion to idols, making it difficult to change their ways.

questions.question: Why would Israel's turning to idol worship lead to shame and disappointment?
options: Because idols cannot bring true wealth
Because idols cannot provide real help and salvation
Because idol worship would cause them to lose allies
Because idols required costly sacrifices
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that the idols Israel trusted would not save them in times of trouble, but would bring shame.

questions.question: What is the most important reminder from today's passage when we encounter difficulties?
options: To diligently seek new solutions
To call upon and seek the God who can truly save us
To seek comfort and help from friends
To reflect on our past successful experiences
questions.explanation: Jeremiah emphasizes that turning to idols for help in trouble was futile for Israel; only turning to God could bring salvation. This reminds us that in any difficulty, only God is the ultimate helper.

en.reflection: Have you ever, like Israel, departed from the fountain of living water in some area, pursuing things that cannot truly satisfy you?
reflectionOptions: Relying on my own strength instead of God under pressure
Seeking human approval instead of God's favour
en.prayer: Lord, forgive me, for at times I, too, like Israel, forsake You, the fountain of living water, and pursue empty things that cannot truly satisfy me. Help me to turn back to You and depend solely on You, for You alone are my satisfaction and salvation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to list any things you might be relying on besides God, and pray to Him to help you refocus on Him.

en.focus: Even when we turn away from God, He continually calls us to return, for His love and mercy endure forever.

questions.question: In Jeremiah 3:1, what metaphor does God use to describe Israel's unfaithfulness?
options: A prodigal son
A lost sheep
A promiscuous wife
A withered vine
questions.explanation: God compares Israel's unfaithfulness to a wife who has played the harlot with many lovers, yet He still calls her to return.

questions.question: God repeatedly calls Israel to return. What promise does He give to those who return?
options: Increased wealth and power
Peace and security
Healing for their waywardness and making them His people
Destruction of all their enemies
questions.explanation: God promises to heal Israel's waywardness, restore them as His people, and provide them with shepherds after His own heart.

questions.question: Why does God continue to call Israel to return, even after repeated unfaithfulness?
options: Because God needs their strength
Because of God's enduring love and mercy
Because God fears losing them
Because God wants them to punish themselves
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD is 'merciful' and 'will not remain angry forever,' indicating His call stems from unchanging love and compassion.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us today when we feel spiritually weak or have strayed?
options: We can return to God by our own efforts alone
God's grace is only for those who have never erred
No matter how far we have strayed, God waits to heal and restore us
Once we stray, there is no chance to return to God
questions.explanation: God's call to unfaithful Israel demonstrates that His mercy and healing are available to all who are willing to return, no matter how far they have strayed.

en.reflection: Is there any area in your life where you feel you have strayed from God, and He is gently calling you to return?
en.prayer: Loving Father, thank You for Your unchanging love that calls me back even when I stray. Please heal my waywardness, help me to know You more deeply, and turn my whole heart back to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to confess any areas where you may have strayed and respond to God's call to return.

en.theme: Return to God, and He Will Restore You
en.focus: God calls His people to return from their rebellion, promising genuine restoration and cleansing when they sincerely turn back to Him.

questions.question: How does God describe the house of Israel in Jeremiah 3:19-20?
options: His beloved children
Rebellious children
Faithful servants
Wise people
questions.explanation: God describes the house of Israel as “rebellious children” because they had turned away from Him.

questions.question: What does God promise to those rebellious children who return?
options: To give them more land
To heal their faithlessness
To make them the head of nations
To destroy all their enemies
questions.explanation: God promises, “Return, you faithless people; I will heal your faithlessness.”

questions.question: What does Jeremiah 4:3-4 emphasize as crucial for God's people?
options: Building tall city walls
Observing sacrificial laws
Breaking up their unplowed ground and removing the foreskin of their hearts
Expanding their commercial trade
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes “break up your unplowed ground; do not sow among thorns” and “remove the foreskin of your hearts,” pointing to inner cleansing and repentance.

questions.question: According to today's scripture, what is the primary sign of truly returning to God?
options: Verbally confessing wrongdoings without changing behavior
Acknowledging one's sin and seeking God's healing
Only calling out to God for help in times of trouble
Believing that offering more sacrifices will gain God's favor
questions.explanation: The rebellious children confess, “We have sinned against the LORD our God,” and cry out, “Heal our faithlessness,” indicating that true return involves acknowledging sin and seeking God's healing.

en.reflection: In your life, what 'unplowed ground' needs to be broken up by God, or what 'foreskin of your heart' needs to be removed, so you can turn more fully to Him?
reflectionOptions: Letting go of an idol or bad habit
Forgiving someone who has hurt me
Taking Scripture and prayer more seriously
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for calling me, a rebellious child, to return to You. I confess that I often stray from Your path, and my heart has impurities. Please heal my faithlessness, help me break up the unplowed ground of my heart, and remove everything that is not pleasing to You. May I turn to You with all my heart and experience Your cleansing and restoration. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to quietly reflect and write down or pray about one 'impurity of heart' you are willing for God to remove, or one area of 'unplowed ground' that needs tending.

en.theme: A Call to Repentance Amidst Judgment
en.focus: As the Lord’s judgment approaches, He calls His people to repent to avoid deeper suffering.

questions.question: What does Jeremiah call the people to do in Judah and Jerusalem in verse 5?
options: Hold a grand feast
Blow the trumpet, set up a signal, and cry out
Build stronger city walls
Seek help from other nations
questions.explanation: The prophet calls the people to blow the trumpet, set up a signal, and cry out in Judah and Jerusalem, warning of impending judgment.

questions.question: From which direction does the passage indicate the Lord will bring disaster?
options: The south
The north
The east
The west
questions.explanation: The Lord declares that disaster and great destruction will come from the north.

questions.question: Why is the Lord’s heart grieved by the condition of His people?
options: Because of their loss of wealth
Because of their rebellion and unrepentance
Because they could not form alliances with other nations
Because they failed to build magnificent temples
questions.explanation: The Lord is grieved by the rebellion and unrepentance of the people of Israel, as their sins will lead to tragic consequences.

questions.question: What is the most important reminder from this passage?
options: God is only a God of punishment
Good deeds alone can prevent all disasters
God desires His people to turn back to Him to avoid judgment due to sin
National strength can resist all external threats
questions.explanation: Despite the severe message of judgment, God's heart is still grieved, showing His desire for His people to turn back and avoid the inevitable consequences of their sin.

en.reflection: In what areas do you feel the Spirit's gentle prompting to turn back to God today?
reflectionOptions: Spending too much time on unimportant things
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me through Jeremiah that You are a just and loving God. Please help me to always be alert, to turn away from sin, and to respond to the Spirit's prompting to return to You promptly. May my heart always be aligned with Yours. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, when you feel restless or distracted, take a minute to be still and invite the Holy Spirit to guide your heart back to God.

en.focus: When sin brings devastation, God’s heart intertwines with His people’s pain, calling them to repentance.

questions.question: How does the prophet Jeremiah express his feelings at the beginning of the passage?
options: Joy and hope
Grief and anguish
Anger and frustration
Calm and submission
questions.explanation: Prophet Jeremiah expresses extreme anguish over the destruction of his people, crying out, 'My anguish, my anguish!'

questions.type: Observe God's description of His people
questions.question: How does God describe His people?
options: Intelligent and wise
God-fearing people
Foolish and senseless
Strong and powerful
questions.explanation: God states that His people are 'foolish and senseless,' wise in doing evil but not knowing Him.

questions.question: What kind of destructive scene is described in the passage?
options: Fertile land and peaceful inhabitants
Desolate land, ruined cities, no inhabitants
A strong nation, with other nations paying tribute
Blessed people, with enemies retreating
questions.explanation: The prophet foretells a desolate land, ruined cities, and no inhabitants, signifying the thoroughness of God's judgment.

questions.question: What is the main message about God's heart we can understand from this passage?
options: God is indifferent to His people's sins
God delights in the suffering of His people
God is deeply grieved by His people's sins, but righteous judgment will still come
God always immediately forgives all sins without repentance
questions.explanation: The passage reveals God's heartbreak over His people's wickedness and the impending judgment, yet His justice demands that judgment be carried out.

en.reflection: After reading today’s scripture, do you sense God’s sorrow over the sins of humanity? How does this remind you to live your life today?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, my heart is moved by Your sorrow over the sins of the world. Help me to understand more deeply the seriousness of sin and grant me strength to turn away from anything that displeases You. May my life bring glory to Your name and be a testimony to Your love and truth. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to pray for those who are living in sin and do not know God.

en.theme: The Gravity of Sin and God's Patience
en.focus: Despite the deep-seated sin of His people, the LORD remains patient, calling them to return, revealing His attributes of both justice and mercy.

questions.question: What kind of people was the prophet Jeremiah searching for in Jerusalem?
options: People living piously
People who act justly and seek truth
People who are wealthy and powerful
People who can prophesy
questions.explanation: Jeremiah was searching the streets of Jerusalem for someone who 'acts justly and seeks truth.' God said He would pardon the city if such a person could be found.

questions.question: How did the passage describe the people's response to God's discipline?
options: They humbly repented
They grew more stubborn and refused to return
They sought help from other nations
They offered more sacrifices
questions.explanation: The text states that despite God's discipline, they 'refused to return' and hardened their hearts, making their faces 'harder than rock.'

questions.question: Why did God say He would attack and destroy idol-worshipping nations, but not Israel?
options: Because Israel is His chosen people, they would not be punished
God said He would attack Israel, but not completely destroy them
God demanded compensation from Israel for His losses
God commanded Israel to attack other nations
questions.explanation: God explicitly stated that He would attack Israel, but would not 'make a complete end' of them, demonstrating His faithfulness to preserve a remnant.

questions.question: What attributes of God toward His people are emphasized in Jeremiah 5:1-19?
options: God is a completely indifferent spectator
God is a judge who only values the law
God is just in judgment, yet full of mercy and patience
God is only concerned with bringing disaster
questions.explanation: God sees the people's sin and executes righteous judgment, but at the same time shows His patience and mercy by not utterly destroying them.

en.reflection: How does today's scripture remind you of God's justice and patience, and areas in your life where you need to return to Him?
reflectionOptions: Repent of sins I have committed
Trust in God's mercy and grace
en.prayer: Righteous and merciful God, I confess that I am often unfaithful and disobedient before You. Thank You for being slow to anger and for giving me opportunities to return. Please help me see the areas in my life that need Your light and change, and grant me a submissive heart. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Reflect on any areas where you have been disobedient or strayed from God recently. Take a moment to confess them to Him and ask for His help to return.

en.theme: The Bitter Consequences of Forsaking God
en.focus: When we turn away from God and pursue our own ways, it inevitably leads to pain and destruction.

questions.question: What challenge does God issue to the people of Israel at the start of this passage?
options: He will send enemies to attack them
He wants them to recall the sins of their ancestors
He wants them to consider His love and faithfulness
He wants them to heed His warning and recognize their rebellion
questions.explanation: God calls on the house of Jacob and the house of Israel to hear His words, pointing out their stubborn and rebellious hearts.

questions.type: Observe God's description of His people
questions.question: How does God describe His people, highlighting their problem?
options: They are wise and discerning
They are God-fearing and obedient
They have stubborn and rebellious hearts, lacking true reverence
They are righteous people seeking God's face
questions.explanation: The text states they have stubborn and rebellious hearts, have turned away from God, and do not fear Him.

questions.question: According to this passage, why do the people experience disaster and judgment?
options: Because they are unable to resist foreign armies
Because they have not offered enough sacrifices
Because of their wickedness and injustice, especially oppressing the poor
Because God is tired of their prayers
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that their iniquities have withheld good from them, and they commit evil, failing to plead the cause of the poor or judge the case of the fatherless.

questions.question: What main truth about sin does this passage remind us of?
options: Sin is unavoidable, so there's no need to worry much
Sin does not bring any real consequences
Sin corrupts social justice, leads to spiritual blindness, and ultimately brings God's judgment
Doing some good deeds can offset the effects of sin
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly emphasizes the people's wickedness (stubbornness, rebellion, oppression, injustice), which led to their not knowing God and brought about His judgment.

en.reflection: Have you ever, like the people in Jeremiah's time, been deaf to God's warnings or strayed from His will in some area?
en.prayer: Loving Father, thank You for reminding me through Jeremiah's warning that my iniquities can separate me from You. Please forgive me for times when my heart is hard or when I stray from Your path. Help me to constantly examine my heart, to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, do a small act of kindness for someone around you who needs justice or help, as a response to God's teaching.

en.focus: The prophet Jeremiah issues a severe warning to Judah, highlighting their sins that will lead to devastating consequences, yet the people refuse to repent.

questions.question: From where does Jeremiah call the people to flee in verse 1?
options: Jericho
Jerusalem
Tekoa
The land of Benjamin
questions.explanation: The prophet calls for the people of Benjamin to flee from Jerusalem and sound the alarm, as disaster approaches from the north.

questions.question: What was the people's response when Jeremiah urged them to listen to the word of the LORD?
options: They immediately repented
They said, "We will not listen!"
They asked for more evidence
They sought other prophets
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that the people said, "We will not listen!", indicating their deafness to God's commands.

questions.question: What prevalent sin does the prophet identify across all levels of society, from common people to religious leaders?
options: Laziness and poverty
Lying and deceit
Greed and dishonesty
Pride and selfishness
questions.explanation: The passage describes how everyone, from the least to the greatest, is greedy for gain, and from prophet to priest, all practice deceit.

questions.question: How did the prophets and priests "heal the wound" of the people lightly?
options: They offered genuine healing and a path to repentance
They said, "Peace, peace," when there was no peace
They encouraged the people to seek help from other nations
They taught the people to atone with sacrifices
questions.explanation: The prophets and priests offered false comfort, proclaiming peace when no true peace existed.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that God is righteous and will judge sin. Is there any sin in your life that you have been 'not listening' to God's warnings about, or 'healing lightly'?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of a hidden sin
Stop deceiving yourself and face the truth
en.prayer: Righteous God, thank You for reminding me through Jeremiah of the seriousness of sin. Please illuminate my heart to see any areas in my life where I have chosen 'not to listen' to Your warnings, or tried to 'heal lightly' my sins. Help me to truly repent and turn back to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend five minutes in quiet reflection today, asking the Holy Spirit to reveal any sins in your life that need repentance, and confess them to God.

en.theme: Stand in the Ancient Paths, Find Rest
en.focus: God calls His people to return to His original ways to find true rest, but they refuse to listen.

questions.question: Where does the LORD call His people to stand, and what does He ask them to inquire about?
options: On the city walls, inquiring about its defenses
On the mountains, asking which path leads to wealth
On the roads, asking for the ancient paths
In the fields, asking which plot is more fertile
questions.explanation: God calls His people to stand on the roads, look and ask for the ancient paths, and find rest.

questions.question: What was the people's response to the LORD's call and command?
options: “We will surely obey”
“We will not walk in it”
“We will consider it”
“We need more time”
questions.explanation: When the LORD called them to stand in the ancient paths and find rest, they replied, 'We will not walk in it.'

questions.question: What does this passage reveal about God's heart for His people?
options: God only desires to punish His people
God wants His people to return to His righteous ways to find true peace and rest
God is completely despairing of His people's rebellion
God believes their religious rituals are more important than their actions
questions.explanation: God desires His people to return to His original ways, the ancient paths, to find true peace and rest, but they refuse.

questions.question: Based on this passage, where should we primarily seek true rest and guidance today?
options: Secular philosophies and novel theories
Societal trends and popular culture
God's ancient truths, His Word, and the paths He has shown
Personal desires and fleeting pleasures
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes standing in the 'ancient paths' and seeking the 'good way,' indicating that true rest and guidance are found in God's unchanging truths and the paths He has revealed.

en.reflection: In which area of your life do you most need to return to God's 'ancient paths' and seek His guidance and rest again?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for calling me to Your ancient paths to find true rest. Please illuminate my heart and show me where I have strayed from Your ways. Help me to turn back, obey Your Word, and find peace in You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a moment to reread Jeremiah 6:16, quietly reflect on what Jesus meant by 'I am the way, the truth, and the life,' and pray to Him for guidance.

en.focus: God calls His people to abandon false worship and sinful living, turning to genuine repentance to receive His favor and presence.

questions.question: Where was Jeremiah instructed to deliver God's message?
options: At the gate of the king's palace
At the gate of the LORD's house
On the highest wall of the city
In the assembly of elders
questions.explanation: The LORD commanded Jeremiah to stand in the gate of the LORD’s house and proclaim His message there to the people of Judah.

questions.question: What would happen if the people did not amend their ways, according to God's warning through Jeremiah?
options: They would become wealthier
They would not be able to live in the land given to them
They would receive more sacrifices
Their enemies would make peace with them
questions.explanation: The LORD states that if they do not amend their ways, He will cast them out of this land, just as He cast out all the people of Ephraim.

questions.question: What does this passage reveal about what God values most from His people?
options: The scale of their sacrifices
Their verbal confessions
Their external religious rituals
Their genuine repentance in heart and actions
questions.explanation: God emphasizes 'amend your ways and your deeds,' turning away from sins like stealing, murdering, committing adultery, swearing falsely, and burning incense to Baal, rather than simply relying on the presence of the temple for security.

questions.question: What reminder does the message of Jeremiah 7 offer us in our lives today?
options: As long as we attend church, our lifestyle doesn't need to change
God will bless us as long as we maintain external rituals
God values our genuine righteousness and holiness in life more
We can continue in sin while enjoying God's presence
questions.explanation: Through Jeremiah, God emphasizes that His people cannot rely solely on the temple or religious rituals but must live out righteousness, holiness, and true repentance in their daily lives. This reminds us that God values our inner condition and actual conduct, not merely outward religious performance.

en.reflection: Today, in your faith journey, is there any 'false sense of security' that might be causing you to neglect the need for genuine repentance?
reflectionOptions: Assuming regular church attendance is enough
Making external offerings without internal change
Becoming accustomed to certain sins without concern
en.prayer: Loving Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me through Jeremiah that You value a truly repentant heart and a life of righteousness and holiness. Please shine Your light upon me, Lord, and reveal any false sense of security or hidden sins in my life. Help me to genuinely turn to You and live a life worthy of repentance. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take five minutes today to quietly reflect on whether there is any area where you genuinely need to repent to God, and then pour out your heart to Him.

en.focus: God desires genuine obedience and integrity from His people, not empty religious rituals.

questions.question: What did the LORD say to the people of Israel at the beginning of this passage?
options: He wanted them to offer more burnt offerings
He had no delight in their burnt offerings and sacrifices
He wanted them to build altars for themselves
He wanted them to stop all sacrifices
questions.explanation: The LORD clearly stated that He did not delight in their burnt offerings and sacrifices, as these were not His original command.

questions.question: What was the main command God gave when He brought the Israelites out of Egypt?
options: To build a magnificent temple
To obey His voice and be His people
To offer various sacrifices
To observe all the feasts
questions.explanation: God’s original command was for the Israelites to obey His voice and to be His people in covenant with Him.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the people's attitude towards God's voice?
options: They listened attentively and obeyed
They eagerly followed God's commands
They did not listen but followed their own stubborn evil hearts
They only obeyed some of the commands
questions.explanation: The people did not listen to God's words; instead, they stiffened their necks and followed their own stubborn, evil hearts.

questions.question: Based on this passage, how does God feel about the people's continuous rebellion and disobedience?
options: Relieved, because they at least offered sacrifices
Helpless, because they were unable to change
Grieved and disappointed, even mentioning their end
Angry, but He would immediately forgive them
questions.explanation: God is deeply grieved by the people's stubbornness and disobedience, even referring to their rejection and tragic death.

en.reflection: Is there an area in your life where you might be 'sacrificing,' but God truly desires your 'obedience'?
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for reminding me through the prophet Jeremiah that You value my obedience and integrity more than empty rituals. Please illuminate my heart to see if there are any areas in my life where I focus on outward forms but neglect genuine obedience to You. Help me to resolve today to listen attentively to Your Word and to do what pleases You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some quiet time today to ask God: What aspect of my life needs more obedience to Your Word, rather than just going through the motions?

en.focus: God grieves deeply over His people's stubborn rebellion, calling them to return, but they refuse to listen.

questions.question: How does the prophet Jeremiah describe the people's attitude toward sin?
options: They quickly repented
They were brave like warriors
They were like a horse charging into battle, not turning back
They sought God's wisdom
questions.explanation: The text states that the people were like a horse charging into battle, refusing to turn back and going their own way.

questions.question: Which birds does Jeremiah mention as knowing their appointed times, contrasting them with the people of Israel?
options: Sparrows
Swallows
Storks and turtledoves
Eagles
questions.explanation: Jeremiah points out that the stork, turtledove, swift, and crane know their appointed times, but God's people do not know the ordinances of the Lord.

questions.question: The people claimed, 'We have the law of the Lord,' but what did Jeremiah reveal about their true condition?
options: They diligently observed the law
They made the law a lie through the false pen of the scribes
They were wiser than other nations
They did not need the law to know God
questions.explanation: Jeremiah reveals that despite their claim to have God's law, the scribes' false pen had made it a lie, and they were not truly obeying it.

questions.question: What was Jeremiah's emotional state in response to the people's rebellion and impending judgment?
options: Joyful and celebratory
Full of hope
Filled with pride
Heartbroken and shedding endless tears
questions.explanation: Jeremiah's heart was broken over the wound of his people and the coming judgment, wishing his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain of tears to weep day and night for them.

en.reflection: Today's passage highlights the danger of rebellion and God's heart. Have you ever, out of stubbornness or disobedience, caused harm to yourself or others, or drifted away from God?
reflectionOptions: Seek reconciliation with someone I've harmed
Return to God's Word for guidance
en.prayer: Gracious Heavenly Father, forgive me for times when I, like the people in the passage, have been stubborn and disobedient to Your known will. Grant me a soft and obedient heart, that I may be sensitive to Your teachings and not stray from Your path. May my life bring glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Quietly reflect on an experience where you were stubborn and confess it to God. Apologize to anyone involved if necessary.

en.theme: The Gravity of Sin and God's Healing
en.focus: We must recognize the deep seriousness of sin and seek God’s healing, rather than relying on false peace.

questions.question: How does the prophet Jeremiah describe the condition of the people he observes?
options: They are all seeking truth
They all love one another
They are all deceptive and do not know God
They are all committed to doing good
questions.explanation: Jeremiah describes the people as forsaking the Lord, acting deceitfully, lying to one another, and not knowing God.

questions.question: Because of the people's sin, what will God do to them?
options: Grant them more wealth and land
Make them stronger and more influential
Make them like a wilderness, consumed by fire
Establish a new peace covenant with them
questions.explanation: God states He will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins and the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant, like a wilderness consumed by fire.

questions.question: What does Jeremiah 9:23–24 emphasize as truly worth boasting about?
options: Human wisdom, might, or riches
Interpersonal relationships and social skills
Knowing the Lord, who exercises steadfast love, justice, and righteousness
Observing all laws and regulations
questions.explanation: The passage states that one should not boast in wisdom, might, or riches, but only in knowing the Lord, who exercises steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.

questions.question: What does this passage remind us today about acknowledging our sin and seeking God?
options: We can disregard the consequences of sin because God always forgives
Outward religious observance is sufficient
We must take our sin seriously and turn to know God, seeking His healing
God's judgment is only for ancient Israel and irrelevant to us
questions.explanation: The passage reminds us of the seriousness of sin and the importance of seeking to know the God who exercises steadfast love, justice, and and righteousness, as only He can bring true healing and salvation.

en.reflection: Today, do you sense any 'wounds' in your life that need God's healing, but you've been trying to cover them up or fix them in other ways?
en.prayer: Healing Lord, I confess that my heart sometimes strays from You, trying to solve problems my own way instead of fully trusting You. Please forgive my sins and heal the wounds in my life. Help me to know Your steadfast love, justice, and righteousness more deeply. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some quiet time today to pray and confess to God an area in your life that needs His healing, asking Him to intervene.

en.focus: The LORD is the one true God, the Creator and Ruler; idols are powerless, man-made nothingness.

questions.question: How does Jeremiah 10 begin with a warning to the people of Israel?
options: Do not fear the statutes of the nations
Do not learn the ways of the nations
You must leave Jerusalem
Prepare for war
questions.explanation: The text clearly states: "Thus says the LORD: 'Do not learn the way of the nations.'"

questions.question: How does the passage describe the making of idols and their inherent nature?
options: They are sacred artworks with healing powers
They are carved by craftsmen from wood, silver, and gold; they cannot speak or walk and must be carried
They are natural wonders with prophetic abilities
They are celestial bodies that guide human destiny
questions.explanation: Idols are made by craftsmen who cut wood from the forest, decorate it with silver and gold, and fasten it with nails and hammers. They cannot speak or walk and must be carried.

questions.question: Compared to idols, where does the unique nature and power of the true God, the LORD, lie?
options: He is more beautiful and beloved than idols
He is the living God, the Creator, who controls the universe, makes the earth tremble, and sends rain and lightning
He can hear prayers but cannot act
He cares only for Israel, not for other nations
questions.explanation: The LORD is the living God, the eternal King. At His wrath the earth trembles. He made the earth by His power, He established the world by His wisdom, and by His understanding He stretched out the heavens. When He utters His voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and He makes the clouds ascend from the ends of the earth.

questions.question: What is the main reminder this passage gives us for our lives today?
options: We should avoid any form of artwork
We should rely completely on our own wisdom and strength to live
We should fear and worship only the true God who created heaven and earth and controls all things, not treating any created thing as an idol
We should learn more about the beliefs and practices of other religions
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that the LORD is the one true God, whose power and works far surpass all empty idols. This reminds us to give our worship and trust solely to Him, and to avoid elevating any created thing (including wealth, fame, power, or anything else) to God's position.

en.reflection: Today, is there anything in your life that has unknowingly taken God’s place in your heart, becoming an ‘idol’ that you rely on or pursue?
reflectionOptions: The opinions or approval of others
en.prayer: Almighty Creator, thank You for being the living God, the one and only Ruler. Please enlighten me and help me examine my heart, removing anything that might be taking Your place. May my heart fear You alone and trust in You alone, giving all glory to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to quietly reflect: what in your life do you often rely on or pursue excessively? Ask God to help you put it back in its proper place and to exalt Him alone.

en.focus: The Lord reminds His people of the covenant with their ancestors and points out the consequences they face due to disobedience.

questions.question: What did the Lord say to Jeremiah in verse 1?
options: To mourn for the sins of the people
To go preach in Egypt
To hear the words of this covenant
To prophesy in Babylon
questions.explanation: The Lord instructed Jeremiah to hear the words of this covenant and proclaim them to the people of Judah and Jerusalem.

questions.type: Understand the nature of the covenant
questions.question: What is the essence of this covenant as mentioned by the Lord in verses 3-5?
options: Blessings are only through sacrifices
Salvation is only by keeping the law
It is a covenant requiring obedience to dwell in the promised land
It is a covenant of unconditional love and grace
questions.explanation: This covenant required the Israelites to obey God's voice and do all He commanded, so they could dwell in the land flowing with milk and honey and be His people.

questions.question: According to verses 7-8, how did the people respond to the Lord's commands?
options: They eagerly obeyed
They only obeyed in some aspects
They heard but did not obey
They refused to listen and followed their own stubborn hearts
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that the people and their ancestors 'did not obey or incline their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart.'

questions.question: What warning did the Lord give to those who broke the covenant?
options: They would become wealthier
They would face all the curses He had commanded
They would be respected by foreign nations
They would receive extra grace
questions.explanation: The Lord warned that because of their disobedience, He would bring upon them all the curses written in the covenant.

en.reflection: Looking back at your life, in what areas do you need to listen more intently to God's Word and obey His will more faithfully?
reflectionOptions: Be more faithful in money management
Be more consistent in daily devotion
en.prayer: Dear Lord, thank You for Your covenant with us, giving us Your teachings and promises. Forgive me for times when I hear but do not obey, or when my heart is rebellious. Help me today to listen more carefully to Your Word and to obey Your will with faith. May my life glorify You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take some time to reread a familiar scripture (e.g., the Lord's Prayer or the Ten Commandments) and reflect on how you can apply it more concretely in your life.

en.focus: Even in confusion and suffering, we can trust in God's justice and His ultimate work.

questions.question: What question does the prophet Jeremiah pose to God in verse 1?
options: Why are Israel's enemies so strong?
Why does the way of the wicked prosper, and all who are treacherous thrive?
Why is my message not being heard?
Why do You allow false prophets to rise?
questions.explanation: Jeremiah opens by questioning God about the prosperity of the wicked and the thriving of the treacherous.

questions.question: How does God respond to Jeremiah in verse 5, indicating the increasing challenge he faces?
options: He will immediately punish the wicked
He will grant Jeremiah more power
If you have raced with men on foot and they have wearied you, how can you compete with horses?
He will change people's hearts to listen to Jeremiah
questions.explanation: God reminds Jeremiah that the challenges he faces will become greater, like competing with horses.

questions.question: What is the main message this passage helps us understand?
options: God is full of wrath towards His people and will no longer show them favor
A just God will ultimately judge the wicked and discipline His people
People who do good will never suffer
The prophet's job is to constantly complain about God's plans
questions.explanation: The passage shows that while God allows the wicked to prosper for a time, He will ultimately bring justice and discipline His people, with a promise of future restoration.

questions.question: How does this passage help us when we see injustice in our lives?
options: It encourages us to take immediate retaliatory action
It makes us feel hopeless because God seems indifferent
It reminds us that God's eyes see everything, and His justice will ultimately prevail
It teaches us to focus only on our own well-being and not care about others' suffering
questions.explanation: Despite Jeremiah's confusion, God's response indicates He knows all things and will bring justice in His time and way, giving us hope.

en.reflection: In your life, are there situations of 'injustice' or 'wicked prosperity' that confuse you? How do you bring these before God?
reflectionOptions: Pour out my confusion and frustration to God
en.prayer: Righteous Father, when my heart is confused by injustice, help me to trust in Your wisdom and perfect justice. I know Your eyes see all, and You will execute judgment and salvation in Your time and way. Grant me patience and hope to continue following You faithfully. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to surrender any confusion or perceived injustice in your heart to God, trusting that He is in control.

en.focus: Through Jeremiah, God warns His people that their pride and wickedness have made them like a defiled waistband and shattered jars, leading inevitably to judgment.

questions.question: What object did God command Jeremiah to use to symbolize the people of Israel and Judah?
options: A clay pot
A linen belt
A mud bowl
A pair of leather shoes
questions.explanation: God commanded Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and wear it around his waist as a symbol.

questions.question: Why did God command Jeremiah to hide the belt in a rock crevice and later retrieve it?
options: To allow the belt to absorb moisture
To make the belt ruined and useless
To make the belt emit a fragrance
To turn the belt into a souvenir
questions.explanation: The progression from the belt being close to the prophet's waist to being hidden and decaying symbolizes how Israel's pride would be ruined by God, rendering them useless.

questions.question: Besides the belt, what other object does God use to illustrate how He will fill the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem with drunkenness?
options: Empty granaries
Shattered wine jars
Dried-up springs
Collapsed houses
questions.explanation: God says: 'I will fill all who live in this land—the kings who sit on David’s throne, the priests, the prophets and all those living in Jerusalem—with drunkenness, like wine jars.'

questions.question: What is the primary message this passage teaches us?
options: God is always lenient with His people, and there will be no judgment
Human pride and wickedness lead to defilement and destruction
Offering enough sacrifices can offset all sins
Changing circumstances are more important than changing hearts
questions.explanation: The passage clearly indicates that the stubbornness, pride, and wickedness of the people of Israel, leading them to abandon God, ultimately resulted in God's righteous judgment.

en.reflection: Are there areas of 'defilement' or 'pride' in your life that you need to acknowledge and repent of before God?
en.prayer: Righteous God, I thank You for reminding me through Jeremiah of the seriousness of sin and Your commitment to holiness. Please shine Your light on me, help me see all defilement and pride in my life, and grant me a repentant heart. Help me break free from the bondage of sin and draw closer to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Quietly reflect on what God has revealed to you through today's scripture, and confess one thing you feel proud of or sinful about to God.

en.theme: Cry in Drought and God's Response
en.focus: In times of disaster, God's people cry out to Him, but God declares judgment for their sins while still holding promises of mercy.

questions.question: What kind of disaster is described at the beginning of Jeremiah 14?
options: An earthquake
Famine and drought
A plague
An invading army
questions.explanation: The passage vividly describes the land parched, animals suffering, and city gates mourning due to drought.

questions.question: What does Jeremiah confess to God in his prayer?
options: The people's wisdom and ability
The people's faithfulness to God
The people's iniquities and backsliding
The people's resistance to paganism
questions.explanation: Jeremiah confesses the people's numerous iniquities, appealing to God for forgiveness and mercy.

questions.question: How does God respond to the prayers of the people and the prophet?
options: He immediately grants their requests
He declares that sword, famine, and plague will come
He tells them to seek other gods
He praises their faith
questions.explanation: God clearly states that He will not accept the people and will send sword, famine, and plague because of their sins.

questions.question: What does this passage remind us about facing difficulties today?
options: God will always change our circumstances immediately if we just keep praying
We should first examine our sins, seek God's forgiveness, and trust in His sovereignty
God's judgment has nothing to do with us when we face difficulties
We can solve all problems by our own strength
questions.explanation: The passage reminds us that in times of trouble, we should examine our hearts, confess our sins, and turn to God for His mercy and guidance, rather than just demanding that He fulfill our desires.

en.reflection: In your life, is there any sin you need to confess to God, which might be affecting your relationship with Him or your current situation?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me through today's Scripture that in times of trouble, I should first examine my heart. Lord, I confess my iniquities and shortcomings; please forgive me and help me turn back to You. Grant me strength to face challenges with faith and to trust in Your lovingkindness and justice. In Jesus' name, I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to confess one deep-seated weakness or sin to God and ask for His forgiveness and help.

en.focus: Even in extreme difficulty and suffering, we can trust that God is just, loving, and present with us.

questions.question: What will be the ultimate outcome of God’s judgment on Judah?
options: Abundant harvest and peace
Disease, sword, famine, and captivity
Total destruction of their enemies
Wealth and prosperity
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that His judgment will include the sword, famine, plague, and captivity as punishment for the people's sins.

questions.question: What is Jeremiah's main complaint to God?
options: He did not receive enough food
He was persuaded and forced by God to speak, enduring much suffering for it
He was not appointed as a leader
He was not respected by the people
questions.explanation: Jeremiah feels he was 'persuaded' or 'deceived' by God into speaking His word, which resulted in great suffering and isolation.

questions.question: How does God respond to Jeremiah's complaints and suffering?
options: God tells Jeremiah his suffering is meaningless
God promises to make Jeremiah a fortified wall of bronze and to deliver him
God demands Jeremiah to stop complaining
God says He will give him more wealth as compensation
questions.explanation: God promises to make Jeremiah a fortified wall of bronze that no one can overcome, and that He will deliver him from the hands of the wicked.

questions.question: What important reminder does this passage offer us when we are facing difficulties today?
options: God's servants do not experience suffering
We should avoid all painful experiences
Even in pain and oppression, God remains with His servants, granting strength and deliverance
God will immediately change our circumstances if we complain
questions.explanation: Despite Jeremiah's immense suffering and struggles, God remains with him, promising strength, protection, and deliverance, showing that God does not abandon His servants in times of trouble.

en.reflection: Is there a situation in your life right now that makes you feel pain, loneliness, or misunderstanding? How do you bring these feelings to God?
reflectionOptions: Pour out my struggles to God
Remind myself of God's promised presence
en.prayer: Lord, my heart sometimes feels confused and pained, like Jeremiah's. Please help me to trust in Your justice and love even in hardship. Thank You for promising to be with me, and to grant me strength and deliverance. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a moment to be still and express your truest feelings and struggles to God, trusting that He hears you.

en.theme: God's Righteous Judgment and Future Restoration
en.focus: God judges His people for their sins, but His faithfulness guarantees future restoration and return.

questions.question: What did God command Jeremiah not to do as a symbol of the coming judgment?
options: Do not mourn for the dead
Do not marry or have children
Do not participate in feasts
All of the above
questions.explanation: God commanded Jeremiah not to marry or have children (v. 2), not to enter a house of mourning (v. 5), and not to sit with those feasting (v. 8), as a sign of the impending disaster.

questions.question: What sin did the LORD accuse His people of, leading to His wrath and judgment?
options: They did not cultivate the land properly
They abandoned God to serve other gods
They did not pay their tithes on time
They did not observe the Sabbath
questions.explanation: God states that His people abandoned Him and served other gods, provoking His anger, which was the main reason for their judgment.

questions.type: Understand the hope in the passage
questions.question: Despite the message of judgment, how does the passage hint at future hope?
options: God will send new prophets
God will bring them back from the land of the north
God will grant them a stronger army
God will change His laws
questions.explanation: God prophesies that in the future, His people will be brought back from the land of the north, indicating a hope for restoration.

questions.question: What attitude should we have when facing God's discipline or difficulties in life, as reminded by this passage?
options: Complain about God's strictness
Deny our own faults and blame others
Examine our actions and trust in God's ultimate salvation and restoration
Believe that God's love has left us
questions.explanation: The passage identifies the people's sins as the cause for judgment but also emphasizes God's ultimate salvation and restoration, encouraging us to examine ourselves and trust Him in difficult times.

en.reflection: Have you ever experienced God's discipline due to your own faults? How did you respond to it?
en.prayer: Righteous and loving God, thank You for revealing Your holiness and justice to me. Help me to examine my heart, and if there is any way I have strayed from You, please discipline and guide me back. May I always live in awe of You, knowing also that You are a God of grace and salvation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a moment reflecting on God's hatred of sin, and confess any ways you may have strayed today, asking for His forgiveness and guidance.

en.focus: God knows the depths of the human heart, and our hope lies in trusting Him, the fountain of living water.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 17:1, how is Judah's sin recorded?
options: Engraved on tablets of stone
Written on scrolls of parchment
Inscribed with an iron stylus and diamond point on their hearts and on the horns of their altars
Written with ink on their doorposts
questions.explanation: The passage states that Judah's sin is inscribed with an iron stylus and a diamond point on the tablet of their hearts and on the horns of their altars.

questions.question: How does Jeremiah 17:5–8 distinguish between those who trust in man and those who trust in the Lord?
options: Those who trust in man enjoy peace, while those who trust in God experience hardship
Those who trust in man are like a bush in the desert, while those who trust in God are like a tree planted by water
Those who trust in man gain wealth, while those who trust in God live in poverty
Those who trust in man are wise, while those who trust in God lack discernment
questions.explanation: The verses use vivid metaphors: those who trust in man will be like a bush in the desert, gaining nothing, while those who trust in the Lord will be like a tree planted by water, yielding fruit without ceasing.

questions.question: What truth does Jeremiah 17:9–10 teach us about the human heart and God?
options: The human heart is upright, and God cannot fully know it
The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick, but God searches and tests it
The human heart is simple, and God only looks at outward appearance
The human heart is unknowable, even to God
questions.explanation: This passage reveals the deceitfulness and corruption of the human heart, emphasizing that only the Lord can search and test the heart and mind, giving to each person according to their ways.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 17:13, what will be the end for those who forsake the Lord?
options: Their names will be written in heaven
They will acquire great wealth
Their names will be written in the dust, because they have forsaken the fountain of living water
They will be respected and loved by people
questions.explanation: Those who forsake the Lord will have their names written in the dust, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living water.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that the human heart is unfathomable, yet God knows it completely. What hidden thought or worry do you most need to bring to God in trust today?
en.prayer: O Lord, fountain of living water, my heart can sometimes be like a bush in the desert, deceitful and full of worries. Search my heart, guide me, and help me to trust in You alone, like a tree planted by water, always bearing fruit. May my hope never be put to shame. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a few minutes today quietly opening your heart to God, asking Him to search your deepest thoughts and feelings.

en.theme: God the Potter, We the Clay
en.focus: God has absolute sovereignty to change His dealings with individuals or nations, depending on their response to Him.

questions.question: Where did the word of the Lord command Jeremiah to go?
options: The temple
The king's palace
The potter's house
The city gate
questions.explanation: The Lord commanded Jeremiah to go down to the potter's house, where he would hear the Lord's words.

questions.question: What did the potter do when the pot he was shaping was spoiled in his hands?
options: He threw it away
He reshaped it into another pot, as seemed good to him
He sold it as is
He put it aside for later
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that when the pot was marred in the potter's hand, he “reshaped it into another pot, as seemed good to him.”

questions.question: According to this passage, what causes God to change His mind concerning a nation or an individual?
options: God's changing moods
The amount of wealth a person possesses
Whether people turn from evil or sin and repent to God
God's predetermined plan, which cannot be altered
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that He will change His plans (to bring disaster or prosperity) based on whether a nation or individual repents of their evil deeds or turns from their sins.

questions.question: As God's people, how does this passage encourage us when facing difficulties and shortcomings in our lives?
options: We can complain to God because He is unfair
We can give up completely because we cannot change
We can trust that God is able to reshape us and encourages us to repent and return to Him
We can try to fix everything through our own efforts
questions.explanation: This passage reminds us that God is our Potter, and He has the sovereignty and power to reshape us. Even if we are like 'marred clay,' if we repent, He can mold us into useful vessels as He sees fit. This offers encouragement for repentance and hope.

en.reflection: Is there a 'marred pot' area in your life that you need to surrender to God today, allowing Him to reshape it?
en.prayer: My Potter, Lord, I confess that I often feel like marred clay, with many imperfections and flaws. According to Your lovingkindness and sovereignty, I ask You to reshape me, making me into a vessel pleasing to You. Help me to repent today and fully surrender myself to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment, cup your hands together, imagine yourself as clay in God's hands, and softly say, “Lord, I am Your clay, please mold me.”

en.theme: The Broken Jar and God's Fierce Anger
en.focus: God uses Jeremiah's symbolic actions and prophecies to reveal that His judgment on His rebellious people is real and unavoidable.

questions.question: What object did the LORD instruct Jeremiah to use to symbolize His judgment on Judah?
options: A golden cup
A wooden staff
A clay jar
A stone
questions.explanation: The LORD told Jeremiah to buy a clay jar to symbolize Judah being shattered like the jar.

questions.question: What did God say He would make Jerusalem become?
options: A city of gold
A fruitful vineyard
A desolation and an object of horror
A place of refuge
questions.explanation: God declared He would make the city an object of horror and scorn, and that it would be devastated.

questions.question: After Jeremiah proclaimed God's judgment in the temple courtyard, what did Pashhur do?
options: He praised Jeremiah's courage
He believed Jeremiah's words were true
He struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks
He invited Jeremiah to share a meal
questions.explanation: Pashhur, after hearing Jeremiah, struck him and put him in the stocks in anger.

questions.question: What is the primary message this passage conveys about God's attitude toward sin?
options: God is always lenient with sin, without punishment
God is righteous in His judgment, which is real and inescapable
God only punishes foreign nations, not His own people
God's judgment is merely a threat and will not actually occur
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God's righteous and severe judgment against rebellion and sin is real, and He will carry out what He has declared.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that God is righteous and holy, and He hates sin. In what areas of your life do you need to seriously examine yourself and ask God to help you turn back to Him?
reflectionOptions: Let go of a hidden sin
Repent of specific words or actions
en.prayer: Righteous and holy Heavenly Father, You are a God who hates sin, yet You are also full of compassion. Search my heart, and if there are any words, actions, or thoughts displeasing to You, please forgive me and help me to genuinely repent and turn back. May I always live in awe of You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to quietly examine your heart and pray to God about one area you realize you need to improve or repent of.

en.focus: Even in the deepest pain and confusion, we can trust in God's sovereignty and His ultimate deliverance.

questions.question: What tone does the prophet Jeremiah use in his prayer to God at the beginning of this passage?
options: Gratitude and praise
Submission and reverence
Complaint and accusation
Joy and hope
questions.explanation: Jeremiah expresses a sense of being 'deceived' or 'overpowered' by God, becoming a laughingstock to all, indicating complaint and confusion.

questions.question: When Jeremiah decided to no longer speak in the Lord's name, what did he feel internally?
options: A sense of ease and freedom
A burning fire in his heart, unbearable
A feeling of peace and security
Indifference
questions.explanation: Jeremiah tried to refrain from speaking in the Lord's name, but His word was like a burning fire shut up in his bones, making it unbearable.

questions.question: Despite Jeremiah's immense suffering and despair, what did he believe the Lord would do to those who attacked him?
options: The Lord would ignore them
The Lord would help them succeed
The Lord would punish them and put them to shame
The Lord would reconcile with them
questions.explanation: Jeremiah believed the Lord was with him like a mighty warrior, and those who persecuted him would stumble and be utterly shamed.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us when we face misunderstanding, ridicule, or persecution for serving the Lord?
options: It encourages us to stop proclaiming God's word
It reminds us to fight back with our own strength
It encourages us to trust that God will vindicate us, even in pain
It implies that God is indifferent to our suffering
questions.explanation: Although Jeremiah complained, he ultimately entrusted judgment and vindication to God, believing God would act justly on his behalf, which is a great encouragement to us.

en.reflection: In your life, have you ever experienced suffering for the sake of the Lord, feeling 'deceived' or 'forsaken' by God? How did you respond then?
reflectionOptions: Poured out my pain and confusion to God
Sought help and intercession from others
en.prayer: Almighty Father, when I face misunderstanding, ridicule, or pain while serving You or following Your will, and even feel Your silence, help me, like Jeremiah, to honestly express my heart to You, even with complaints. Strengthen my faith, knowing that You are a faithful God and will vindicate Your servants. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, if you have any complaints or confusion towards God, take five minutes to honestly write them down or express them to God, trusting that He hears you.

en.focus: Even in the most challenging times, God remains our refuge and source of wisdom. We must turn to Him for guidance.

questions.question: When King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon was attacking Jerusalem, whom did King Zedekiah send to Jeremiah?
options: Eliashib the priest and Samuel the prophet
Gedaliah son of Pashhur the priest and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah
Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and Gedaliah son of Shaphan
Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and Ahikam son of Hilkiah
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that King Zedekiah sent Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and Gedaliah son of Shaphan to Jeremiah.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of King Zedekiah sending envoys to Jeremiah?
options: To ask Jeremiah for military strategies
To inquire about the movements of the Babylonian army
To inquire of the LORD if He would perform a miracle to make the king of Babylon withdraw
To ask Jeremiah to pray for their sins
questions.explanation: They went to Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD through him, hoping God would perform a miracle to make King Nebuchadnezzar withdraw.

questions.question: What kind of predicament was Jerusalem facing at that time, according to the passage?
options: A severe famine
Being besieged by the mighty Babylonian army
A failed alliance with Egypt
An outbreak of civil strife
questions.explanation: The passage clearly mentions, “King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and his whole army were attacking Jerusalem,” indicating they were under siege.

questions.question: When we face great difficulties or uncertainties, what does this passage remind us to do first?
options: Immediately seek human help and advice
Solve problems with our own wisdom and experience
Offer sincere inquiry and prayer to God
Put it aside for now and wait for things to improve naturally
questions.explanation: King Zedekiah, in despair, sent people to inquire of God, reminding us that in adversity, we should first seek God's guidance and help.

en.reflection: When you face a significant challenge or decision, do you, like King Zedekiah, primarily seek God's guidance?
reflectionOptions: Admit that I often forget to seek God first
Be willing to bring my difficulties to God more often
Need to learn how to quietly wait on God in adversity
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being my refuge and source of wisdom. When I am troubled by life's difficulties or uncertainties, please help me, like King Zedekiah, to turn to You first and offer my sincere inquiries. May I seek Your will in all things, rather than relying on my own understanding. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray about a current challenge or dilemma you are facing, asking God for clear guidance and direction.

en.focus: God's judgment on disobedience is certain, yet His righteousness also offers hope to those who seek Him.

questions.question: Which king did Jeremiah instruct the people not to weep for?
options: Jehoahaz
Jehoiakim
Jehoiachin
Zedekiah
questions.explanation: The passage tells the people not to weep for King Josiah, who had died, but for Jehoahaz (Shallum), who was taken into exile and would never return.

questions.question: How is Jehoiakim's reign described, contrasting with his father Josiah?
options: He acted justly and enjoyed peace
He built lavish palaces through injustice, unlike his righteous father
He feared God and brought prosperity to the nation
He followed his father's ways and did what was right in God's eyes
questions.explanation: Jehoiakim built grand palaces through unjust means, neglecting the poor, in stark contrast to his father Josiah's righteous rule.

questions.question: What did God's judgment on Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin (Coniah) signify?
options: God shows favoritism to those in power
God has clear judgment for unjust and disobedient rulers
God protects the royal lineage regardless of their actions
God cares only about religious rituals, not social justice
questions.explanation: God's severe judgment on Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin demonstrates His intolerance for injustice and disobedience, even from kings.

questions.question: From this passage, how should we view our own authority and responsibilities in life?
options: Success is paramount, regardless of the methods used
We should emulate worldly leadership models
No matter our position, we should strive to act justly, show mercy, and walk humbly with God
God's judgment is only for kings, not for us
questions.explanation: The examples of the kings remind us that no matter our position, God values whether we act justly, show mercy, and obey His will.

en.reflection: This passage reminds us that God is a righteous judge. In what areas do you need to examine yourself today and seek to walk more uprightly before God, aligning with His will?
reflectionOptions: How I treat family and friends
My attitude in work or ministry
How I use my resources and time
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You for the teachings in Jeremiah that remind me You are holy and hate sin. Please illuminate my heart to see any areas in my life that are not pleasing to You. Grant me a repentant spirit and the strength to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, try to practice 'doing justice and loving mercy' through a specific action, such as helping someone in need or praying about a social injustice.

en.theme: The Responsibility of Shepherds and God's Promise
en.focus: God promises to raise up a righteous Branch and personally shepherd His flock, in stark contrast to false shepherds.

questions.question: To whom does God pronounce judgment at the beginning of Jeremiah chapter 23?
options: The people of Israel
The kings of the nations
The shepherds who destroy and scatter His flock
The pagan prophets
questions.explanation: The passage begins by declaring woe to the shepherds who are destroying and scattering God's flock.

questions.question: Regarding the scattered flock, what action does God promise to take Himself?
options: Hand them over to other nations
Allow them to remain scattered forever
Gather them from all lands and raise up shepherds for them
Destroy all who oppressed them
questions.explanation: God promises to personally gather His flock from where they have been scattered and set up shepherds over them who will care for them.

questions.question: God promises to raise up a 'righteous Branch' for David. What will this Branch bring?
options: Economic prosperity
Military victories
Justice and righteousness, enabling Judah and Israel to dwell securely
The establishment of powerful empires worldwide
questions.explanation: This righteous Branch will reign as king, act wisely, and execute justice and righteousness on earth, allowing Judah and Israel to dwell securely.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us to trust in God's control over the future today?
options: It reminds us that hard work alone can change the future
It teaches us that God will fulfill His promises for His people according to His righteousness and love
It tells us that relying on human wisdom can solve all problems
It implies that God only rewards those who have never made mistakes
questions.explanation: Despite the failures of false shepherds and the nation's corruption, God promises His personal intervention, raising up a righteous king to shepherd and save His people. This reminds us of God's faithfulness and that He will fulfill His promises according to His righteousness and love.

en.reflection: In the midst of today's changing world, which of God's promises brings you peace and hope?
reflectionOptions: God is sovereign and personally cares for me
God will fulfill His plans according to His justice and love
Jesus Christ is the righteous Branch who will execute justice and righteousness
en.prayer: Faithful Father, thank You for revealing Your righteousness and love to us in this passage. When the world is full of chaos and uncertainty, help me to trust in Your promises, knowing that You are the Good Shepherd who personally cares for Your flock. May I live out justice and compassion in my life because of the hope You give. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to reflect on how Jesus has been your righteous Shepherd, and offer Him thanks.

en.focus: God is omnipresent; He is not only far away but also intimately near to us. We cannot hide from Him.

questions.question: Does the Lord say He is 'a God nearby'?
options: Yes
No
The text does not mention it
Only in specific situations
questions.explanation: The Lord explicitly states, 'Am I only a God nearby,' implying He is indeed a God nearby as well as far away.

questions.question: What contrast does the Lord make about Himself in this verse?
options: A God nearby and a God far away
Lord of all in heaven and Lord of all on earth
Creator of all things and Sustainer of all things
A God of power and a God of grace
questions.explanation: The Lord Himself asks, 'Am I only a God nearby,' which naturally sets up a contrast with 'a God far away.'

questions.question: Which attribute of God is primarily emphasized in this verse?
options: God's love
God's justice
God's omnipresence
God's omnipotence
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Am I only a God nearby, and not a God far away?' clearly emphasizes that God is present everywhere, both near and far, signifying His omnipresence.

questions.question: What reminder does understanding God's omnipresence give us for our daily lives?
options: We can act as we please because God won't always be around
We should try harder to conceal our mistakes
Everything we do, wherever we are, is in God's sight
We only need to revere God in church
questions.explanation: God's omnipresence means that our every action, thought, and intention is known to Him, reminding us to live a life that honors Him.

en.reflection: Where have you experienced God's presence today, or in which area of your life do you need to invite Him more deeply?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the omnipresent God, always with me no matter where I am. Help me to be continually aware of Your presence and, because of it, to live a life that pleases You. May my thoughts and actions bring You glory. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take one minute today to be still and quietly reflect in your heart: 'God, You are here; You are with me.'

en.focus: God pronounces judgment due to persistent rebellion, but also repeatedly calls His people to return, and His ultimate plan will be fulfilled.

questions.question: In which king's reign and year was this message in Jeremiah 25 given?
options: The fourth year of King Josiah
The fourth year of King Jehoiakim
The fourth year of King Zedekiah
The fourth year of King Manasseh
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that this message came in 'the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah.'

questions.question: For how many years had God been sending messages to the people through Jeremiah?
options: Ten years
Twenty years
Twenty-three years
Thirty years
questions.explanation: God says, 'For twenty-three years—from the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah until this very day—the word of the Lord has come to me.'

questions.question: What was the main reason God decided to judge Judah and Jerusalem?
options: They had not built enough temples
They had not paid their tithes on time
They did not listen to God’s words, did not repent, and served other gods
They did not participate in military wars
questions.explanation: God said, 'Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways and your evil practices, and you can stay in the land the Lord gave to you and your ancestors forever and ever. Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them; do not arouse my anger with what your hands have made. Then I will not harm you. But you did not listen to me.'

questions.question: How did God prophesy He would punish rebellious Judah and the surrounding nations?
options: By causing them to suffer seven years of famine
By making them serve the king of Babylon for seventy years
By making them serve the king of Babylon for seventy years, after which the king of Babylon would also be punished
By causing them to suffer seventy years of plague
questions.explanation: God said, 'This whole country will become a desolate wasteland, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years. “But when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Babylonians, for their wickedness; I will make it desolate forever.'

en.reflection: Like the Israelites of old, do you sometimes ignore God's repeated warnings? What warning from God do you most need to heed today?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your constant reminders and calls, even when I often rebel. Please forgive me for sometimes ignoring Your word. Help me to listen to Your warnings today and turn back to You. May Your word bear fruit of obedience in my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time today reflecting on a reminder God has given you through Scripture or circumstances, and pray about it.

en.focus: God is the Judge of all the earth, and His judgment begins with His own people and extends to all nations who reject Him.

questions.question: What kind of vessel did God tell Jeremiah to take and make the nations drink from?
options: A golden cup
A cup full of wine
A cup full of water
A silver bowl
questions.explanation: God commanded Jeremiah to take the cup of His wrathful wine and make all the nations drink from it.

questions.question: Among the listed nations, which one was named first to drink from this cup?
options: Egypt
Philistia
Jerusalem and the towns of Judah
Babylon
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that Jeremiah was to begin by making Jerusalem and the towns of Judah drink from the cup.

questions.question: What is the nature of God's judgment on the nations as revealed in this passage?
options: Random and without purpose
Only directed at Israel's enemies
Just, universal, and inescapable
Can be avoided by wealth or power
questions.explanation: God's judgment is universal, covering all peoples and kings, showing that He is the sovereign ruler and judge of all the earth, and none can escape.

questions.question: What should be our response when we see God's judgment on the nations?
options: Feel fear and despair, as no one is safe
Feel sorrow for all who reject God and pray for them
Rejoice that we are not among the judged nations
Believe it doesn't concern us and continue with our lives
questions.explanation: Recognizing God's righteous judgment, we should feel sorrow for the outcome of those who reject God and pray for their repentance, while also being vigilant in our own obedience to God.
questions.evidence: Jeremiah 25:29-38 (especially v. 31, which speaks of the Lord contending with the nations, indicating the universality of judgment and thus our call to compassion for the world)

en.reflection: What are your feelings and thoughts when confronted with God's righteousness and His judgment over all the earth? How does this impact your view of yourself and the world?
reflectionOptions: A deeper understanding of God's justice and power
A greater burden for those who do not know God
A reflection on my own obedience to God
en.prayer: Almighty God, You are the supreme Judge, and all things are under Your control. Open my eyes to know Your justice and mercy more deeply. May I live with reverence, always obeying Your will, and pray for those in this world who do not know You, that they too may turn and come to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for three friends or family members who do not know God, asking Him to have mercy on them and enable them to know and accept Jesus Christ as their Savior.

en.theme: A Call to Repentance and a Choice for Life
en.focus: God calls His people to repent, warns of the consequences of disobedience, but also promises forgiveness and life for those who turn back to Him.

questions.question: What message did Jeremiah deliver to the people in the temple courtyard?
options: God would bless Judah and make it the greatest nation
God would protect the temple forever because of His presence
If the people did not repent, the temple and Jerusalem would be destroyed like Shiloh
God would raise up a new king to lead the people to victory over their enemies
questions.explanation: Jeremiah clearly conveyed God's warning: if the people did not repent and obey His words, the temple and Jerusalem would suffer the same fate as Shiloh.

questions.question: What was the reaction of the priests, prophets, and all the people when Jeremiah delivered this message?
options: They immediately knelt in repentance, pleading for God's mercy
They seized Jeremiah, intending to put him to death
They welcomed Jeremiah's message and asked him to speak more
They mocked Jeremiah, thinking he was a madman
questions.explanation: When the priests, prophets, and all the people heard Jeremiah's words, they seized him and declared that he deserved to die.

questions.question: How did Jeremiah respond to those who sought to kill him, despite the threat of death?
options: He denied being a prophet and tried to flee
He pleaded for his life and promised not to deliver any more negative messages
He insisted his message was from the LORD and called them to repent to avoid disaster
He cursed those who sought to kill him and prophesied worse punishment for them
questions.explanation: Jeremiah courageously told them that he was sent by the LORD to speak these words and urged them to change their ways and obey the LORD to prevent disaster.

questions.question: What is the most important reminder for us today from Jeremiah 26?
options: We should avoid any unpleasant messages and only listen to what sounds good
God's judgment on sin is real, and repentance is key to forgiveness and life
As long as we worship in the temple, no disaster will come upon us
A prophet's words are always popular and bring immediate change
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that God's warnings about sin are serious, and He calls His people to repent to avoid judgment and receive forgiveness.

en.reflection: Today, is there any area in your life where God is calling you to repent and turn back to Him?
reflectionOptions: Confess and give up a habit displeasing to God
Repair a relationship damaged by my actions
Be more faithful in obeying God with my finances
