God is indifferent to sin, allowing it to run its course
questions.explanation: Through His judgments on various nations, God reveals that He is not only the God of Israel but also the supreme ruler who governs all the earth and exercises justice.

en.reflection: In light of God's justice and sovereignty, what burden or worry do you most need to entrust to Him today?
en.prayer: Sovereign Lord, You are the Judge of all the earth and also a God of mercy. Help me to understand Your justice and love more deeply. When I face anxieties and uncertainties in life, may I trust in Your sovereignty alone and cast all my burdens upon You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute quietly reflecting on God's greatness and sovereignty, offering Him praise.

en.focus: God is a righteous judge; He will justly judge rebellious nations and deliver His people.

questions.question: Which nation is the subject of the prophecy in Jeremiah chapter 50?
options: Assyria
Egypt
Babylon
Philistia
questions.explanation: The chapter clearly states at the beginning that this is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans.

questions.question: What is used to describe Babylon's downfall?
options: Her wise men will be killed
Her idols will be put to shame, and her warriors terrified
Her granaries will be burned
Her walls will be torn down
questions.explanation: The passage describes that her idols will be put to shame, her detestable things terrified, and her warriors dismayed.

questions.question: What promise does God make to His people Israel when Babylon is judged?
options: They will receive new land
They will seek the LORD their God with Judah, weeping as they return
They will become stronger than other nations
They will forget all past suffering
questions.explanation: The passage promises that Israel and Judah will seek the LORD their God together, weeping as they return to Zion.

questions.question: How does this passage remind us of God's character today?
options: God only cares about His people, not other nations
God is righteous, and He will judge all sin and pride
God always punishes all sin immediately
God's power is limited and cannot fully control the world
questions.explanation: This passage shows God's judgment on Babylon and His deliverance of Israel, revealing Him as sovereign, righteous, and faithful.

en.reflection: Are there any 'Babylonian' forms of pride, idols, or injustice in your life that you need to lay down and turn towards God's righteous path?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of a sin
Release an excessive pursuit of material things
Forgive someone who has hurt me
en.prayer: Righteous Judge, I acknowledge that You are the sovereign God. Help me to examine my heart and remove all pride and selfish desires that do not honor You. May I seek You alone and walk in Your righteous ways. In Jesus' name, I pray. Amen.
en.action: Today, try to commit one 'idol' or source of pride in your life to God through prayer.

en.focus: God is a righteous judge who will justly punish those nations that oppress His people.

questions.question: Who does God command to attack Babylon?
options: Merathaim and Pekod
Judah and Israel
Egypt and Assyria
Edom and Moab
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 50:21 mentions God commanding an attack on Merathaim and Pekod, which represent certain places or allies of Babylon.

questions.question: How is the scene described when Babylon is attacked?
options: A time of peace and quiet
A sound of battle and great destruction
Celebration and dancing
Peaceful negotiations
questions.explanation: The text describes a sound of battle and great destruction when Babylon is attacked, indicating a fierce war.

questions.question: Why does God judge Babylon?
options: Because Babylon had strong military power
Because Babylon was too wealthy
Because Babylon acted arrogantly against the Holy One of Israel and defied the LORD
Because Babylon did not invite God to their feasts
questions.explanation: God judges Babylon because of their arrogance against the Holy One of Israel and their defiance of the LORD; their pride and hostility towards God are the reasons for judgment.

questions.question: What can we learn about God's character from this passage?
options: God is indifferent to justice in the world
God is a righteous judge who will hold the wicked accountable
God only cares about the Israelites, not other nations
God only cares about sacrifices, not human actions
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that God is righteous and will judge nations that oppress His people and act with arrogance.

en.reflection: Are there any 'Babylon-like' areas of pride or injustice in your life that God is calling you to examine and repent of?
reflectionOptions: Arrogant attitude towards others or God
Lack of justice in certain areas
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You that You are the sovereign Lord who will judge the world with justice. Help me to examine my heart and remove all pride and injustice, so that I may always live humbly and obediently before You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to confess and repent of any pride or injustice you might find in your life.

en.theme: God, the Redeemer of the Oppressed
en.focus: God will surely advocate for His oppressed people and judge those who oppressed them.

questions.question: The inhabitants of Babylon are called “oppressed” because who led them captive and refused to let them go?
options: Assyria
Egypt
Israel
Babylonian captives
questions.explanation: The text states that those who carried Israel and Judah captive are the ones who refused to let them go.

questions.question: Who is called “the LORD of hosts” and “their Redeemer”?
options: The King of Persia
The prophet of Israel
The King of Babylon
The LORD God
questions.explanation: The passage clearly identifies the LORD as the “LORD of hosts” and “their Redeemer.”

questions.question: Why does God say He will “plead their case” for Israel against the Chaldeans?
options: Because Israel was stronger than Babylon
Because the Chaldeans worshipped false gods
Because they oppressed Israel and refused to release them
Because God wanted to prove He is the only true God
questions.explanation: God promises to plead the case for Israel and Judah because Babylon (the Chaldeans) had oppressed them, carried them captive, and refused to let them go.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us today when we feel oppressed or face injustice in the world?
options: God will immediately remove all injustice
We should fight back with our own strength
God is righteous, He cares for the oppressed, and will advocate for them
We should completely avoid any conflict or injustice
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God is the Redeemer of the oppressed. He sees those who are captive and mistreated, and promises to advocate for them, offering great comfort and hope.

en.reflection: In what area of your life are you currently feeling oppressed, experiencing injustice, or needing God to advocate for you?
en.prayer: Righteous Redeemer, I thank You that You are a God who cares for the oppressed. When I face injustice or feel weak in this world, please remind me of Your faithfulness and power. I trust that You will advocate for me and bring justice in Your perfect timing and way. Grant me peace and patience as I wait for Your action. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment of quiet reflection to specifically tell God about a situation where you feel injustice or need His advocacy.

en.focus: God is a righteous judge who will justly judge all evil in the world, and His promises will never fail.

questions.question: How does the LORD declare He will treat Babylon?
options: He will make Babylon strong
He will make Babylon a city of destruction
He will make Babylon the leader of nations
He will make Babylon at peace with other nations
questions.explanation: God declares that He will raise up destroyers against Babylon, making it a desolate city.

questions.question: What does the LORD command the people of Israel to do?
options: Stay in Babylon and enjoy comfort
Flee from Babylon to save their lives
Fight alongside Babylon in war
Pray for Babylon's prosperity
questions.explanation: God commands His people to flee from Babylon to avoid being destroyed with it in judgment.

questions.question: What ability of God is described in Jeremiah 51:15–19?
options: He can change hearts and bring repentance
He created and governs the universe
He can raise the dead
He can make the poor rich
questions.explanation: This passage emphasizes that the LORD is the one true God who created the heavens and earth and controls natural phenomena, possessing supreme power.

questions.question: What is the main message this passage conveys to us today?
options: People can change the world by their own strength
God will tolerate sin forever and not judge
God's judgment is real and just, and He is in control
Working hard will prevent all disasters
questions.explanation: This passage strongly declares that God's judgment against sin is real and unavoidable, and that He is the all-powerful God who controls everything.

en.reflection: In the face of injustice and evil in the world, how does this passage strengthen your faith in God's sovereignty and justice?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me God will ultimately judge all things
It helps me trust more in God's power
It prompts me to pray for those who suffer
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You that You are the Lord over all, Your judgment is just and righteous, and Your promises never fail. Please help me to firmly trust in Your power and love amidst the chaos and injustice in the world. May Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Pray for an issue you perceive as unjust, asking God to bring about justice according to His will.

en.focus: God's righteous judgment will come upon all who are arrogant and oppressive, and He will vindicate His people.

questions.question: How does God describe His instrumental use of Babylon?
options: His sword and shield
His battle-ax and weapons of war
His servant and messenger
His judge and lawyer
questions.explanation: God says Babylon is His “battle-ax” and “weapons of war” to shatter nations.

questions.question: What specific sins of Babylon are repeatedly mentioned as reasons for God's judgment?
options: Idolatry and sorcery
Pride and violence, devouring Israel
Greed and injustice
Breaking covenants and unfaithfulness
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly mentions Babylon's pride (seeing itself as a mountain) and its sin of devouring Jacob and Israel as reasons for God's judgment.

questions.question: What will be the outcome of God's judgment on Babylon?
options: Babylon will become an impregnable city
Babylon will prosper forever
Babylon will become a desolate wasteland, uninhabited
Babylon will become a model for other nations
questions.explanation: God declares that Babylon will become a desolate wasteland, uninhabited, where even its stones cannot be used for cornerstones or foundations.

questions.question: What is the primary message this passage conveys to God's people?
options: God's judgment is arbitrary and unpredictable
God's promises are always delayed
God is righteous; He will punish oppressors and vindicate His people
People should rely on their own strength to fight injustice
questions.explanation: This passage emphasizes God's justice and sovereignty, assuring His people that He will punish wicked Babylon in due time and vindicate suffering Israel.

en.reflection: How does this passage remind you of God's character and actions when you face injustice or feel oppressed in your life?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me that God is the ultimate judge
It helps me to quietly wait for God's vindication
It encourages me to pray for those who suffer
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You that You are the Lord of history, and all things are under Your control. When I witness injustice and evil in the world, help me to look to You, trusting that Your judgment will ultimately come, and You will vindicate Your people. Grant me peace to rest in Your faithfulness. In Jesus' name, I pray, Amen.
en.action: Meditate on a verse (e.g., Jeremiah 51:35) that reminds you God is just and will vindicate His people.

en.focus: God calls His people to flee from Babylon, which faces judgment, and to trust in His promises.

questions.question: How does God warn His people at the beginning of the passage?
options: To rejoice in Babylon's prosperity
To be wary of Babylon's temptations
To go out from Babylon and save themselves
To live in peace with the Babylonians
questions.explanation: God warns His people to go out from Babylon and save themselves, lest they be caught in its iniquity.

questions.question: What fate is described for Babylon in the passage?
options: Its wealth will be divided among other nations
It will suffer a great earthquake
It will be swallowed by the deep sea
It will become desolate and uninhabited
questions.explanation: The passage prophesies that Babylon will become desolate and uninhabited, a horror.

questions.question: How does God want His people to respond to the coming judgment in this passage?
options: Actively resist Babylonian rule
Rejoice at Babylon's destruction
Trust God's promises, be alert, and obey His call
Pray for the Babylonians for their forgiveness
questions.explanation: God calls His people to be alert, to come out of Babylon's wickedness, and to trust His promises, for He will accomplish what He has spoken.

questions.question: What does this passage remind us of for our lives today?
options: We should avoid all contact with the secular world
When faced with sinful temptations, we should firmly choose to depart and obey God
We don't need to care about social injustices
Simply attending church guarantees our salvation
questions.explanation: Just as God called His people to flee from Babylon's wickedness, we too must be alert and, when the world tempts us away from God, firmly choose to depart and obey Him.

en.reflection: In your life, what are some 'Babylons' you need to be alert to and 'flee' from?
en.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for being a faithful and covenant-keeping God, whose promises never fail. Grant me wisdom to discern the 'Babylons' in my life and help me courageously flee from sin and anything that draws me away from You. May I wholeheartedly trust in Your protection and salvation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a few minutes today reflecting on anything in your life that you need to resolve to let go of or distance yourself from, and pray to God about it.

en.focus: Even in the darkest of judgments, God remains sovereign and preserves a glimmer of grace and hope for His people.

questions.question: Who was the last king of Judah?
options: Josiah
Jehoiakim
Zedekiah
Jehoiachin
questions.explanation: Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, reigning in Jerusalem for eleven years and doing what was evil in the eyes of the Lord.

questions.question: After the Babylonian army captured Jerusalem, what did they do to the temple and city walls?
options: Rebuilt the temple and walls
Demolished the temple and walls
Converted the temple into a Babylonian shrine
Strengthened the city walls for defense
questions.explanation: Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD and the king's house, and broke down all the walls around Jerusalem.

questions.question: From this painful history of captivity, what can we learn about God's attitude towards sin?
options: God is lenient towards sin and will not punish it
God is righteous concerning sin and will judge it
God only punishes the sins of Gentiles, not His own people
God is indifferent to sin
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that Judah suffered God's judgment for its sins (especially Zedekiah's rebellion), leading to the destruction of the kingdom and captivity. This demonstrates God's righteousness in judging sin.

questions.question: What was the final outcome for King Jehoiachin of Judah, who was in captivity, as mentioned at the end of the story?
options: He died in a Babylonian prison
He was released and restored to his throne
He was shown favor by the king of Babylon, given honor, and ate regularly at his table
He was exiled to a more distant land
questions.explanation: After thirty-seven years of captivity, King Evil-Merodach of Babylon showed favor to Jehoiachin, releasing him from prison and 'exalting him above the other kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king’s table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, every day a portion, until the day of his death.' This foreshadows God's grace and hope even amidst judgment.

en.reflection: This passage contains both severe judgment and a glimmer of grace. What grace have you received from God today that you are most thankful for?
en.prayer: Righteous and loving God, I see that Your judgment of sin is real, and yet You preserve grace even in times of trouble. Thank You for all the grace and hope You have given me. Help me to always live with reverence, turn away from sin, and live a life of gratitude. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to list three graces you believe God has given you today and thank Him for them.

en.focus: When God's people are disciplined for their sins, they experience deep pain, loneliness, and shame, but these experiences also call them back to God.

questions.question: How is Jerusalem (Zion) depicted at the beginning of this passage?
options: A city full of joy
A city sparsely populated
A beloved city
A prosperous and flourishing city
questions.explanation: The passage opens by describing Jerusalem as 'deserted, like a widow,' indicating its desolation.

questions.question: What did Zion's 'lovers' and 'friends' do to her?
options: Helped her rebuild her home
Betrayed her and became her enemies
Mourned for her and comforted her
Suffered with her
questions.explanation: Those she loved have betrayed her and become her enemies.

questions.question: What is identified as the reason for Zion's suffering in the passage?
options: The strength of her enemies
The decrease in population
Harsh environmental conditions
Her many transgressions
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that 'Jerusalem has sinned greatly and so has become unclean.'

questions.question: What is the main message this passage conveys?
options: God always protects His people from all suffering
Suffering happens randomly, unrelated to human actions
God's discipline for His people's sins brings pain and shame, but also calls them to repentance
Suffering will naturally pass if one just waits
questions.explanation: Zion's suffering is due to her many sins, and God uses this discipline to prompt reflection and repentance.

en.reflection: This passage reminds us that sin can bring pain and separation from God. Do you need to examine any 'sins' in your life today that might be causing distance in your relationship with God?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of hidden sins
Draw near to God again, seeking His face
en.prayer: Lord, when my heart strays from You due to sin, I often experience pain and loneliness. Please forgive my sins and turn me back to You. May Your mercy and grace shine upon me once more, restoring my relationship with You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to quietly reflect before God and confess any sins in your life that are causing separation from Him.

en.focus: Amidst profound pain and despair, the sufferer still cries out to God with honesty and trusts in His justice.

questions.question: How does the sufferer describe their pain in verse 12?
options: Unparalleled suffering
Mild discomfort
Temporary inconvenience
Tolerable ordeal
questions.explanation: The sufferer asks passersby if there is any sorrow like theirs, indicating their pain is beyond comparison.

questions.question: What metaphor does the sufferer use to describe God's anger causing their affliction?
options: Burning with fire
Catching in a net
Burdensome weight
Chopping down with an axe
questions.explanation: The text describes the Lord sending fire from on high into their bones and spreading a net for their feet, turning them back.

questions.question: Despite immense suffering, what is the sufferer's attitude towards God?
options: Complete denial of God's existence
Complains about God's unfairness but still cries out to Him
Turns to other gods for help
Believes their suffering is unrelated to God
questions.explanation: The sufferer acknowledges that the Lord has brought this suffering upon them, and in their anguish, they cry out to the Lord, asking Him to deal with those who have caused their suffering.

questions.question: How does this passage help us face pain and injustice in our lives?
options: Encourages us to suppress our feelings
Teaches us to only focus on our own problems
Reminds us that we can pour out our pain to God and trust in His justice
Suggests we avoid reality and not confront difficulties
questions.explanation: The sufferer, in deep anguish, still cries out to God and trusts in His righteous judgment, which encourages us to commit everything to God in our suffering.

en.reflection: What pains or injustices are you currently experiencing that you most need to pour out to God and seek His comfort and justice for?
en.prayer: Lord, my heart is broken by pain and heavy burdens. I know You are just and loving. Please hear my cry, comfort my wounded soul, and help me to look to You alone in my suffering. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment today to pour out your deepest pains and struggles to God in your own words.

en.theme: The Lord's Fierce Wrath and Discipline
en.focus: When God’s wrath is poured out due to sin, His judgment is thorough, yet His justice remains.

questions.question: In verse 1, how did the Lord treat the splendor of Zion?
options: He made it more glorious
He cast it down from heaven to earth
He burned it with fire
He hid it away
questions.explanation: The text states that the Lord “has cast down the splendor of Israel from heaven to earth.”

questions.question: What did the Lord destroy in His anger concerning Judah?
options: Her vineyards and olive groves
Her strongholds and walls
Her temple and altars
Her houses and streets
questions.explanation: Verse 2 mentions that the Lord “has laid in ruins all the strongholds of the daughter of Judah; He has leveled her walls.”

questions.question: Why did the Lord allow such destruction to come upon His people and His sanctuary?
options: Because He delights in destruction
Because foreign gods were more powerful than Him
Because He poured out His fierce wrath on account of their sin
Because He forgot His covenant with His people
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly emphasizes that the Lord acted “in His anger” and with “fierce wrath” in bringing about judgment and destruction, indicating it was a response to the people's sin.

questions.question: How should we respond to God’s seemingly severe discipline?
options: Complain that God is unfair
Turn to other gods for help
Recognize the seriousness of sin and seek repentance and God's mercy
Pretend nothing happened and continue as before
questions.explanation: While the passage describes God's fierce wrath and thorough judgment, understanding that this is due to sin should lead us to consider the gravity of sin and turn to God in repentance and for mercy, rather than complaining or avoiding Him.

en.reflection: Today, do you sense God's displeasure with sin? How does this remind you of your life's priorities?
reflectionOptions: Trust more deeply in God's mercy
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, I am filled with awe as I read of Your fierce wrath and judgment against sin. Help me to recognize the gravity of sin and to truly repent. May my life glorify You and not provoke Your anger. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a moment today reflecting: In what areas might you be taking God's holiness and commands lightly?

en.focus: Even in the deepest sorrow and despair, we can still turn to God, for He is sovereign over all.

questions.question: How did the elders and virgins react externally to the destruction of Jerusalem?
options: They wore festive clothes and tried to flee
They sat on the ground in silence, with dust on their heads
They cursed their enemies and called for vengeance
They sang and danced, celebrating a new beginning
questions.explanation: The elders sat on the ground in silence with dust on their heads, and the virgins bowed their heads to the ground, showing extreme grief and humiliation.

questions.question: According to the passage, what was a significant reason for Jerusalem's tragic situation?
options: The overwhelming power and cunning of the enemies
The prophets spoke false and misleading prophecies
The people did not worship God enough
God's love and protection for Israel were insufficient
questions.explanation: The text states that the prophets saw false and misleading visions and did not expose the people's iniquity, leading to their captivity and tragic state.

questions.question: What was the reaction of those who passed by Jerusalem?
options: They expressed sympathy and pity for Jerusalem
They scoffed, hissed, clapped their hands, and shook their heads
They feared God's power and remained silent
They felt afraid and quickly left
questions.explanation: All who passed by clapped their hands, scoffed, and shook their heads at Jerusalem, saying, 'Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth?'

questions.question: The phrase 'the LORD has done what he purposed' is mentioned repeatedly. What important truth does this reveal to us?
options: God's love and mercy are limited
Humans can easily change God's will
God's judgment on His people is just and faithful, and His plans will ultimately be accomplished
Everything happened by chance, without God's intervention
questions.explanation: The text emphasizes that all this was purposed by the LORD, indicating that God's judgment is not arbitrary but flows from His righteous character and faithful word, and what He has declared will come to pass.

en.reflection: Are there experiences in your life that bring you deep sorrow or despair? How do you perceive God's role in these experiences?
reflectionOptions: Acknowledge my grief and pour out my heart to God
Seek God's Word for comfort and guidance
Remind myself of God's sovereignty, even in pain, and trust Him
en.prayer: Lord, when my heart is overwhelmed with sorrow and despair, please help me. I know You are a sovereign God, and even in pain I cannot understand, Your will is good and righteous. Comfort me, guide me, and enable me to continue trusting You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to pour out your heart's sorrow or confusion to God, believing He hears you.

en.theme: Crying Out to God in Anguish
en.focus: Even in the deepest pain, we can pour out our hearts to God, trusting Him to hear and show mercy.

questions.question: In verse 18, to whom does the prophet appeal to cry out to the Lord?
options: The walls of Judah
The people of Israel
The inhabitants of Jerusalem
The kings of the nations
questions.explanation: The prophet calls on the walls of Daughter Zion (representing Jerusalem and Judah) to cry out to the Lord.

questions.type: Observe the content of the prayer
questions.question: In verse 19, at what time does the prophet urge people to pour out their hearts to the Lord?
options: In the morning
At noon
In the evening
At the beginning of the night watches and throughout the night
questions.explanation: The prophet urges people to rise and cry out in the night, at the beginning of the night watches, and to pour out their hearts to the Lord.

questions.question: What does the prophet ask the Lord to look and see?
options: The wealth and comfort of the people
The suffering and destitution of the people
The military strength of the people
The people's faithfulness to idols
questions.explanation: The prophet asks the Lord to look and see the suffering, such as the children and women being consumed by the enemy.

questions.question: Despite the immense suffering and destruction, how does this passage remind us of God's character?
options: God is distant and unconcerned with human suffering
God is unable to comprehend human pain
God is one who can be called upon and trusted even in desperation
God only punishes sin and shows no compassion
questions.explanation: Even in deep anguish, the prophet calls out to God, trusting that God will look and show mercy, indicating that God is one who can be called upon and trusted even in desperate times.

en.reflection: What is the most painful or despairing thing in your life right now? Are you willing to pour out your heart to God about it?
reflectionOptions: Pour out my anxieties to God
Repent of my weakness and sin
Seek help from brothers and sisters
en.prayer: Lord, my heart is sometimes heavy with pain and despair. Please help me to pour out my heart to You at the beginning of the night watches, and indeed at any time. Look upon my suffering, I pray, and show me Your mercy. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, find a quiet moment to honestly pour out one burden or pain in your heart to God, trusting that He hears.

en.theme: Hope in God's Steadfast Love Amidst Suffering
en.focus: Even in the deepest suffering, we can look to God’s compassion and faithfulness, for His mercies never come to an end.

questions.question: How does the poet describe his suffering?
options: Struck by the rod of God’s wrath
Besieged by enemy armies
Punished for his own sins
Bedridden with illness
questions.explanation: The poet begins by describing himself as the one who has seen affliction under the rod of God’s wrath.

questions.question: What metaphors does the poet use to describe his immense pain?
options: Torn by a lion, caught in a snare
Covered in darkness, crushed by burdens
Walled in by stones, bound by chains
Bitten by snakes, swallowed by floods
questions.explanation: The poet feels like a bear lying in wait or a lion in ambush, and like one caught in a net, describing his pain and despair.

questions.question: Why does the poet not completely despair despite such profound suffering?
options: He believes his own strength can overcome anything
He knows suffering is just a temporary illusion
He still holds onto hope in God's compassion and faithfulness
He receives comfort and help from friends
questions.explanation: Despite describing great pain, the poet acknowledges that the LORD’s steadfast love never ceases and His mercies never come to an end, which gives him hope.

questions.question: When you are at a low point in life, what reminder can this passage offer you?
options: Focus on your feelings and don't seek God
Remember that God is just and His mercies never end
Suffering is God's punishment, so give up completely
Only by your own strength can you overcome difficulties
questions.explanation: This passage reminds us that even in the deepest pain, we should look to God's compassion and faithfulness, for His mercies never come to an end.

en.reflection: What 'affliction' in your life today causes you pain and despair? How will you choose to look to God's compassion in it?
reflectionOptions: Pray for strength in your difficult situation
Meditate on God's promises for comfort
Share with a trusted brother/sister for prayer
en.prayer: Lord, my heart sometimes feels pain and loneliness like the poet's. Please remind me that Your steadfast love never ceases and Your mercies never come to an end. Help me to look to You in my suffering and hold onto Your faithful promises. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take one minute today to quietly pour out your deepest pain to God and meditate on: 'But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope.' (Lamentations 3:21)

en.theme: The LORD's Great Love Never Ends
en.focus: Even in the deepest suffering, we can find comfort and hope in God's faithfulness and compassion.

questions.question: What does the prophet Jeremiah recall when remembering his affliction and wandering?
options: His former wealth
His lost health
His suffering and bitter gall
His glorious past
questions.explanation: Jeremiah recalls his suffering and bitter gall when remembering his affliction and wandering, which caused him great anguish.

questions.question: Amidst memories of deep suffering, what phrase does Jeremiah use to express a turning point of hope?
options: “I will overcome all this”
“Yet this I call to mind and therefore I have hope”
“God has forsaken me”
“My strength is utterly gone”
questions.explanation: After recalling his bitter memories, Jeremiah says, 'Yet this I call to mind and therefore I have hope,' indicating his shift towards hope.

questions.question: Jeremiah's hope is primarily based on which attributes of God?
options: God's strict judgment
God's unpredictability
God's unfailing love, compassion, and faithfulness
God's demands on humanity
questions.explanation: Jeremiah's hope is rooted in the LORD’s great love that never ends, His compassions that never fail, and His great faithfulness.

questions.question: When facing difficulties and distress in our lives, how does this passage encourage us to respond?
options: Complain about circumstances and abandon all hope
Rely solely on our own strength to solve problems
Wait steadfastly for the LORD, trusting in His love and compassion
Seek human help without considering God at all
questions.explanation: The passage encourages us to wait for the LORD, even in distress, trusting in His unchanging love and compassion, for He is our portion.

en.reflection: Is there a situation in your life right now where you feel distressed or discouraged? How can you apply the LORD's unfailing love and compassion to it?
reflectionOptions: Wait patiently for God in hardship
Pour out my heart to God
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your great love never ends, and Your compassions never fail. When I am in distress, please help me fix my eyes on Your faithfulness, so that I may have hope. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a minute to meditate on 'The LORD’s great love never ends; His mercies never cease. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!' (Lamentations 3:22–23).

en.focus: In times of suffering, God calls His people to examine their ways, return to Him, and wait in faith for His compassion.

questions.question: What does the author urge the people to do at the beginning of this passage?
options: Build stronger walls
Seek new allies
Examine their ways and test their actions
Curse their enemies
questions.explanation: The passage opens with a call to 'examine our ways and test them, and let us return to the LORD.'

questions.question: What does the author confess in their prayer?
options: They are more righteous than other nations
They have never sinned
They have rebelled against God, but He has not forgiven
They have rebelled against God, and He has not forgiven them
questions.explanation: The author confesses, 'We have sinned and rebelled; you have not forgiven.' This shows an acknowledgment of their sin, but also the apparent lack of forgiveness from God in their suffering.

questions.question: Despite the suffering, why does the author still hold onto hope?
options: Because they trust in their own strength
Because they see their enemies defeated
Because the LORD’s great love never ends, and His compassions never fail
Because other nations are coming to their aid
questions.explanation: Although this passage describes deep suffering, the broader context of Lamentations 3 emphasizes that the LORD's love and compassion are unfailing, which forms the basis of his hope.
questions.evidence: Lamentations 3:22-23 (This verse is contextual, but crucial for understanding the author's hope)

questions.question: What does this passage remind us to do when facing difficulties today?
options: We can complain to God and do nothing else
We should first examine our hearts and actions, then turn back to God
We should only focus on our feelings and ignore God's will
Difficulties are proof of God's punishment, so there's no need to seek Him anymore
questions.explanation: The passage calls for the people to examine their ways and return to the LORD, reminding us to reflect on our relationship with God during times of hardship.

en.reflection: In what area of your life does God most want you to examine and turn back to Him today?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your unfailing love and never-ending compassion. Please help me, when facing life's challenges, to constantly examine my ways, confess my transgressions, and sincerely turn back to You. May my heart seek only You, and patiently wait for Your salvation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to quietly reflect and either write down or tell God one specific area where you need to turn back to Him.

en.theme: Crying Out and Hoping in Affliction
en.focus: Even in the deepest pain, we can find hope in God's faithfulness and continue to cry out to Him.

questions.question: In his extreme distress, what did the enemies do to the psalmist?
options: Attacked him with schemes
Threw him into a pit
Mocked him with words
Stole his possessions
questions.explanation: The enemies “hunted me down like a bird, without cause” and “threw stones at me”.

questions.question: How did God respond when the psalmist cried out to Him?
options: Immediately removed all suffering
Hid His face and did not listen
Heard the prayer and comforted him
Commanded the enemies to stop persecution
questions.explanation: When the psalmist called out, God heard and told him, “Do not fear!”

questions.question: How does this passage describe God's justice?
options: God immediately judges all evildoers
God will plead His people’s cause and repay them
God does not intervene in worldly sins
God's justice is only expressed through mercy
questions.explanation: The psalmist trusts that God will “plead my cause” and “repay them according to the work of their hands”.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage you when you are in distress?
options: I can rely on my own strength to solve problems
I can boldly pour out my pain and needs to God
I should wait for circumstances to improve before seeking God
I do not need to seek help from anyone
questions.explanation: Despite his desperate situation, the psalmist cried out to God, trusting that God would hear and plead his cause. This encourages us to pour out our hearts to God in any distress.

en.reflection: Is there a difficult situation or injustice in your life right now that you need to pour out to God?
en.prayer: Faithful Lord, thank You for hearing my prayers in my suffering, drawing near to me, and telling me, “Do not fear.” Help me to fix my eyes on Your justice and love, even in the darkest moments. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to pour out one burden or injustice in your heart to God, trusting that He hears you.

en.theme: The Cost of Sin and God's Mercy
en.focus: When people stray from God, sin brings profound and painful consequences, yet God's ultimate mercy and justice will still be revealed.

questions.question: After the siege and destruction of Jerusalem, what happened to the luster of gold?
options: It became even more radiant
It lost its luster and became dim
It was stolen by the enemies
It was buried underground
questions.explanation: The passage describes how the once gleaming gold lost its luster and became dim.

questions.question: What stark contrast is described regarding the nobles and children of Jerusalem after the siege?
options: They became stronger and wiser
They went from abundance to poverty, from being cherished to despised
They went from slavery to freedom
They went from health to sickness
questions.explanation: The precious nobles and children were now regarded as clay pots, their lives debased, even worse off than wild dogs in the field.

questions.question: How does this passage describe Jerusalem's suffering, especially when compared to the destruction of Sodom?
options: Jerusalem's sin was lighter than Sodom's, and its suffering less
Jerusalem's destruction was quicker and more brutal than Sodom's
Jerusalem's destruction was due to lack of food, Sodom's due to fire
Sodom's sin was more severe than Jerusalem's, but the suffering was similar
questions.explanation: The text states that Jerusalem's destruction and suffering were quicker than Sodom's, not inflicted by 'human hands.' This implies the thoroughness and brutality of its destruction.

questions.question: What is the main lesson this passage teaches us about sin and judgment?
options: As long as we are wealthy, we will not suffer
God's people, when they sin, will also face severe consequences, sometimes even exceeding those of other nations
As long as we pray diligently, we can avoid all disasters
God's judgment is only for other nations, not for His people
questions.explanation: The passage clearly reveals that even God's chosen people, when they turn away from Him and disobey Him, will face extremely severe judgment and suffering, sometimes even more so than other nations.

en.reflection: Today's scripture reminds us of the profound consequences of sin. In your life, are there any hidden sins that you need to ask God to reveal, which you need to repent of?
reflectionOptions: Ask God to show me unseen sins
Confess to God and seek forgiveness
en.prayer: Loving Heavenly Father, today's scripture shows me the pain and destruction that sin brings. Please illuminate me and reveal any hidden sins in my life, so that I may genuinely repent before You. Forgive me, and help me to turn away from sin and follow You more closely. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment today to ask God to reveal any sin in your heart that needs repentance, and then confess it to Him immediately.

en.theme: The Bitter Fruit of Sin and God's Judgment
en.focus: When God's judgment comes, His people bear the consequences of their sin, yet God's sovereignty remains over all.

questions.question: Verse 11 states that the LORD has fully poured out His what, igniting a fire in Zion?
options: Wrath
Love
Grace
Mercy
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that the LORD has poured out His 'fierce wrath' and 'anger,' kindling a fire in Zion.

questions.question: According to verse 13, who was identified as the primary reason for Jerusalem's punishment?
options: Foreign enemies
The women of the city
The sins of her prophets and priests
The poor people
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states, 'This happened because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests.'

questions.question: From this passage, where is the deepest despair of the people of Judah evident when facing their suffering?
options: Losing wealth and status
Hoping for Egypt to save them
Discovering that their trusted allies and king could not help
Being unable to rebuild city walls
questions.explanation: The text describes their 'eyes failed,' looking for a nation that could not save them (Egypt), and mourning their anointed king being captured, indicating that all their trusted sources of help had failed.

questions.question: What important reminder does this passage bring to us?
options: We should rely completely on human help
Sin will not have any consequences
God's judgment on sin is real and thorough; we should be vigilant and repent
Having a strong army guarantees victory
questions.explanation: The passage vividly portrays God's judgment on Jerusalem's wickedness and its tragic consequences, reminding us of the seriousness of sin and the necessity of repentance.

en.reflection: Today's scripture reminds us of the seriousness of sin. Is there any hidden sin you need to confess to God and seek His forgiveness and help for?
reflectionOptions: Confess and give up a bad habit
en.prayer: Lord, today's scripture shows me the terrible consequences of sin and Your righteous judgment against it. Please examine my heart, and if there is any hidden sin, illuminate it so I may genuinely repent. Help me not to rely on human help, but to look solely to Your salvation and mercy. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Quietly reflect on a sin you've recently committed or one that has been troubling you. Confess it to God and ask for His forgiveness and help to overcome it.

en.theme: The End of Pride and the Hope of Humility
en.focus: God's sovereignty is revealed in His judgment of Edom and His promise of restoration for Zion.

questions.question: Who is singled out to be put to shame despite their joy and gladness?
options: Babylon
Egypt
Edom
Assyria
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that the people of Edom will be put to shame despite their joy and gladness.

questions.question: What is the contrasting fate described for Edom and Zion (God's people) in Lamentations 4:21–22?
options: Edom will prosper forever, while Zion will suffer eternally
Edom's iniquity will be pardoned, while Zion's will be increased
Edom will be punished, while Zion's iniquity will be pardoned
Both Edom and Zion will face complete destruction
questions.explanation: The passage prophesies that Edom will be punished by God, while Zion's iniquity will be pardoned, and she will no longer be exiled.

questions.question: What important message does this passage convey about God's character?
options: God is indifferent to His people
God is only concerned with punishment, not forgiveness
God is a righteous judge and a merciful forgiver
God's love is unconditional, and He will not punish any sin
questions.explanation: The passage prophesies God's judgment on Edom, showing His righteousness, and promises forgiveness for Zion, revealing His compassion and faithfulness.

questions.question: What can we learn from this passage today?
options: We should gloat over the misfortunes of others
Being God's people means we don't need to repent for our sins
To be wary of pride and to trust in God's justice and mercy
Worldly suffering is random and unrelated to God's actions
questions.explanation: Edom's pride and downfall warn us against arrogance, while Zion's hope in God's forgiveness encourages us to trust in God's character.

en.reflection: Have you ever gloated over someone else's struggles or been proud of your own circumstances? How does this passage remind you to be humble and trust God?
reflectionOptions: Seek God's mercy for your own or others' suffering
Deepen your trust in God's justice and forgiveness
en.prayer: Righteous and merciful Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Your character in this passage. Forgive me for times I have been proud or self-righteous, forgetting my own weaknesses. Help me to always humble myself before You, trust in Your righteous judgment, and experience Your forgiving grace more deeply. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for someone you know who is facing challenges, asking God to show them mercy, and remind yourself not to be proud of your own situation.

en.theme: Crying Out for God's Mercy in Distress
en.focus: Even in the deepest suffering, we can pour out our pain to God and seek His mercy and restoration.

questions.question: What does the author of Lamentations ask God to do at the beginning of chapter 5?
options: Completely punish their enemies
Bring justice quickly
Remember and look on our disgrace
Grant them more wealth
questions.explanation: The author begins by pleading with God to remember their plight and witness the disgrace and suffering they endure.

questions.question: What specific hardships did the people experience in their daily lives after the captivity, as described in the passage?
options: Lost all relatives and became isolated
Their houses were occupied by foreigners, and they had to pay for water and wood
Suddenly suffered an earthquake, and the city became ruins
Were afflicted by disease with no one to heal them
questions.explanation: The text states that their inheritance has been turned over to foreigners, their homes to aliens, and they had to pay for water and wood.

questions.question: In the midst of great suffering, where does the author ultimately place his hope?
options: In his own ability to find a way out
In the compassion of other nations
In God re-establishing their kingdom
In God reigning forever, with His throne enduring to all generations
questions.explanation: Despite profound suffering, the author proclaims God's eternal sovereignty and His throne enduring to all generations, indicating that his ultimate hope rests in God's unchanging nature.

questions.question: From Lamentations chapter 5, what do we learn about how we can respond to God in suffering?
options: Complain about God's injustice and turn away from Him
Silently endure everything without crying out to God
Pour out our pain and difficulties to God in detail, asking for His grace to turn us back
Focus only on our own abilities and try to save ourselves
questions.explanation: The author clearly states their distress to God and pleads for God to remember, look, and restore them, showing that even in despair, we can confide in God and seek His mercy.

en.reflection: What is your greatest difficulty or worry in life right now? How are you willing to honestly pour it out to God today?
en.prayer: Eternal Lord, Your throne endures to all generations. Please remember the suffering I am experiencing and look upon my difficulties. I bring all my burdens and worries before You, asking You to turn me back with Your mercy and renew my days. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment and, in your own words, pour out your deepest worries and difficulties to God, as you would speak to a loving Father.

en.focus: God reveals His immeasurable glory and power to His people in unexpected places.

questions.question: Where was the prophet Ezekiel when he saw the vision at the beginning of the book?
options: In the temple in Jerusalem
In the king's palace in Babylon
By the Chebar Canal in the land of the Babylonians
On the banks of the Nile in Egypt
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that Ezekiel was among the exiles by the Chebar Canal in the land of the Babylonians when he saw the vision.

questions.question: What were the four faces of each living creature in the vision?
options: A human, a lion, an ox, an eagle
A human, a leopard, a bear, an eagle
A human, a dog, a horse, an eagle
An angel, a cherub, a seraph, a living creature
questions.explanation: Each living creature had four faces: a human face in front, a lion face on the right, an ox face on the left, and an eagle face on the back.

questions.type: Observe the movement of the creatures
questions.question: What was a distinctive characteristic of how these living creatures moved?
options: They turned their bodies slowly
They only moved in one direction
They went straight forward without turning
They frequently stopped to rest
questions.explanation: The creatures “went straight forward; they did not turn as they moved,” indicating the directness and steadfastness of their movement under God's guidance.

questions.question: What is the primary message about God conveyed by Ezekiel's vision?
options: God is present only in the temple
God's power is limited and cannot intervene in the exiles' situation
God's glory and sovereignty transcend everything, and He is with His people even in exile
God has completely abandoned His people
questions.explanation: In the desperate context of exile, God reveals His transcendent glory and sovereignty to Ezekiel, showing that He has not abandoned His people but remains in control.

en.reflection: In your life today, do you sense God revealing His presence and guidance to you in unique ways?
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You that You are the Lord above all, and Your glory and presence are not limited by any circumstances. Open my eyes and heart, that I may know You more deeply each day and experience Your real guidance and comfort. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a minute today to quietly reflect: How is God making His presence known to me in my circumstances?

en.focus: Ezekiel's vision reveals God's transcendence, sovereignty, and glory, assuring His presence with His people even in exile.

questions.question: What was beneath the four living creatures in Ezekiel's vision?
options: An altar of gold
A burning furnace
Wheels on the ground
A flowing river
questions.explanation: The text clearly states there were wheels on the ground beside the living creatures.

questions.question: How were the wheels described in appearance?
options: Like Pharaoh's chariots
Like water mill wheels
Like the color of beryl
Like the appearance of jewels
questions.explanation: The appearance and structure of the wheels were like the color of beryl.

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of how the wheels and living creatures moved in Ezekiel's vision?
options: They moved independently without connection
They could only go straight, not turn
They moved wherever the Spirit went, in unison
They moved randomly with no fixed pattern
questions.explanation: Wherever the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

questions.question: What is the climax of the entire vision?
options: The living creatures making a loud sound
A brilliant rainbow in the sky
A throne with the likeness of God upon it
The wheels shining with fiery light
questions.explanation: Above the expanse over the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire, and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance, which was the appearance of the glory of the LORD.

en.reflection: How does this vision of God's glory encourage you in times of uncertainty or difficulty in your life?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me that God is sovereign and present with me
It motivates me to seek God's will more deeply
It helps me release worries and trust God's guidance
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for revealing Your glory and sovereignty through Ezekiel's vision. Please help me to look to You in all circumstances, trusting that Your Spirit is guiding my life. May I always feel Your presence and find strength and comfort in it. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to meditate on God as the all-controlling, glorious King who is with you, even in difficulties.

en.focus: God calls Ezekiel to deliver His message to a rebellious people, empowering him to fulfill his mission.

questions.question: How does God address Ezekiel at the beginning of the passage?
options: My servant
Son of man
Prophet of Israel
My chosen one
questions.explanation: God addresses Ezekiel as 'son of man,' emphasizing his humanity and frailty while also signifying his role as God's representative on earth.

questions.type: Observe the people God sends him to
questions.question: What kind of people is Ezekiel sent to confront?
options: A humble people seeking God
A devout people following the law
A rebellious and stiff-necked people
A people full of faith in God
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly describes these people as 'rebellious,' 'unyielding and hardened in spirit.'

questions.question: What is God's mission for Ezekiel?
options: To lead the people to repentance and establish a new kingdom
To speak God's words to the people, whether they listen or not
To perform signs and wonders to prove God's power
To record visions for future generations
questions.explanation: God explicitly tells Ezekiel to speak His words to them, regardless of whether they choose to listen.

questions.question: What did God give Ezekiel to help him face his difficult mission?
options: An army to protect him
The ability to speak with eloquence
A heart as hard as diamond
Authority to change circumstances at will
questions.explanation: God made Ezekiel's forehead as hard as a diamond, harder than their foreheads, so he could stand firm against the rebellious people.

en.reflection: In what area of your life or challenging situation do you need God's strength and courage to face today?
reflectionOptions: Speaking truth to family or friends
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for calling me and empowering me to fulfill Your will. Help me, like Ezekiel, to faithfully speak Your words and be strong and courageous in You, even when facing difficulties and opposition. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for someone in your life whom you find difficult to communicate with or serve, asking God for wisdom and courage.

en.focus: God calls Ezekiel to be a watchman for the house of Israel, faithfully delivering His word to a rebellious people.

questions.question: What is the first instruction God gives to Ezekiel?
options: You shall speak My words to them
Arise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you
Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel
Go to the exiles, to your people, and speak to them
questions.explanation: God first tells Ezekiel, “Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak My words to them.”

questions.question: How does God prepare Ezekiel to face the rebellious people?
options: He grants him a life of material wealth
He makes his forehead harder than their foreheads and his spirit more unyielding than theirs
He gives him eloquent speech to persuade everyone
He provides him with a strong army for protection
questions.explanation: God promises Ezekiel strength to confront the people's stubbornness, making his “forehead harder than their foreheads and his spirit more unyielding than theirs.”

questions.question: What is Ezekiel's responsibility as a watchman?
options: To bless the people and protect them from disaster
To speak God’s word, warn the wicked to turn, and encourage the righteous
To lead the people in revolt against their enemies and rebuild their homes
To intercede for the people so they are spared punishment
questions.explanation: The watchman's duty is to hear God's word and deliver it to the people, warning the wicked and encouraging the righteous.

questions.question: How does Ezekiel’s experience remind us of the importance of faithfulness to God’s word today?
options: Once we hear God’s word, we don’t need to share it
We should only speak God’s word to those who are willing to listen
We have a responsibility to faithfully deliver God’s message, regardless of the response
God’s word is too complex for everyone to understand
questions.explanation: Ezekiel was called to proclaim God’s word whether the people listened or not. This reminds us that as Christians, we also have a responsibility to faithfully share God’s word, even when it's challenging.

en.reflection: Is there a message God wants you to deliver in your life, whether to an individual or a group, that you have been hesitant or found difficult?
reflectionOptions: Share the Gospel with a family member
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for choosing me and giving me Your precious Word. Help me to be a courageous and faithful watchman for You, delivering Your message in due season to those who need to hear it, whether it is admonition or comfort. May Your word in my mouth be life and hope. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for a friend or family member who needs to hear God's word, and ask God for wisdom and courage to speak to them at the right time.

en.focus: God uses symbolic actions to reveal the coming judgment and consequences of disobedience to His people, calling them to repentance.

questions.question: What did God command Ezekiel to use to represent the city of Jerusalem?
options: A piece of wood
A brick
A stone
A clay tablet
questions.explanation: God commanded Ezekiel to take a brick and engrave the city of Jerusalem on it.

questions.question: For how many days was Ezekiel commanded to lie on his left side to bear the iniquity of the house of Israel?
options: 40 days
150 days
390 days
520 days
questions.explanation: God commanded Ezekiel to lie on his left side for 390 days to bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.

questions.question: What main message did Ezekiel's series of symbolic actions convey?
options: God would give abundant blessings to Israel and Judah
God's judgment on Israel and Judah was serious and real
God would immediately forgive all the sins of Israel and Judah
God wanted Israel and Judah to attack neighboring nations
questions.explanation: Ezekiel was commanded to perform a series of difficult and unusual symbolic actions (like lying on his side, eating limited food) to foreshadow the coming judgment of siege, famine, and exile for Jerusalem.

questions.question: Ultimately, what response did God desire from His people through these severe prophecies of judgment?
options: To continue their own way of life
To be fearful but refuse to change
To recognize their sin and repent to God
To question God's justice and power
questions.explanation: God's purpose in prophesying judgment was to awaken His people to their rebellion and sin, leading them to repent and seek His mercy.
questions.evidence: Ezekiel 4:17 ("They will lack food; they will be appalled at each other and waste away because of their sin" implies the suffering of judgment was to make them realize their iniquity.)

en.reflection: When God, through circumstances or Scripture, reminds you of areas in your life that need adjustment or turning back to Him, how do you respond?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being a just God whose judgment aims to awaken us. Please grant me a humble and teachable heart so that when I face difficulties or hear Your reminders, I can timely examine my life and repent, turning back to You. May my life bring glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to quietly reflect on anything God might be nudging you about recently that requires seeking His heart, and pray about it.

en.focus: Even in severe judgment, God preserves a remnant for restoration among His people.

questions.question: What did God instruct Ezekiel to use to symbolize the inhabitants of Jerusalem?
options: Clay
Hair and beard
Stones
Wood
questions.explanation: God commanded Ezekiel to shave his hair and beard, using these to symbolize the fate of Jerusalem's inhabitants.

questions.question: How did Ezekiel dispose of the symbolic hair to foretell the fate of Jerusalem's inhabitants?
options: Burned it all
Chopped some with a sword, burned some, scattered some to the wind, and kept a few strands in his garment
Threw it all into a river
Buried it all in the ground
questions.explanation: Ezekiel divided the hair into three parts: one part burned, one chopped with a sword, one scattered to the wind, and a few strands kept in his garment, foreshadowing different outcomes.

questions.question: What was the main reason for God's severe judgment on Jerusalem?
options: They did not offer sacrifices on time
They failed to build a grand temple
They rebelled against God’s ordinances and statutes, doing more evil than the surrounding nations
They did not form alliances with other nations
questions.explanation: God judged Jerusalem because they rebelled against His ordinances and statutes, doing more evil than the surrounding nations, and defiled His sanctuary.

questions.question: Despite the severe judgment, what glimmer of hope did God provide in this passage?
options: He promised to rebuild the temple immediately
He promised more wealth for the survivors
He would preserve a small remnant, keeping them in His garment
He would make a covenant with all foreign nations
questions.explanation: God mentioned keeping a few strands of hair in his garment, symbolizing the preservation of a remnant for hope.

en.reflection: In God’s severe judgment, He still preserves grace and a remnant. What reminder and comfort does this bring to you?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me of God's justice and holiness
It comforts me that God never completely abandons His people
It prompts me to take my faith more seriously
en.prayer: Righteous and holy God, thank You for reminding me of Your majesty and faithfulness through the message of judgment in Ezekiel. Help me to always live with reverence and to obey Your will. I also offer thanks for Your preserved grace and hope. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to reflect on God's grace and mercy in your life, and give thanks for it.

en.focus: God’s judgment on Israel stems from their idolatry, but its ultimate purpose is for them to know Him.

questions.question: To whom was Ezekiel instructed to speak, and what was the message about?
options: Kings of Judah, rebuking their injustice
Mountains of Israel, declaring judgment on idolatry
People of Babylon, prophesying their downfall
Pharaoh of Egypt, warning him of his pride
questions.explanation: God’s word came to Ezekiel, instructing him to speak to 'the mountains of Israel,' proclaiming impending judgment.

questions.type: Observe the objects and reasons for judgment
questions.question: According to this passage, why was Israel to be judged?
options: For not observing the Sabbath
For paying tribute to neighboring nations
For worshipping idols on every high hill and under every green tree
For not listening to the prophets
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly emphasizes that the reason for judgment was Israel's idolatry on every high hill, mountain, green tree, and thick oak.

questions.question: What is the ultimate purpose of God's judgment on Israel?
options: To utterly destroy Israel without mercy
So that they may know that He is the LORD
To show the nations Israel's weakness
To make them reflect on their cultural traditions
questions.explanation: The purpose of God's judgment is for the people of Israel to 'know that I am the LORD.'

questions.question: What important truth can we learn from this passage?
options: Only gentiles worship idols
God tolerates His people's idolatry
God is holy and must judge any form of idolatry
We only need to worship God in church
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that God does not tolerate idolatry among His people. His holiness demands judgment on sin, and through it, He calls His people back to Him.

en.reflection: Are there any people, things, or pursuits in your life that have taken God's place and become an 'idol'?
reflectionOptions: A craving for comfort and ease
en.prayer: Holy Lord, thank You for being a righteous judge and a loving God. Please enlighten me and remove any idols in my heart that have taken Your place. Help me to treasure You above all else and worship You all my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some quiet time today to reflect on areas where you might be valuing people or things more than God, and repent before Him.

en.focus: When judgment arrives, only God provides true peace and protection, not worldly possessions or idols.

questions.question: What recurring message does God emphasize in Ezekiel chapter 7?
options: His people will gain more wealth
His people will live in peace with their enemies
The end has come, and judgment is imminent
His people will build a magnificent temple
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly declares, “The end has come,” “An end has come,” and “Your end is coming,” signifying the approaching judgment.

questions.question: How will people regard their silver and gold when judgment comes?
options: They will hide their silver and gold for future use
They will throw their silver and gold into the streets as defiled
They will use their silver and gold to bribe their enemies
They will use their silver and gold to buy food
questions.explanation: The text states that on the day of judgment, people will consider their silver and gold defiled and throw them into the streets, because these cannot save them.

questions.question: What attributes of God are revealed concerning His sinful people in Ezekiel 7?
options: He is an indifferent God who does not care for His people
He is faithful to His covenant and also just in judging sin
He is always immediately forgiving and never holds people accountable
He values sacrifices more than actions
questions.explanation: God declares His judgment through Ezekiel, showing that He will by no means clear the guilty, and He faithfully carries out His warnings.

questions.question: What is the most significant reminder from this passage for us today?
options: We should strive to accumulate more wealth for future security
We should trust ourselves completely and not rely on God
We should revere God's justice and seek true peace and security in Him
We should ignore spiritual warnings and pursue immediate pleasures
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that worldly wealth and idols are worthless in the face of judgment; true security is found only in turning to and fearing God.

en.reflection: In your life, is there anything you once mistakenly believed would bring security, but in reality, cannot withstand the 'end' in life?
en.prayer: Righteous Father, You are a holy and faithful God. Help me to always fear You and not build my security on the fleeting things of this world. May I look solely to You and find true peace and protection in You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a minute today to reflect on anything that is replacing God in your heart, and ask God to help you let it go.

en.theme: Witnessing God's Glory and Israel's Sin
en.focus: God reveals to Ezekiel the detestable practices of His people in the temple, demonstrating His justice and holiness, and His deep abhorrence of sin.

questions.question: Under what circumstances was the prophet Ezekiel brought to Jerusalem by the Spirit of God?
options: While he was preaching outside the city
While he was sitting in his house with the elders of Judah before him
While he was fasting and praying
While he was being pursued by enemies
questions.explanation: The text states that Ezekiel was sitting in his house with the elders of Judah before him when the Spirit lifted him to Jerusalem.

questions.question: What detestable idol did Ezekiel first see in the temple courtyard that provoked God's wrath?
options: An idol of Baal
An Asherah pole
The idol of jealousy
A golden calf
questions.explanation: The first idol Ezekiel saw is called 'the idol of jealousy,' indicating it directly challenged God's uniqueness and holiness.

questions.question: What is the core message of this passage?
options: God's glory had completely departed from the temple
The people's sinful acts were permitted by God
God clearly sees and is angered by the detestable things His people are doing in the temple
The prophet Ezekiel merely had a dream
questions.explanation: God led Ezekiel to witness various hidden idolatries and sins in the temple, revealing His awareness and indignation at His people's wickedness.

questions.question: How does this passage remind us about God's character?
options: God is loving, so He overlooks our sins
God is omniscient, He sees everything hidden in our hearts and actions
God only cares about temple worship, not personal life
God's anger at sin is temporary and will soon pass
questions.explanation: God revealing hidden abominations to Ezekiel emphasizes His omniscience and omnipotence, that He sees all, including our deepest motivations and actions.

en.reflection: The people of Israel in this passage were committing abominations in secret. Today, are there any 'secret places' in your life that you need to open up to God and repent of?
reflectionOptions: An inner attachment to an idol (e.g., money, power)
en.prayer: Almighty and all-knowing God, thank You for Your holiness and righteousness. You see all things. Please shine Your light into the hidden places of my life and reveal any sin that displeases You. Grant me a repentant heart and help me to turn to You, worshipping You alone. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time today reflecting and asking the Holy Spirit to reveal any 'secret places' in your life that need to be confessed and repented of before God.

en.focus: God's judgment is righteous when His people rebel, yet He preserves those who are faithful and revere Him.

questions.question: How many men did Ezekiel see being called to carry out judgment on Jerusalem?
options: Three men
Five men
Six men
Seven men
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that 'six men' came from the direction of the upper gate facing north, each with a weapon of destruction in his hand.

questions.question: On whose foreheads did God command the man clothed in linen to put a mark?
options: All residents of Jerusalem
Those who sigh and groan over all the abominations committed in the city
The priests and Levites
Those who had committed sins in the city
questions.explanation: The LORD commanded the man clothed in linen to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over all the abominations committed in the city, to protect them from judgment.

questions.question: Where did God command the slaughter to begin?
options: Outside the city walls
With the elders and officials
At the sanctuary
With the children and women
questions.explanation: The LORD commanded them to 'begin at My sanctuary,' indicating that judgment would first come upon the very place meant for God's worship.

questions.question: What primary attribute of God does this passage teach us?
options: God is only loving and never judges
God is righteous; He judges sin but also preserves the faithful
God only judges Gentiles, not His own people
God overlooks sin and will eventually forgive everyone
questions.explanation: This passage reveals God's righteousness; He carries out judgment on sin, but also preserves those who genuinely revere Him and grieve over sin.

en.reflection: Have you, like those who sighed and groaned, ever grieved over sin in your life or in your community? How does this remind you of God's justice and grace?
reflectionOptions: Pray for the sins of the church or nation
Trust more deeply in God's preservation
en.prayer: Righteous and holy God, I acknowledge that You are the One who searches hearts. Please forgive me for all the ways I have sinned against You. Grant me a heart that grieves over sin, so I may sigh and groan over my own and the sins around me. Thank You for Your grace and preservation even in judgment. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for one sin you are aware of (either your own or in society), asking God for mercy and change.

en.focus: Though God's glory temporarily departs from the temple, His presence and sovereignty remain in control.

questions.question: From which part of the temple did the prophet see the glory of God depart in the vision?
options: The inner court
The outer court
The threshold of the temple
The Most Holy Place
questions.explanation: The glory of the LORD first went up from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple before gradually leaving the temple.

questions.question: In the vision, what was the glory of God riding on as it departed?
options: A pillar of cloud
A pillar of fire
The wings of the cherubim
Wind and thunder
questions.explanation: The glory of the LORD ascended from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple and departed carried by the cherubim.

questions.question: What did the departure of God's glory from the temple signify for the Israelites at that time?
options: God had completely abandoned His people
God was judging His people, but His sovereignty and presence still had a deeper purpose
The Israelites were free to worship other gods as they pleased
The temple was no longer important
questions.explanation: While the departure of God's glory from the temple indicated judgment upon His people, the text also emphasizes that the movement of the cherubim and wheels was guided by the Spirit of God, showing that God remained in control and His presence was not entirely absent.

questions.question: From this passage, how should we understand God's presence?
options: God's presence is limited to physical temples or churches
God's presence is unchanging and will not depart due to human sin
God's presence may temporarily withdraw due to human rebellion, but His sovereignty and care never change
Humans can guarantee God's presence by doing good deeds
questions.explanation: God temporarily withdrew His glorious presence from the temple due to the sins of the Israelites, but He remained in control, guiding the movement of the cherubim and wheels, foreshadowing His ultimate plan for the restoration of His people.

en.reflection: In your life, are there any actions or attitudes that make your heart feel as though God's presence has 'departed'?
en.prayer: Lord, I confess that my heart sometimes deviates from You, causing me to lose a sense of Your presence. Please forgive me and turn me back to You. May my life be a dwelling place for Your glory, that Your Spirit may always work within me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time today in prayer, asking God to cleanse your heart and reinvite His glory to fill your life.

en.focus: Even in judgment, God faithfully promises to gather His people and give them new hearts and spirits.

questions.question: Who did the prophet Ezekiel see in his vision at the gate of the temple?
options: The elders and officials of Israel
Priests and Levites
Common people and foreigners
Sadducees and Pharisees
questions.explanation: Ezekiel saw seventy elders of Israel, and among them were Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, leaders of the people.

questions.question: What sins did God accuse these leaders of committing?
options: Greed for money and power
Setting up idols, plotting evil, and shedding innocent blood
Disobeying the law and not offering sacrifices
Intermarrying with foreigners
questions.explanation: God said they were plotting evil, making idols in the city, and shedding much innocent blood.

questions.question: In the passage, what attitude does the statement, 'This city is a pot, and we are the meat,' reflect in these leaders?
options: They believed they could protect the city from enemies
They longed for God's protection, like meat safely cooked in a pot
They believed they were safe within the city and would not be destroyed
They felt they were innocent victims
questions.explanation: This statement reflects their belief that they were safe in Jerusalem and would not be destroyed by the Babylonians. However, God declared that the slain were the 'meat,' and these wicked leaders would be driven from the city.

questions.question: After Pelatiah's death, what hope do Ezekiel's prayer and God's response offer us?
options: God will immediately stop all judgment and suffering
God will continue to punish all sinful people without forgiveness
Even in judgment, God will preserve hope and promise restoration for the remnant of His people
Human efforts in prayer can change God's plans
questions.explanation: Even when judgment came, Ezekiel prayed for the remnant of Israel, and God promised to gather them, give them new hearts and spirits, and remove their hearts of stone so they would obey Him.
