en.reflection: Is there a 'heart of stone' in your life that needs God to transform? How are you willing to respond to God's discipline and allow Him to give you a new heart and spirit?
reflectionOptions: Confess my sins and seek forgiveness
Diligently read Scripture and pray for God's will
Lay down pride and self-righteousness, repent humbly
en.prayer: Almighty God, I thank You that You are a righteous judge and a loving redeemer. Please examine my heart, remove every 'heart of stone' within me, and grant me a heart of flesh that obeys You and loves You. May my life glorify Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time before God today, asking Him to reveal areas in your life that need transformation, and pray over them.

en.theme: God Promises a New Heart and Spirit
en.focus: Even in exile, God faithfully promises to gather His people and give them new hearts and spirits.

questions.question: What did God say about those who remained in Jerusalem and mocked the exiles?
options: They would prosper forever
God would give them more land
God would drive them out of Jerusalem
They were God's true people
questions.explanation: God stated through Ezekiel that those remaining in Jerusalem would be driven out because of their wickedness.

questions.question: What did God promise the exiled Israelites?
options: They would return to Jerusalem immediately
God would be a sanctuary for them in their exile
They would receive new wealth
They could forget God's laws
questions.explanation: God promised that He Himself would be a temporary sanctuary for them among the nations where they were scattered.

questions.question: What does it mean for God to give His people a 'new heart' and a 'new spirit'?
options: God would make them more intelligent
God would transform their nature to enable them to obey Him
God would make them physically stronger
God would give them more time to decide whether to follow Him
questions.explanation: God promised to remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh, enabling them to obey His statutes and have a true relationship with Him.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage us in difficult circumstances today?
options: We can change all difficulties if we try hard enough
God is only with us when things are going well
God is with us and promises renewal even in hardships
We can rely on our own strength to get through everything
questions.explanation: Even in the despair of exile, God's promise to be a sanctuary and to give a new heart and spirit shows His presence and hope in all circumstances.

en.reflection: Are there times in your life when you feel exiled or lost? How does God reveal Himself as your sanctuary and promise a new heart and spirit to you today?
reflectionOptions: Desiring God to renew my heart and spirit
en.prayer: Faithful God, thank You that even when I feel lost or trapped, You are with me and act as my sanctuary. Please remove my heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh, so I may know You more deeply and obey You fully. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to reflect on how God is your 'sanctuary' in your current difficulties.

en.focus: Through Ezekiel's symbolic actions and messages, God foretold the impending exile and destruction of Jerusalem, reminding His people that His word would not fail.

questions.question: What specific action did God command Ezekiel to perform to foreshadow the fate of the house of Israel?
options: Build a miniature temple in the city
Carry baggage out through a hole dug in the wall
Shout messages of judgment at the city gate
Fast forty days and nights to intercede for the people
questions.explanation: God commanded Ezekiel to carry his baggage out through a hole in the wall, like an exile, symbolizing the impending exile of Jerusalem's inhabitants.

questions.question: Why did God instruct Ezekiel to perform these symbolic actions in broad daylight, before the eyes of the people?
options: To attract a larger crowd to hear his preaching
So the people would see with their own eyes and understand these were signs for them
To train Ezekiel's courage and faith
So these actions could be recorded for future generations
questions.explanation: God explicitly stated that these actions were to be a sign for the people, so they would see and understand what was coming upon them.

questions.question: What is the main message of Ezekiel chapter 12?
options: God will always protect Jerusalem and prevent its destruction
The people of Israel could avoid exile through their own efforts
God's judgment is real and will surely come to pass, even if people do not believe it
The prophet's predictions are false and should not be taken seriously
questions.explanation: This chapter emphasizes that God's word and prophecies are true and will certainly be fulfilled, and the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of its people are inevitable judgments, regardless of their belief.

questions.question: How should we respond to the certainty of God's word being fulfilled?
options: Ignore it, assuming it won't happen to us
Try to change our circumstances rather than ourselves
With reverence, obey and trust in God's word
Only believe the prophecies we find pleasant to hear
questions.explanation: Ezekiel reminds us that God's word is true and reliable. Therefore, we should receive it with reverence, obeying and trusting in His word, whether it be a promise or a warning.

en.reflection: Is there an area in your life where you need to remind yourself that God’s promises or warnings are real and will surely come to pass?
en.prayer: Almighty God, I thank You that Your word is true and reliable, never failing. Help me to receive every word from You with reverence and obedience. May I not only hear but also act upon it, for Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend five minutes today meditating on a Bible verse you've recently read, reminding yourself that God's word is true and powerful.

en.focus: God severely condemns false prophets who mislead His people with false messages and declares His intention to personally rescue His people.

questions.question: How does God address the false prophets at the beginning of the passage?
options: Shepherds of Israel
Foolish prophets
Priests of the nations
Lying philosophers
questions.explanation: God calls these prophets 'foolish prophets' because they follow their own spirit and speak visions they have not seen.

questions.type: Observe the actions of false prophets
questions.question: What image is used to describe the false prophecies?
options: Idols made of gold
A wall daubed with whitewash
A net woven with silk threads
A crown made of thorns
questions.explanation: The passage describes false prophets as those who daub a wall with whitewash, covering up its weaknesses, which will ultimately collapse in a storm.

questions.question: What is God's intention towards His people who have been misled by false prophets?
options: To let them continue to be deceived
To personally rescue them from the false prophets' hands
To command them to discern right from wrong themselves
To be disappointed and give up on them
questions.explanation: God declares that He will personally rescue His people from the hand of the false prophets, so they will no longer be misled.

questions.question: How does this passage remind us to discern truth today?
options: Only listen to those who preach good news
Rely on our own feelings and intuition
Test all teachings and prophecies against the Scriptures
Believe that the opinion of the majority is always right
questions.explanation: We must test all teachings and messages against God's Word, the Bible, to discern truth from falsehood.

en.reflection: In your life, what voices or messages do you need to carefully discern and test with God's Word?
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for being the God of truth, who does not allow falsehood to deceive Your people. Grant me wisdom to discern, so that I may test all voices and messages with Your Word and not be led astray by false teachings. May my heart follow You alone. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Read a short passage from the Bible today and meditate on its truth, allowing God's Word to be the standard in your heart.

en.focus: God calls His people to abandon their heart-idols and genuinely return to Him for life.

questions.question: What did the elders of Israel have in their hearts when they came before Ezekiel?
options: Reverence for God
Remorse for their sins
Their idols
A desire for wisdom
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that the elders had their idols set up in their hearts when they came to the prophet.

questions.question: How did God respond to the Israelites who harboured idols in their hearts but still came to inquire of Him?
options: He immediately granted their prayers
He remained silent to them
He answered them according to their many idols
He sent angels to instruct them
questions.explanation: God declared that for those who come to inquire of Him with idols in their hearts, He would answer them according to their many idols, meaning He would let them reap the consequences of their idolatry.

questions.question: Why did God deal severely with the Israelites who had idols in their hearts?
options: Because God detested them and wanted no relationship with them
To make them aware of their sin and to turn the house of Israel back from straying from God
To demonstrate His judgmental power to the nations
To punish them so they could never again draw near to God
questions.explanation: God explicitly stated His purpose was to take hold of the house of Israel, so they might realize their sin and turn back from their apostasy.

questions.question: What important reminder does this chapter offer us today?
options: God will hear our prayers as long as we attend church
God only cares about our external actions, not our inner heart
God demands that we genuinely forsake all idols that hinder our closeness to Him and turn to Him wholeheartedly
We can seek both God's help and worldly assistance when facing difficulties
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God values the purity of one's heart and genuine repentance, not merely outward inquiry.

en.reflection: Today, is there anything in your life that occupies a deep place in your heart, such that it has become an 'idol' between you and God?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being the God who searches hearts. Please shine Your light on me and reveal any idols that may exist in my heart. Help me to bravely remove them. May my heart be solely devoted to You, loving and serving You with all my being. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a few quiet minutes today asking the Holy Spirit to reveal any hidden idols in your heart, confess them to God, and ask for His help to let them go.

en.focus: Even in judgment, God preserves a remnant, revealing His justice and mercy, so that people may know His ways.

questions.question: When a land sins, what four 'severe judgments' does God say He will bring upon it?
options: Sword, famine, wild beasts, plague
Flood, earthquake, drought, locusts
War, slavery, disease, poverty
Fire, hail, darkness, pestilence
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that God will send the sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague as severe judgments.

questions.question: When God mentions that even righteous individuals like Noah, Daniel, and Job in the land could only save themselves, not others, what is repeatedly emphasized?
options: The unchanging nature of God's promises
The severity of sin
The importance of individual responsibility
The strictness of the law
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly stresses that these three righteous men could only save their own lives by their righteousness, implying the importance of individual accountability before God and the pervasive nature of sin preventing them from interceding for others.

questions.question: Why does God still leave a 'survivor' or remnant after inflicting such severe judgments?
options: To prove He cannot completely eradicate sin
So they can go preach the gospel in other nations
So their conduct and actions may comfort the people and make them know God's justice
He suddenly changes His mind about judgment
questions.explanation: God leaves a remnant so that their conduct and actions may be seen by those in exile, bringing comfort and demonstrating that God's judgments are just and well-deserved.

questions.question: How does today's passage help us understand God's justice and mercy?
options: God only brings judgment and never shows mercy
God preserves a remnant even in judgment, revealing His fairness and love
God will remove all judgment based on people's good deeds
God cares only for the righteous, not for sinners
questions.explanation: The passage clearly shows God's justice in His judgment of sin, but His mercy is also evident in preserving a remnant for His purposes, ultimately allowing the world to recognize His just and merciful ways.

en.reflection: Today’s passage reminds us that even in deep sin, God still has His plan and mercy. How do you view God's just judgment of sin, and how have you experienced His mercy in difficult times?
reflectionOptions: Confess my sins and seek God's forgiveness
Give thanks for God's mercy in my life
en.prayer: Righteous and merciful Lord, thank You for helping me understand Your attributes more deeply through Your Word today. I know You are a God who hates sin, yet Your mercy never abandons those who seek You. Help me to always live with reverence, turn away from sin, and live a life pleasing to You, so that others may know Your justice and love through me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Reflect on any areas in your life that need repentance, and spend a minute confessing them to God, asking for His forgiveness and guidance.

en.focus: God reminds His people that if they do not bear fruit, they are like a useless vine, destined for fire.

questions.question: What metaphor does God use to describe Jerusalem in this passage?
options: A tree of gold and silver
An olive tree
A vine
A cedar tree
questions.explanation: The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, using the metaphor of a vine to describe Jerusalem.

questions.question: Compared to other trees, what characteristic of vine wood is emphasized in this passage?
options: It is exceptionally hard, suitable for building
It is fragrant, suitable for incense
It is very soft, easy to carve
It is useless, only fit for fuel
questions.explanation: The text states, “Is wood from the vine ever used to make anything? Is it used to make a peg to hang anything on?” highlighting its uselessness.

questions.question: What fate does the parable of the burned vine foreshadow for Jerusalem and its inhabitants?
options: Blessing and prosperity
Worship by foreign nations
Divine judgment and destruction
Elevation to leadership among nations
questions.explanation: God clearly states that just as the vine is consumed by fire, the inhabitants of Jerusalem will also be consumed by fire, which is His judgment.

questions.question: What reminder does this passage offer for our lives today?
options: Outward appearance is sufficient
God values our bearing of fruit more
Material wealth is more important than spiritual life
Having religious rituals is enough
questions.explanation: This passage reminds us that God does not just value our existence, but more importantly, whether we bear fruit that aligns with our lives; otherwise, we are like a useless vine facing judgment.

en.reflection: In what areas do you need to strive harder today to bear fruit pleasing to God, instead of being a 'useless vine'?
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for using the parable of the vine to remind me that You value the fruit my life bears. Help me not to have only an outward show of godliness, but to live a life worthy of You. May my words and actions always bring glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Consider how you can concretely demonstrate one aspect of the 'fruit of the Spirit' (Galatians 5:22-23) today.

en.theme: God's Love and Pain for Jerusalem
en.focus: God uses a vivid analogy to depict His profound love and grace for Israel (Jerusalem), and how she betrayed that love.

questions.question: How does God describe the origin of Jerusalem (Israel)?
options: An infant abandoned in an open field
A noble princess
The daughter of a wealthy merchant
An adopted orphan
questions.explanation: God describes Jerusalem (Israel) as an infant, cast out into the open field at birth, with no one to pity her.

questions.question: What did God do for this abandoned infant?
options: Left her to fend for herself to see if she would survive
Just watched her from afar
Had compassion on her, let her grow, and made a covenant with her to be His wife
Entrusted her to others for upbringing
questions.explanation: God had compassion on her, let her grow, adorned her with His splendor, and finally made a covenant with her, making her His own as His wife.

questions.question: How did Jerusalem treat this grace and her covenant with God?
options: Faithfully served God and spread His name
Formed alliances with neighboring nations to resist enemies
Used God's gifts and reputation to commit prostitution with nations and worship idols
Built a strong army to protect herself
questions.explanation: Jerusalem used the splendor, riches, and reputation God had given her to commit prostitution with nations and worship idols, betraying God.

questions.question: What is the most important reminder for us from this passage?
options: We can protect ourselves if we are strong enough
God's love is conditional, and we must first be worthy
All our blessings come from God, and betraying Him brings sorrow and judgment
God is very strict with His people and does not easily forgive
questions.explanation: The passage highlights God's unconditional love and grace for Israel, and how Israel betrayed that love, indicating that all blessings originate from God, and betraying Him brings sorrow and judgment.

en.reflection: Looking back at your life, what blessings has God given you, and in what ways might you have taken His love for granted?
reflectionOptions: Admitting to taking credit for God's blessings
Committing to respond more faithfully to God's love
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for choosing me with Your unconditional love and grace, just as You chose Jerusalem. Please forgive me for ever taking Your love for granted and for misusing Your blessings. Help me to love You more faithfully today and to glorify You with my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to silently list three instances of God's grace in your life and offer Him thanks for each one.

en.focus: Despite Israel's betrayal, God faithfully remembers His covenant and promises restoration and purification.

questions.question: How does God describe Jerusalem's (Israel's) betrayal?
options: She quietly worshipped idols
She committed adultery by allying with Egypt and Assyria
She openly proclaimed God's law
She only had relations with Babylon
questions.explanation: The text describes Jerusalem's alliances with foreign nations like Egypt and Assyria as committing adultery, signifying her breach of the covenant with God.

questions.question: How does God say He will deal with the nations Jerusalem once courted?
options: God will make them love Jerusalem more
God will make them attack and shame Jerusalem
God will make them renew their covenant with Jerusalem
God will make them send gifts to Jerusalem
questions.explanation: God prophesies that the nations Jerusalem once courted will gather against her, strip her naked, tear down her houses, and stone her as judgment for her prostitution.

questions.question: What is God's ultimate purpose in carrying out His judgment?
options: To destroy Jerusalem forever
To make Jerusalem understand that God stopped her from prostituting herself
To make Jerusalem an object of scorn for other nations
To make Jerusalem completely forget her past
questions.explanation: God states that when His wrath is spent, His jealousy will depart, and she will no longer be a prostitute nor remember her disgrace, so that she may know that God has stopped her from her prostitution.

questions.question: Despite Jerusalem's betrayal, what will God ultimately do for her?
options: God will completely abandon her and never remember her
God will punish her and then cut ties with her
God will remember His covenant and establish an everlasting covenant with her
God will let her bear all the consequences alone
questions.explanation: God promises, 'Yet I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you.' Even after judgment, God still offers grace and a covenant.

en.reflection: This passage reminds us that even when we fail and betray, God remains faithful. How can you better trust in God's faithfulness today, even when you feel unworthy or disappointed?
reflectionOptions: Repent of my transgressions and seek God anew
Meditate on God's faithfulness and release self-condemnation
Seek prayer and support from other believers
en.prayer: Lord, You are a faithful God. Even when I, like Jerusalem, have turned away from You, You still remember Your covenant. Thank You for never giving up on me. Help me today to know Your love and faithfulness more deeply, and to live a life worthy of Your covenant. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to list specific examples of God's faithfulness in your life and offer Him thanks for them.

en.focus: Through parables, God reveals His supreme sovereignty over nations and His people, along with His plan of salvation.

questions.question: What image does the prophet Ezekiel use to describe the 'house of Israel'?
options: A pruned olive tree
A hunted lamb
A great eagle with powerful wings
A great cedar tree
questions.explanation: The text uses the image of a 'great cedar tree' to symbolize the house of Israel, specifically the kingdom of Judah.

questions.question: What do the 'two great eagles' mentioned in the passage represent?
options: The kings of Egypt and Assyria
The kings of Babylon and Egypt
The kings of Israel and Judah
The kings of Persia and Greece
questions.explanation: The first great eagle represents the king of Babylon, and the second represents the king of Egypt, both of whom had dealings with Judah.

questions.question: How does God promise to treat the 'tender sprig'?
options: Let it wither and neglect it
Transplant it to barren land
Plant it on the high mountain of Israel, making it a majestic cedar
Burn it as a punishment
questions.explanation: God promises to personally take a tender sprig from the top of the tall cedar and plant it on the high mountain of Israel, where it will become a majestic cedar, symbolizing the Messiah's kingdom.

questions.question: How does this passage offer comfort to believers in difficult situations?
options: By trying harder, we can change our destiny
God will eventually punish all enemies, so we don't need to do anything
Even in humanly hopeless situations, God is sovereign and can accomplish His plan of salvation
Safety is found by aligning with powerful worldly forces
questions.explanation: Even in the desperate situation of Judah's rebellion and impending destruction, God declares His supreme sovereignty and promises to personally plant a sprig, foreshadowing His future salvation and the Messiah's kingdom. This demonstrates God's hope and power in dire circumstances.

en.reflection: This passage shows that God remains in control even in the most difficult or seemingly hopeless situations. What area of your life today most needs you to surrender control to God?
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for being the sovereign Lord of all. When I feel confused or helpless amidst life's changes, please help me to look to You and trust that You can plant hope even from seemingly dry ground. May my heart turn solely to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to reflect on a challenge you are currently facing, then say to God, 'Lord, You are the sovereign God, and I surrender this to You.'

en.focus: God judges individuals based on their actions, not their parents' sins, and calls everyone to turn back to Him and live.

questions.question: What proverb was being used in the land of Israel that God declared was wrong?
options: The fathers eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.
As you sow, so shall you reap.
Good deeds are rewarded, evil deeds are punished.
Man can conquer nature.
questions.explanation: The passage begins by mentioning the proverb in the land of Israel: 'The fathers eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' This reflected a misunderstanding of sin and punishment.

questions.question: In response to this proverb, what truth did God emphasize?
options: All souls are mine; the soul who sins shall die.
I will punish the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation.
People have no ability to choose their own path.
The righteous and the wicked ultimately have the same end.
questions.explanation: God clearly states, 'Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die.' This emphasizes that each person is responsible for their own actions.

questions.question: What is God's desire concerning the wicked who repent?
options: He desires the wicked to perish forever, no longer disturbing society.
He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that they turn from their ways and live.
He is not interested in the repentance of the wicked because their sins are too great.
He accepts only the repentance of the righteous, not the wicked.
questions.explanation: God clearly declares, 'Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?' This reveals God's merciful heart, desiring people to repent and live.

questions.question: What is the main message this passage helps us understand today?
options: Our destiny is solely determined by our family's past sins.
God judges each person fairly and desires all to repent.
Once a mistake is made, there is no chance to turn back.
Doing a little good can cancel out all sins.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God is a righteous judge who judges according to each person's actions, and He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls everyone to repent, turn from sin, and receive life.

en.reflection: Have you ever felt powerless due to past guilt or the actions of others? How does this passage encourage you to re-examine your choices today and turn to God?
reflectionOptions: Trust in God's grace of forgiveness and release old burdens.
Repent of my own wrongs to God and seek His guidance.
Stop blaming myself for others' mistakes and live a new life.
en.prayer: Righteous and loving Father, thank You that You judge me by my own actions, not by the transgressions of my parents. Help me to take responsibility for my own life and repent of my sins. I do not want to go my own way, but let my heart turn to You, depart from all unrighteousness, and receive the life You offer. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to confess a specific area where you need to repent to God, and ask Him to help you turn back to the right path.

en.focus: Through a lament, God warns His people that their sinful actions will lead to tragic consequences.

questions.question: For whom was the prophet Ezekiel commanded to sing a lament?
options: The restoration of Israel
The princes of Israel
The fall of Jerusalem
The rebuilding of the temple
questions.explanation: The passage begins by stating, “Raise a lament concerning the princes of Israel.”

questions.question: What animal is used to describe the mother of Israel?
options: A lioness
A she-wolf
A she-bear
A doe
questions.explanation: The text describes the mother as a lioness, crouching among lions.

questions.question: What do the captured “lion cubs” in the passage symbolize?
options: Enemies of Israel
Exiled kings of Israel
The future Messiah
Foreign rulers
questions.explanation: The passage depicts two of the lioness's cubs being captured and taken to Egypt and Babylon, symbolizing the kings of Israel being led into foreign captivity.

questions.question: What is the main message conveyed by this lament?
options: God's love never changes
The kings of Israel were innocent
Sinful actions lead to painful consequences and God's judgment
Israel's future is bright and hopeful
questions.explanation: This lament clearly illustrates the tragic end of Israel's kings (the lion cubs) due to their wicked actions, serving as a warning about the consequences of sin and God's judgment.

en.reflection: This lament reminds us that the path of sin ultimately leads to tragic ends. In what area do you need to be vigilant today and turn back to God?
en.prayer: Loving Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me of the consequences of sin through Your Word. Please help me to be vigilant and not stray from Your path. May my heart always turn back to You and obey Your will, so that I may not fall into the trap of sin. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, reflect on an experience where your sin led you into difficulties, and confess and repent of it to God.

en.theme: God's Patience and Judgment on a Rebellious People
en.focus: Despite Israel's repeated rebellion, God endures for the sake of His own name, exercising both righteous judgment and ultimate redemption.

questions.question: What was God's response when the elders came to inquire of Him?
options: He immediately answered all their questions
He refused to be inquired of by them
He sent an angel to answer
He demanded more sacrifices from them
questions.explanation: God explicitly stated that because of their idolatry, He would not allow Himself to be inquired of by them.

questions.question: In God's review of Israel's history, at what stage did He mention Israel began to rebel against Him?
options: After entering the land of Canaan
During the time of the Judges
While they were in the land of Egypt
After the establishment of the kingdom
questions.explanation: God pointed out that Israel began to rebel against Him and did not cast away the idols of Egypt while they were still in Egypt.

questions.question: Despite Israel's repeated rebellion, why did God not completely destroy them?
options: Because they eventually repented
Because God was not powerful enough
For the sake of His own name, to prevent desecration among the nations
Because Moses interceded for them
questions.explanation: God stated that He did not destroy them for the sake of His own name, so that His name would not be profaned in the sight of the nations.

questions.question: From this passage, how should we respond to God's judgment of sin and His patience?
options: Assume God will not ultimately punish sin
Continue our own way of life without worry
Recognize God's justice and holiness, and repent of our sins to Him
Focus only on God's grace and ignore His judgment
questions.explanation: This passage reminds us that God's holiness and judgment of sin are real, but He also endures because of His faithfulness. This should motivate us to humbly repent and turn back to Him.

en.reflection: Have you ever taken God's patience for granted regarding your sin? What specific area of rebellion or unbelief do you most need to repent of to God today?
reflectionOptions: Let go of an idol or dependency in your heart
Re-submit to God in a specific area
en.prayer: Holy and righteous God, thank You for Your patience for the sake of Your own name, and for not dealing with me according to my sins. Forgive my rebellious heart that has taken Your commands and grace lightly. Help me to repent today, to cast away all idols from my heart, and to turn solely to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a few moments to quietly reflect on any 'idols' in your life (e.g., money, status, pleasure) and confess them to God, asking for His help to let them go.

en.focus: God judges Israel for their rebellion, but His faithfulness and concern for His holy name will ultimately lead to their return and restoration.

questions.question: What behavior did God repeatedly accuse the Israelites of in the passage?
options: Failing to observe the Sabbath
Offering sacrifices to idols on every high hill and under every leafy tree
Not offering firstfruits on time
Forgetting the law given by Moses
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that the Israelites defiled themselves by offering sacrifices to idols on high hills and under leafy trees.

questions.question: Despite the Israelites' continuous rebellion, for what reason did God say He did not completely destroy them?
options: Because of their large numbers
Because He remembered His covenant with Abraham
Because of His name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations
Because His servant Moses interceded for them
questions.explanation: God stated that He acted for the sake of His name, so that it would not be profaned before the nations, which is why He did not utterly destroy them.

questions.question: God promised to gather the Israelites from the nations and lead them to where?
options: The land of Egypt
The wilderness of the peoples
The Promised Land
The land of Chaldea
questions.explanation: God promised to gather the Israelites and bring them into 'the wilderness of the peoples,' where He would enter into judgment with them face to face.

questions.question: How does this passage reveal God's attributes?
options: God is a strict judge who only cares about punishment
God is a gracious Father who never rebukes
God is both just and faithful; He judges sin but also keeps His promises for His name's sake
God is fickle, and His decisions often change
questions.explanation: The passage shows God as both a righteous judge who punishes Israel's rebellion and a faithful covenant-keeper who brings about salvation and restoration for the sake of His name.

en.reflection: This passage reminds us of God's justice and faithfulness. In what area of your life do you most need to turn back to God today, to experience His faithfulness and restoration more deeply?
reflectionOptions: Confess and forsake an idol (e.g., money, status, pleasure)
Trust God's leading in difficult circumstances
en.prayer: Just and faithful God, I confess that sometimes I, like Israel, allow my heart to stray from You and pursue idols. Please forgive me and lead me by Your Spirit to turn back. May my life bring glory to Your holy name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to consider if there are any 'idols' in your life that have taken God's place, and repent to God.

en.focus: God's righteous judgment is inevitable, but even in judgment, He offers the promise of restoration.

questions.question: What did the prophet Ezekiel see in a vision as a symbol of the Lord's judgment on Israel?
options: A burning altar
A drawn sword
A withered tree
A crumbling wall
questions.explanation: The Lord commanded Ezekiel to prophesy that He would draw His sword and cut off both the righteous and the wicked from Israel.

questions.question: Which areas were subject to this sword of judgment?
options: Only Jerusalem
Only Judah
The whole land of Israel, including Jerusalem and Judah
Only foreign nations
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that this sword would judge the whole land of Israel, including Judah in the south and Jerusalem.

questions.question: Why did God say His sword would cut off both the righteous and the wicked?
options: Because God cannot distinguish between good and evil
Because the whole nation was corrupt, and no one was exempt from judgment
Because God delights in destruction
Because the righteous committed the same sins as the wicked
questions.explanation: God's words indicate that the entire land of Israel was filled with wickedness, and no one could escape this righteous judgment, even those seemingly 'righteous'.

questions.question: What attitude should we adopt when facing God's righteous judgment?
options: Complain that God is unfair
Be indifferent, thinking it doesn't concern us
Confess our sins and turn back to God
Try to hide our transgressions
questions.explanation: When God's righteous judgment comes, the correct attitude is to humbly confess our sins and genuinely repent, seeking God's forgiveness and mercy.
questions.evidence: (This is an application question, the answer is based on the overall theme of the passage and general biblical teaching, not a direct verse quotation)

en.reflection: Today's scripture shows us God's righteous judgment against sin. Have you ever felt uneasy or in need of God's forgiveness for your own transgressions or the sins of this world?
en.prayer: Righteous God, I confess that You are holy, and Your judgment against sin is perfectly just. Please forgive my transgressions and help me to live in a way that pleases You. May I see Your love and the hope of salvation even in Your judgment. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to confess and repent of a past transgression to God.

en.focus: God severely condemns Jerusalem for the sins of its inhabitants, yet still seeks an intercessor.

questions.question: What major sins is Ezekiel told fill Jerusalem?
options: Idolatry and profaning the Sabbath
Bloodshed and worshiping false gods
Oppressing the foreigners and greed
All of the above
questions.explanation: The passage lists various sins committed by the inhabitants of Jerusalem, including bloodshed, idolatry, oppressing the vulnerable, greed, and profaning holy things.

questions.question: What emotions does God express regarding Jerusalem's sins?
options: Indifference
Anger and abhorrence
Sadness and disappointment
Tolerance and understanding
questions.explanation: God expresses through the prophet strong anger, abhorrence, and grief over the sins committed in Jerusalem, calling them 'detestable practices'.

questions.question: Why does God say He will 'pour out My wrath' on Jerusalem?
options: Because He enjoys destruction
Because the people's sins have reached their limit and demand righteous judgment
Because He had no other way to punish them
Because He wanted foreign nations to mock Israel
questions.explanation: God's wrath is poured out because of the people's persistent and escalating sins, which is the inevitable outcome of His righteous judgment.

questions.question: In this severe message of judgment, what aspect of God's heart is revealed?
options: He is only concerned with judgment, not human repentance
He is still looking for a righteous person to stand in the gap, showing His slowness to anger
He believes no one is innocent, so there is no need to search
He only wishes for Israel's destruction
questions.explanation: Despite the overwhelming sin, God still searches for someone to stand in the gap for the land, revealing that while He justly judges, He is also merciful and does not desire anyone to perish.

en.reflection: Today's scripture reminds us of the seriousness of sin and reveals God's justice and mercy. Do you see any 'gaps' in your own life that need repentance?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent, asking God for cleansing
Ask God to help me be an intercessor
en.prayer: Righteous Father, Your word is a double-edged sword, revealing the stains of sin in my life. Please forgive all my transgressions and cleanse my heart. May I know Your justice and mercy more deeply, and be willing to intercede before You for the sins of this generation. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, offer a short prayer to God for the sins and injustices present in your city or country.

en.theme: Rebellion and Restoration: God's Judgment and Love
en.focus: God severely condemns His people's betrayal, but His judgment aims to awaken them to repentance.

questions.question: What metaphor does God use in this passage to describe Israel and Judah?
options: Two trees
Two sisters
Two shepherds
Two cities
questions.explanation: God uses two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, to represent Samaria (Israel) and Jerusalem (Judah).

questions.question: What was the main spiritual act of betrayal by these two sisters against God?
options: They did not build the temple well
They did not observe the Sabbath
They committed adultery with foreign nations and worshipped their idols
They did not manage the land well
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly points out their alliances with foreign nations like Assyria and Babylon, imitating their promiscuity and idol worship, which is seen as spiritual adultery.

questions.question: How does God specifically describe Oholibah's (Judah's) sin?
options: Her sin was lighter than Oholah's (Israel's)
Her sin was exactly the same as Oholah's
Her sin was worse than Oholah's
God did not specifically mention her sin
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that Oholibah (Judah), after witnessing Oholah's (Israel's) punishment, did not take warning but instead became even more promiscuous.

questions.question: What important reminder does this passage offer us today?
options: God only cares about our outward actions, not our hearts
We can freely imitate worldly trends without being affected
God abhors idolatry and spiritual adultery, and His people must be faithful and devoted
As long as we pray, God will forgive all sins without the need for repentance
questions.explanation: Through the judgment of Israel and Judah, God reminds us that He is a holy and jealous God, demanding unwavering faithfulness from His people and separation from all forms of idolatry and spiritual betrayal.
questions.evidence: Ezekiel 23: The entire passage emphasizes God's wrath and judgment against betrayal.

en.reflection: Today, are there any 'idols' or 'worldly temptations' in your life that are diverting your loyalty to God?
en.prayer: Holy and righteous God, You are a jealous God. Please forgive me for any unfaithfulness, worldly imitations, and sins that have drawn me away from You. Help me to examine my heart, remove all idols, and find my joy solely in You, loving and following You with all my heart. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend five minutes in quiet reflection today, considering what might be subtly replacing God in your heart, and confess it to Him.

en.focus: God's righteous judgment on sin aims to purify His people and turn them back to Him.

questions.question: What primary sins of Oholah and Oholibah (Samaria and Jerusalem) were judged by God?
options: Idolatry and harlotry
Poverty and hunger
Disregarding the Sabbath
Oppressing the fatherless and widows
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly highlights their judgment for idolatry and harlotry with foreign nations, referring to seeking political alliances and adopting their religious practices.

questions.question: How does God describe the judgment He will bring upon Oholah and Oholibah to punish them?
options: A great flood
A deadly plague
A consuming fire
Using their beloved foreign allies to attack them
questions.explanation: God states He will stir up their 'lovers' – the very foreign nations they relied on – to come against them, bringing disgrace and destruction.

questions.type: Understand the purpose of the passage
questions.question: What is the ultimate purpose of God's judgment on Oholah and Oholibah?
options: To utterly destroy them without any remnant
To show them that alliances with foreign nations are wrong
To put an end to harlotry and cleanse the land of impurity
To demonstrate His righteousness and power to all nations
questions.explanation: God clearly states that the purpose of the judgment is to stop harlotry, prevent others from following their example, and purify His holy land.

questions.question: What does this passage remind us about how believers, saved by grace in Christ, should respond to God's holiness and righteousness?
options: We don't need to worry about sin, as grace covers everything
We should actively examine and abandon any behavior displeasing to God
Focus only on external religious rituals to maintain a good image
Believe that God's judgment only applies to people in the Old Testament
questions.explanation: Although we are justified by faith, God remains holy and righteous. This passage reminds us to actively examine and abandon sin, living a life worthy of our calling, as God's ultimate purpose is to purify His people.
questions.evidence: Ezekiel 23:48–49 (God's ultimate purpose of judgment implies His demand for holiness from His people)

en.reflection: Today, is there any 'spiritual harlotry' in your life – placing your trust and reliance on things other than God?
reflectionOptions: Over-reliance on money and material possessions
Seeking human approval more than God's pleasure
Being consumed by a particular hobby or habit
en.prayer: Holy and righteous God, I confess that my heart sometimes strays from You, seeking satisfaction and security outside of You. Please forgive me for any spiritual harlotry and cleanse my heart. May my life find joy in You alone and rely solely on You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to list things in your life you might be over-relying on or consumed by. Confess them to God and ask Him to help you recenter your life on Him.

en.theme: The Boiling Pot: Judgment on Jerusalem
en.focus: God uses the parable of the boiling pot to declare the severe judgment awaiting Jerusalem and its inhabitants.

questions.question: In what year, month, and day did God speak to Ezekiel to declare the siege of Jerusalem?
options: The ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day
The tenth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day
The eighth year, in the ninth month, on the ninth day
The eleventh year, in the twelfth month, on the fifth day
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states the exact date when the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel concerning the siege.

questions.question: What vessel does God use to symbolize Jerusalem and its inhabitants?
options: A golden cup
A boiling pot
A clay jar
An oil lamp
questions.explanation: God instructs Ezekiel to prophesy against the rebellious house, using the imagery of 'setting on the pot' to represent Jerusalem.

questions.question: What does the 'filth' of the meat (the inhabitants of the city) in the pot refer to?
options: The uncleanliness of their living conditions
Their physical diseases
Their various sins and injustices
Their ignorance of the law
questions.explanation: The text explains the 'filth' of the pot as the 'bloodshed' and 'idolatry,' representing the wickedness and injustice of Jerusalem's inhabitants.

questions.question: God mentions that one reason for Jerusalem's judgment is her 'uncleanness.' What does this remind us of?
options: God does not care about our sins, only our worship rituals
God has holy requirements for sin and will execute judgment according to His justice
As long as we do the right things outwardly, our inner state doesn't matter
God will not judge us as long as we have a large population
questions.explanation: God's judgment on Jerusalem, particularly the descriptions of its 'filth' and 'uncleanness,' highlights God's holy nature regarding sin and His righteous judgment.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us of God's holiness and justice, and reveals the seriousness of sin. In your life, what 'filth' is God calling you to repent of and cleanse?
en.prayer: Holy and righteous Lord, thank You for reminding me through today's Scripture of Your holiness and Your hatred of sin. Please examine my heart and reveal any areas of 'filth' in my life that displease You. Help me to truly repent, and cleanse me with the precious blood of Jesus, so that I may live a holy life that is pleasing to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend a minute in quiet prayer, asking God to illuminate areas in your life that need cleansing, and commit to seeking repentance and change in those areas.

en.focus: God is a righteous judge who brings retribution upon nations that gloat over the suffering of His people, revealing His sovereignty and holiness.

questions.question: Which nations are primarily targeted by God's judgment in this passage?
options: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon
Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia
Tyre, Sidon, Syria
Persia, Greece, Rome
questions.explanation: God explicitly names the Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and Philistines as recipients of His judgment.

questions.question: What is the primary reason for these nations' judgment?
options: They failed to provide military aid to Israel
They worshipped idols and did not know the true God
They rejoiced over Israel's calamity and sought revenge
They hindered Israel's trade routes
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly emphasizes that these nations gloated, clapped their hands, stamped their feet, and took revenge out of ancient hatred for Israel's suffering.

questions.question: What is God's ultimate purpose in judging these nations?
options: To completely annihilate all foreign nations
To show the nations that He is the LORD, the God who executes judgment
To make Israel the dominant world power
To restore peace and harmony among the nations
questions.explanation: God repeatedly declares that He will execute judgment so that they 'will know that I am the LORD.' This indicates God's purpose is to reveal His sovereignty and justice through judgment.

questions.question: How does this passage help us understand God's character?
options: God only cares about Israel and not other nations
God is a harsh and unforgiving deity
God is just, and He will punish those who harm His people and gloat over their misfortune
God's judgments on nations are random and without specific reasons
questions.explanation: The passage highlights God's justice; He will vindicate His people and punish nations that gloat over their suffering and seek revenge, thereby demonstrating His holiness and sovereignty.

en.reflection: Have you ever secretly rejoiced over someone else's downfall or expressed ungodly attitudes in your words?
reflectionOptions: Admit to having a gloating mindset
Reflect on whether I lack compassion for others
Ask God to help me cultivate a more godly attitude
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You for being the sovereign Lord over all, whose judgments are just and true. Please forgive me if I have ever gloated over another's suffering or harbored ungodly attitudes. Grant me a compassionate heart, to imitate Christ and love my neighbor as myself. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for someone you typically don't like or someone who is currently facing difficulties, asking God to have mercy on them.

en.focus: God’s sovereignty is revealed in the rise and fall of nations, and His judgment declares that He is the one true God.

questions.question: What was the reason prophesied for the overthrow of Tyre?
options: It rejoiced over Jerusalem's downfall
It competed with Israel for trade
It refused to worship the LORD
It allied with Egypt against Babylon
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that Tyre gloated over Jerusalem's destruction, thinking it would increase its own trade opportunities.

questions.question: What kind of destruction was prophesied for the city of Tyre?
options: Its walls would be rebuilt, but its wealth plundered
It would be scraped bare and become a place for spreading nets
It would be flooded and become a desolate wasteland
It would be besieged but ultimately preserved
questions.explanation: The LORD declares that He will attack Tyre, making it like a bare rock, a place for spreading nets, and never to be rebuilt.

questions.type: Understand the purpose of the prophecy
questions.question: What was God's ultimate purpose in judging Tyre?
options: To give the Israelites a sense of revenge
To make the king of Babylon famous
To let the nations know that He is the LORD
To make the people of Tyre recognize their sin and repent
questions.explanation: God repeatedly states that the purpose of His judgment is for the nations, including Tyre, to know that He is the LORD.

questions.type: Understand the application of the passage
questions.question: What important lesson can we learn from Tyre's fate?
options: God's judgment is only for Gentiles and irrelevant to us
We can secure safety through political alliances
Any pride that exalts itself and gloats will ultimately fall before God
Material wealth is the only sign of God's blessing
questions.explanation: Tyre was judged for its pride and gloating over Jerusalem's fall, reminding us that God values humility and controls all things; any self-exaltation will ultimately fall.

en.reflection: In what areas of your life today might you be demonstrating pride, and where do you need to humble yourself and acknowledge God's sovereignty?
en.prayer: Almighty LORD, You are the sovereign ruler over all nations and peoples. Please help me to remove pride from my heart and to look to You alone in both prosperity and adversity. May my life honor Your name, knowing that You alone are God. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to confess any pride you may have had to God, seeking His forgiveness and help.

en.focus: Earthly prosperity and self-reliance cannot withstand God’s judgment; true security rests only in Him.

questions.question: What does the prophet Ezekiel liken the city of Tyre to?
options: A mighty fortress
A magnificent ship
A majestic palace
A fertile vineyard
questions.explanation: The passage describes Tyre in detail as a beautifully built and well-equipped ship, symbolizing its prosperous trading empire.

questions.question: What was the geographical scope of Tyre's trading partners?
options: Mainly concentrated in North Africa
Mainly concentrated in Western Europe
Very wide-ranging, from all over the world
Mainly concentrated in the Middle East
questions.explanation: The text lists partners from Persia, Lud, Put, Tarshish, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Dedan, and many other regions, showing the vastness of its trade network.

questions.question: What was the primary reason for Tyre's downfall?
options: Strikes by natural disasters
Betrayal by its allies
Its own excessive pride and self-reliance
Depletion of resources leading to decline
questions.explanation: Tyre's immense wealth and power led to its pride and self-reliance, believing itself to be perfect, which ultimately brought about God's judgment and destruction.

questions.question: What significant spiritual lesson can we learn from Tyre’s experience?
options: Striving for wealth and power is the primary goal in life
If you are strong enough, you can never be defeated
All earthly glories can vanish in an instant; only God's grace endures
The secret to success is establishing trade relations with more nations
questions.explanation: Tyre's downfall reminds us that all earthly splendor and riches are temporary, and only reliance on God provides eternal security.

en.reflection: Is there an area in your life where you are overly relying on your own abilities or worldly resources, neglecting God's sovereignty?
en.prayer: Dear Lord, thank You for reminding me through the example of Tyre that all earthly glories will pass away. Please help me examine my heart, so that I may not become proud or self-reliant due to any worldly achievements, nor overly dependent on temporary resources. May my heart solely rely on You, knowing that You are my Rock and eternal security. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to reflect on people or things in your life that you are proud of or overly reliant on. Then, quietly say to God, “Lord, my heart desires to rely on You alone.”

en.theme: The End of Pride and the Glory of God
en.focus: God's sovereignty will be displayed over all earthly powers, no matter how self-exalting they become.

questions.question: What did God, through the prophet Ezekiel, say about the king of Tyre?
options: He was a righteous ruler
He was proud due to his wealth and thought himself a god
He would become an ally of Israel
He would build an impregnable wall
questions.explanation: God stated that the king of Tyre was proud due to his wealth, considered himself a god, and sat in the seat of God.

questions.question: What was the ultimate purpose of God's judgment on the king of Tyre and Sidon?
options: To demonstrate the king of Tyre's wisdom and power
To show Sidon's wealth and prosperity
To reveal that the Lord is God and holy
To demonstrate Israel's military strength
questions.explanation: God clearly stated that His judgment was to make people know that 'I am the LORD' and to show His holiness.

questions.question: After judging Tyre and Sidon, what promise did God give to the people of Israel?
options: They would become world dominators
They would never again have enemies
They would dwell securely, and God would remove all who despise them
They would receive more wealth and authority
questions.explanation: God promised Israel that after His judgment on those who despised them, they would dwell securely and know that He is their God.

questions.question: What lesson about pride can we learn from the example of the king of Tyre?
options: Possessing wealth and wisdom is the root of pride
Pride causes one to exalt oneself, forget God's sovereignty, and ultimately leads to destruction
Pride is harmless as long as one does not publicly claim to be God
Pride can help one achieve greater accomplishments
questions.explanation: The king of Tyre's pride, stemming from his perceived wisdom and wealth, led him to consider himself a god, which ultimately resulted in his destruction. This reminds us that pride is a manifestation of forgetting God's sovereignty, and its outcome is tragic.

en.reflection: Today's scripture reminds us that God is the supreme sovereign, and He detests pride. Is there any area in your life where you are relying on your own wisdom or ability, exalting yourself, and forgetting God's sovereignty?
en.prayer: Almighty God, You are the one true Sovereign, and Your wisdom and power surpass all. Please forgive the pride in my life, those moments when I acted by my own understanding and ability, forgetting Your sovereignty. Help me to humble myself and always magnify You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, when you achieve something or feel proud, pause and silently say, “All this is by God's grace; glory belongs to God.”

en.theme: The Fall of Egypt and the Restoration of Israel
en.focus: God's sovereignty is displayed in the rise and fall of nations, and He will fulfill His promises to His people in His timing.

questions.question: What is God's primary accusation against Pharaoh?
options: He worshiped idols
He oppressed the Israelites
He boasted of creating and owning the Nile River
He formed alliances with foreign nations
questions.explanation: God accuses Pharaoh of claiming that he made the Nile River and that it belonged to him.

questions.question: What will God do to Egypt?
options: Make it the richest nation on earth
Allow it to be conquered and desolate for forty years
Ensure it will never again have a king
Cause it to ally with Israel against Babylon
questions.explanation: God states that He will bring a sword against Egypt, making the land desolate and waste for forty years, and it will be the lowest of kingdoms.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of God's judgment on Egypt?
options: To utterly destroy the Egyptians
To display His wrath to the nations
To make Pharaoh know that He is the LORD
To prevent other nations from allying with Egypt
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that His judgment is so that the Egyptians may know that He is the LORD.

questions.question: How does this passage offer comfort to the exiled Israelites?
options: By reminding them that Egypt was a strong ally
By predicting that Israel would be ruled by Babylon forever
By promising that God would judge their oppressors and restore Israel in the future
By encouraging them to seek freedom through their own strength
questions.explanation: God judged Egypt because it was an unreliable 'reed staff' for Israel. God promises that after Egypt's judgment, He will make a horn grow for the house of Israel and open Ezekiel's mouth among them, pointing to future restoration.

en.reflection: This passage reminds us that God is in control, even in difficult times. What worry or hope do you most need to surrender to God today, trusting in His sovereignty and promises?
reflectionOptions: The faith of my family members
en.prayer: Lord, You are the God who rules over all; the rise and fall of nations are in Your hands. When my heart is anxious or feels helpless, help me to look to You and trust that Your promises will not fail. May Your will be done in my life and in the lives of those I care about. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to reflect or write down one thing you want to surrender to God today, trusting in His ultimate control.

en.theme: The Fall of Egypt and the Judgment of the LORD
en.focus: God's sovereignty is revealed in His judgment over nations, proving that even powerful Egypt cannot escape.

questions.question: Which two specific nations or regions are mentioned as victims in God's judgment on Egypt?
options: Assyria and Babylon
Libya and Lydia
Cush and Put
Philistia and Tyre
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that 'Cush and Put, Lud and all Arabia, and Libya' will fall with Egypt.

questions.question: Which nation does God say He will use as His instrument to judge Egypt in this passage?
options: Assyria
Babylon
Persia
Rome
questions.explanation: God states through Ezekiel that He will 'bring the might of Babylon's king, Nebuchadnezzar, against them.'

questions.question: What is the ultimate purpose of God's judgment on Egypt?
options: To show that He is stronger than the gods of Egypt
To utterly destroy the people of Egypt
So that they 'will know that I am the LORD'
To allow Babylon to rule Egypt permanently
questions.explanation: God repeatedly states that the purpose of His judgment is for the nations and Egypt to 'know that I am the LORD,' recognizing His uniqueness and sovereignty.

questions.question: What important truth about God's reign can we learn from this passage?
options: God only cares about Israel and not other nations
God is not interested in the fate of nations, letting them develop on their own
God controls all nations and the course of history, and His sovereignty is unchallengeable
As long as a nation is strong, it can escape God's judgment
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows God's judgment on mighty Egypt and prophesies its fall, demonstrating that He is the supreme ruler who controls nations and historical events.

en.reflection: How does understanding God as the sovereign ruler of all nations influence your perspective and prayers regarding current world events?
reflectionOptions: Avoid excessive worry about world affairs
en.prayer: Almighty Father, You are the supreme ruler over all nations and peoples. Help me to trust in Your sovereignty amidst global turmoil, and to pray for the society and nation I live in. May Your name be glorified throughout the earth, and may Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, specifically pray for the leaders and people of Singapore, asking for God's grace and guidance.

en.theme: The Fall of Pride and God's Sovereignty
en.focus: God reminds Egypt and Assyria that any seemingly great power, if arrogant, will ultimately fall under God's judgment. Only God is supreme.

questions.question: What kind of tree is used in Ezekiel 31 to metaphorically represent the glory of Assyria?
options: A cedar
An olive tree
A grapevine
A palm tree
questions.explanation: The passage uses a tall cedar tree to symbolize the splendor of Assyria, with its luxuriant branches reaching to the clouds.

questions.question: What caused the metaphorical cedar tree to grow so tall?
options: Its own effort to grow upward
Fertile soil and abundant water
Nourishment from other trees
A special gift from God
questions.explanation: The text states that this cedar tree grew tall and its branches spread wide because it was nourished by deep waters.

questions.question: What was the ultimate fate of this metaphorical cedar tree (Assyria)?
options: It would become an eternal king
It would be lifted to heaven
It would be cut down due to pride and go to the realm of the dead
It would become more humble
questions.explanation: This cedar, symbolizing Assyria, because of its height and pride, was ultimately cut down and sent to the realm of the dead with the uncircumcised.

questions.question: What is the primary message conveyed by this passage?
options: God's kingdom will eventually perish
Earthly powers can last forever
God will humble all proud and arrogant powers
Human efforts can surpass God's plans
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that no matter how mighty an earthly power, if it harbors pride, it will ultimately be brought low under God's judgment.

en.reflection: Is there any area in your life where, because of some achievement or ability, pride has taken root, and you need God's reminder and humbling?
en.prayer: Almighty God, You are the sovereign Lord over all. Search my heart, and if I have become proud because of any gift or achievement, please remind me and humble me before You. May I honor You alone and give all glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take a minute to silently reflect and offer to God anything you are proud of in your life, asking Him to help you remain humble.

en.theme: The Fall of Pharaoh and Egypt
en.focus: God's sovereignty is demonstrated in His judgment of pride and evil, making His name known to all nations.

questions.question: In which year, month, and day did the word of the Lord come to Ezekiel in chapter 32?
options: Tenth year, first day of the twelfth month
Eleventh year, first day of the first month
Twelfth year, first day of the second month
Thirteenth year, first day of the third month
questions.explanation: The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel on the first day of the second month of the twelfth year.

questions.question: What animal does God use to symbolize Pharaoh, king of Egypt?
options: A lion
A sea monster (great fish)
A crocodile
A wild ox
questions.explanation: God compares Pharaoh to a great crocodile in the Nile, stirring up the waters and making them muddy.

questions.question: What is the ultimate purpose of God's judgment on Egypt?
options: To make the Israelites feel superior
To make all nations fear God's power
To make all nations know that He is the LORD
To make Egypt disappear forever
questions.explanation: God states that He will execute judgment so that all nations may know that He is the LORD.

questions.question: What important truth about God can we learn from this passage?
options: God only cares about the destiny of Israel
God's power is limited by earthly powers
God is the sovereign ruler of history and judge of all nations
God's judgment on sin is random
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that God is the sovereign ruler over all, exercising absolute judgment over the pride and evil of the world, thereby manifesting His glory.

en.reflection: Are there any areas of pride or self-reliance in your life that you need to examine and surrender to God's sovereignty?
en.prayer: Almighty Lord, You are the sovereign ruler over all nations and history. Help me to humble myself, recognize my smallness, and surrender every area of my life to Your authority. May my life glorify Your name and make known to the world that You are the Lord. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to quietly reflect and, in prayer, surrender one thing you are most skilled at or proud of to God, acknowledging that it all comes from Him.

en.focus: As God's people, we are called to be watchmen, to warn those who stray, and to be accountable to God for our own actions.

questions.question: How does God define the role of a watchman in this passage?
options: Managing the city's finances
Explaining the law to the people
Blowing the trumpet to warn of danger
Prophesying future events
questions.explanation: God clearly states that the watchman is to blow the trumpet and warn the people when he sees the sword coming upon the land.

questions.question: If the watchman fails to give warning and people die, how will God hold him accountable?
options: God will forgive the watchman because the people did not listen anyway
God will hold the watchman accountable for their blood
God will directly punish the people, unrelated to the watchman
God will appoint a new watchman
questions.explanation: If the watchman does not blow the trumpet and the sword comes, God will hold the watchman accountable for the blood of the people.

questions.type: Understand God's attitude towards the wicked and righteous
questions.question: What is God's attitude toward the wicked turning from their ways and repenting?
options: God is indifferent to the death of the wicked
God desires the wicked to turn from their ways and live
God only saves the righteous and gives no chance to the wicked
God will immediately punish all wicked people
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live.

questions.question: What is the main teaching about personal responsibility in this passage?
options: Individual actions are irrelevant to salvation
One good deed ensures eternal salvation
Each person is accountable to God for their actions; the righteous will die if they sin, and the wicked will live if they repent
Human destiny is entirely predetermined by God, irrespective of actions
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly emphasizes that the outcome for both the righteous and the wicked depends on their current actions and whether they repent. Each person is responsible for their own path.

en.reflection: As a follower of Christ, how can you be a 'watchman' in your family, church, or community today, lovingly reminding others with truth?
reflectionOptions: Pray for family and share your faith
Encourage church members to repent or return
Share the gospel with an unbelieving friend
en.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for Your Word that reminds me of my responsibility as Your child. Grant me courage and wisdom to lovingly and truthfully warn those around me who may be straying from Your path. Help me also to constantly examine my own heart, turn from all wicked ways, and live a life that pleases You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for a friend, family member, or church member whom you feel needs the gospel or a loving reminder, and look for an appropriate opportunity to reach out to them.

en.theme: The LORD is the Good Shepherd
en.focus: God declares Himself to be the true Shepherd of His people, who will personally feed, seek, and save His flock.

questions.question: What was the main reason God rebuked the shepherds (leaders) of Israel through Ezekiel?
options: They failed to build strong city walls
They did not lead the people into battle
They fed themselves instead of the flock
They did not collect taxes on time
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that these shepherds cared only for their own gain and neglected their responsibility to feed, seek, and heal the flock.

questions.question: What did God promise to do personally for His flock?
options: Grant them more wealth and land
Establish a powerful empire for them
Seek the lost, bring back the scattered, bind up the injured, and strengthen the sick
Allow them to choose their own new shepherds
questions.explanation: God promised to intervene personally, like a good shepherd, actively seeking, healing, and feeding His flock.

questions.question: What did God's 'covenant of peace' with His flock primarily entail?
options: The people could do as they pleased without discipline
Freedom from wild beasts, fruitful land, and no more shame
God would give them silver and gold, making them leaders among nations
God would grant military power to conquer all enemies
questions.explanation: The 'covenant of peace' meant God would remove all threats, allowing His people to live in security and abundance, free from shame.

questions.question: From this passage, how should we view God's care for us?
options: God is only concerned with our material wealth
God is an indifferent bystander
God is an active Shepherd who seeks, feeds, and saves us
We must strive on our own to receive God's blessings
questions.explanation: The core message is that God declares Himself to be the active, personal, and loving Shepherd who cares for His people.

en.reflection: In what area do you most need to experience God's care as the Good Shepherd today?
en.prayer: Yahweh, my Good Shepherd, thank You for actively seeking and feeding me. When I feel lost, hurt, or weary, please personally care for me, guide me, heal me, and grant me true peace and satisfaction. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment and say to God, “Lord, You are my Good Shepherd, and I surrender myself completely to You.”

en.theme: God's Judgment and Promise of Restoration
en.focus: God executes righteous judgment on wickedness and promises to restore His people and land for the sake of His holy name.

questions.question: What did God declare concerning Mount Seir in chapter 35?
options: It would become fertile land
It would become a desolate wasteland
It would be given to Israel
It would be occupied by other nations
questions.explanation: God declared that Mount Seir would become a desolate wasteland because of its enduring hostility towards Israel.

questions.question: Whose name does God repeatedly emphasize He will act for in chapter 36?
options: The name of the people of Israel
The name of King David
His own holy name
The name of the prophets
questions.explanation: God emphasized that He would act for the sake of His own holy name, which Israel had profaned among the nations.

questions.question: What is the primary reason God promised to bring the people of Israel back to their own land?
options: Because the Israelites repented
Because God was angry with the nations
Because God wanted to show His holiness and power
Because the Israelites deserved to regain their inheritance
questions.explanation: God promised to restore Israel not because they deserved it, but to demonstrate His holiness and power before the nations, removing the disgrace His name had suffered.

questions.question: How does this passage encourage you to trust more in God's justice and faithfulness today?
options: Realizing God will judge all evil
Believing God always fulfills His promises
Understanding God ultimately acts for His own glory
All of the above
questions.explanation: This passage shows us that God's judgment on evil is real, His promises to His people are faithful, and ultimately, all this is to display His own glory.

en.reflection: Have you ever doubted God's justice or faithfulness due to injustice around you or your own weaknesses? How does this passage comfort and remind you?
reflectionOptions: It reminds me that God will judge all evil.
It strengthens my faith in God's promises.
It helps me see God is in control, acting for His glory.
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for being a righteous Judge and a faithful Covenant-Keeper. Please help me to trust in Your wisdom and power amidst the world's chaos and my personal struggles. May Your holy name be glorified in my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Think of one injustice you have worried about, and commit it to God, trusting that He will enact justice in His own time and way.

en.focus: God acts to turn His people back to Him and to cleanse them anew.

questions.question: What does God promise to do for the land of Israel?
options: Make it desolate and uninhabited
Make it fertile again, bearing abundant fruit
Allow foreigners to occupy it permanently
Turn it into a desert, barren and lifeless
questions.explanation: God promises that the land of Israel will again grow grain and bear fruit to feed His people.

questions.question: What change does God say He will bring about in the people of Israel?
options: Let them continue in their wickedness
Make them more arrogant
Remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh
Make them forget God's statutes
questions.explanation: God promises to remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh, enabling them to obey Him.

questions.question: What is the primary reason God promises to restore Israel?
options: Because the Israelites deserve His grace
So that other nations may know God's name
To vindicate His holy name
To punish the surrounding nations
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that He acts not for Israel's sake, but for His holy name, which they profaned among the nations.

questions.question: According to this passage, where does true change and restoration in our personal lives come from?
options: Mainly through our own efforts and determination
It is God's initiative to cleanse us and give us a new heart
Changing external circumstances automatically changes the inner self
It can be achieved through human wisdom and strategies
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes God's active role in cleansing, gathering, and giving a new heart and spirit to His people, all of which are His sovereign grace.

en.reflection: What are the 'stony' areas in your life that need God to replace them with a 'heart of flesh' so you can obey Him more fully?
en.prayer: Holy God, thank You for being a God who restores and cleanses. Please search my heart and remove any hard, disobedient 'stony hearts' within me. Grant me a soft 'heart of flesh' that loves and obeys You, so that my life may bring glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to quietly pray, asking God to reveal areas in your life that need His renewal and cleansing.

en.focus: God actively renews the hearts of His people, enabling them to obey His statutes and experience His promised abundance.

questions.question: What kind of new heart does God promise to give His people?
options: A heart as hard as stone
A heart insensitive to God
A heart of flesh
A heart full of pride
questions.explanation: God promises to remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh.

questions.question: What is the purpose of God putting His Spirit within His people?
options: To make them smarter than others
To enable them to walk in His statutes and keep His ordinances
To give them supernatural powers
To make them independent of God
questions.explanation: God puts His Spirit within His people so that they may walk in His statutes and be careful to obey His ordinances.

questions.question: Why does God cleanse, restore, and multiply His people?
options: Because His people deserve these blessings
To demonstrate the holiness of His name to the nations
To allow His people to rule over other nations
To prove that His people are better than others
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that He does these things not for their sake, but for the sake of His holy name, to show the nations that His name is holy.
