questions.question: Which two nations does God declare judgment against at the beginning of Amos chapter 2?
options: Moab and Judah
Judah and Israel
Moab and Ammon
Moab and Edom
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that God will judge Moab and Judah.

questions.question: What was the specific reason God judged Moab?
options: They did not keep God's law
They burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes
They oppressed the poor
They worshiped idols
questions.explanation: God judged Moab because they burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes, an act of extreme cruelty and disrespect.

questions.type: Understand the reason for judging Judah and Israel
questions.question: What was the primary reason God judged Judah and Israel?
options: They were unable to resist foreign enemies
They rejected God's laws and commands, despising His instruction
They did not offer enough sacrifices
They failed to expand their territory
questions.explanation: God judged Judah and Israel because they despised His law, did not keep His commands, and were led astray by false idols.

questions.question: What is the most important lesson we can learn from this passage today?
options: God only judges foreign nations, not His people
God holds His people to a higher moral standard and judges them more severely
Religious rituals can exempt us from God's judgment
The God of the Old Testament is cruel, while the God of the New Testament is loving
questions.explanation: This passage shows that God holds His covenant people (Judah and Israel) to a higher moral standard and judges them more severely because they knew God's law but still rebelled.

en.reflection: Are there any areas in your life where you know God's will but have not yet obeyed?
en.prayer: Righteous God, Your judgments are perfectly just. Please forgive me for areas in my life where I have known Your will but have been disobedient. Help me to humbly obey Your Word and live a life that pleases You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take time today to meditate on one of your favorite Bible verses and ask God to help you live out its teaching.

en.focus: God will execute righteous judgment because of Israel's sin and rebellion, for He is a covenant-keeping God of love.

questions.question: To whom does God specifically speak in Amos 3:1?
options: The people of Egypt
The people of Moab
The whole family of Israel
The people of Assyria
questions.explanation: God clearly states that He is speaking to “the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt.”

questions.question: According to Amos 3:2, why will God punish Israel?
options: Because Israel was the most powerful nation
Because Israel was uniquely 'known' by God, yet more corrupt than other nations
Because Israel was the only nation that worshipped idols
Because Israel did not suffer in Egypt
questions.explanation: God says, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” This highlights their greater responsibility due to their special relationship with God.

questions.question: Amos 3:3-8 presents a series of questions and analogies. What is their main point?
options: To emphasize the mysteries and laws of nature
To illustrate the inevitable connection between God and His prophet, and the certainty of God's judgment
To encourage Israelites to explore cause-and-effect relationships more
To express human ignorance and fear of the future
questions.explanation: These analogies (e.g., two walking together, lion roaring, snare catching) aim to show that events have causes, and that when the Lord speaks, His prophet must speak, indicating the reality and inevitability of God's judgment.

questions.question: According to Amos 3:9-11, what were the main sins of Israel?
options: They failed to build a strong army
They hoarded violence and plunder in Samaria and did not know how to do right
They did not build magnificent temples
They failed to establish friendly relations with neighboring nations
questions.explanation: The passage points out that Samaria was full of “oppression” and “plunder,” and they “do not know how to do right,” but instead “store up violence and robbery in their fortresses.”

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that God is righteous and will not clear the guilty. In your daily life, what words, actions, or attitudes do you need to be mindful of to avoid displeasing God?
reflectionOptions: My relationships with family and neighbors
en.prayer: Righteous God, thank You for reminding me of Your holiness and justice through the book of Amos. Please shine Your light upon me and help me examine my heart, removing all sin and unrighteousness that displeases You. May my conduct always bring glory to Your name, so that I may not fall under Your judgment. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to confess and repent to God for an instance where you may have acted unjustly or unrighteously.

en.focus: God judges His people for their sins and unrepentance, yet His ultimate purpose is to call them back to Himself.

questions.question: What does Amos call the women of Samaria?
options: Princesses of Judah
Cows of Bashan
Sheep of Israel
Ladies of Zion
questions.explanation: The prophet Amos sternly calls the wealthy women of Samaria 'cows of Bashan', condemning their luxurious lifestyle and oppression of the poor.

questions.question: What forms of discipline did God use to call Israel back to Him?
options: Granted abundant harvests and wealth
Sent foreign invaders but no famine
Caused famine, plague, sword, and disaster
Helped them win wars and expand territory
questions.explanation: The passage mentions God bringing famine, lack of water, blighted crops, plagues, the sword, and destroyed cities, yet they still did not return to Him.

questions.question: What is the main point of the repeated phrase, 'yet you have not returned to me'?
options: God's judgment on Israel was random
Israel remained unresponsive and hardened to God's discipline
God's love for Israel had completely disappeared
Israel believed they had not sinned and did not need to return
questions.explanation: Despite God's various forms of discipline, Israel consistently refused to return to Him, demonstrating their stubbornness and unrepentant hearts.

questions.question: According to Amos 4:12, what does 'prepare to meet your God, O Israel' remind us of today?
options: We should actively seek worldly success
We must prepare ourselves to finally meet God by examining our hearts and repenting
God will always be patient, so we don't need to rush to repent
It is enough to appear outwardly religious
questions.explanation: This verse calls Israel to take God's judgment and His call seriously, to prepare their hearts to meet the righteous and holy God. It serves as a similar reminder for us today.

en.reflection: Today's passage reminds us that God is both just and loving. His discipline aims to call us back to Him. Have you noticed God's warnings or discipline in your life? How will you respond?
reflectionOptions: Give thanks for God's discipline in my life
Ask God to help me be more sensitive to His presence and guidance
en.prayer: Righteous and loving God, thank You for reminding me through Your Word that You are the One who rules over all and judges all. Please help me to always maintain a watchful and humble heart, eager to respond to Your call. May my heart continually turn back to You, so that I do not miss Your grace due to a hardened heart. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to quietly pray before God about any areas in your life that may need repentance and turning back to Him.

en.focus: True life is not found in religious rituals, but in seeking justice, hating evil, and having an authentic relationship with God.

questions.question: What kind of message does the prophet Amos declare for Israel at the beginning of this chapter?
options: A declaration of victory
A lament
A prayer of blessing
A psalm of thanksgiving
questions.explanation: Amos begins with a lament for the house of Israel, foretelling their tragic end.

questions.question: What does the LORD repeatedly urge the people of Israel to seek through Amos?
options: To seek Bethel
To seek Gilgal
To seek Beersheba
To seek the LORD
questions.explanation: God explicitly commands the Israelites to 'seek the LORD and live,' rather than seeking the places of idol worship.

questions.question: According to this passage, how does God view those who 'turn justice into bitterness and cast righteousness to the ground'?
options: He will continue to tolerate their sins
He will bless their wealth
He will despise their festivals and offerings
He will help them become stronger
questions.explanation: God clearly states that He despises and rejects the festivals and offerings of those who are hypocritical, acting unjustly while pretending to worship Him.

questions.question: What does this passage remind us about seeking God today?
options: Attending church activities is enough
God values our inner justice and actions more than external rituals
We can sin while worshipping God
Seeking God is only necessary when we face difficulties
questions.explanation: The book of Amos emphasizes that God requires inner integrity and righteous actions, which are far more important than formal religious rituals.

en.reflection: In what areas of your life might you be going through the motions instead of genuinely 'seeking the LORD' or living out His righteousness?
en.prayer: Righteous God, help me to genuinely seek You, not just through outward rituals, but by living out Your truth in my inner justice and actions. Help me to hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the gate, so that Your life may always be in me. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, choose one small action where you can show justice or compassion to someone, and put it into practice.

en.focus: God desires justice and righteousness, not mere religious rituals; He will judge those who offer hypocritical worship.

questions.question: What scene does the prophet Amos describe at the beginning of the passage?
options: People rejoicing at the city gates
Wailing in all the streets and squares
People offering abundant sacrifices in the temple
The king hosting a feast for the prophet in the palace
questions.explanation: The passage describes wailing in all the streets and squares, with farmers called to mourn and those skilled in lamentation summoned to weep.

questions.question: What was God's reaction to the festivals, sacrifices, and songs offered by the Israelites?
options: He delighted in their rich worship
He encouraged them to engage in more of these activities
He detested and rejected their hypocritical worship
He considered them irrelevant
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that He hates their festivals, takes no pleasure in their sacred assemblies, will not accept their burnt offerings or grain offerings, and will not listen to their songs.

questions.question: What does God most desire to see from His people?
options: More elaborate religious rituals
Justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like a never-failing stream
The building of taller temples
Displaying strong military power to neighboring nations
questions.explanation: God clearly states His desire: 'But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream.'

questions.question: What is the main warning this passage gives us?
options: Simply attending church activities pleases God
God values our inner integrity and pursuit of justice more than outward forms
Offering the most expensive sacrifices can atone for all sins
God is not concerned with social justice, only personal faith
questions.explanation: The book of Amos repeatedly emphasizes that God detests superficial religious rituals and instead values whether His people live out fairness and justice in their lives.

en.reflection: In what area of your life today does God value your inner integrity and righteous actions more than outward appearances?
reflectionOptions: Your motives in work or service
en.prayer: Righteous Father, I confess that sometimes I focus more on external religious forms, neglecting true justice and compassion in my heart. Help me to live a life where justice rolls on like a river and righteousness like a never-failing stream. May my worship not just be with my lips, but a genuine outflow of my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, when interacting with someone, intentionally look for an opportunity to practice fairness and justice, even in a small way.

en.focus: Judgment approaches when people indulge in pleasure and wealth, yet remain indifferent to God's justice and the suffering of the poor.

questions.question: Who does the prophet Amos denounce?
options: Those who turned away from God to worship idols
Those who are at ease in Zion and secure in Samaria
Those Israelite soldiers who lost battles
Those who failed to observe the Sabbath
questions.explanation: The passage begins by denouncing those who are at ease in Zion (Jerusalem) and secure in Samaria, feeling safe in their positions.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the lifestyle of these complacent people?
options: They worked diligently to accumulate wealth
They were busy worshipping God but neglected the poor
They reclined on beds of ivory, ate choice lambs and calves, drank wine from bowls, but were not grieved over the ruin of Joseph
They were concerned with politics and tried to change the nation's direction
questions.explanation: The text vividly portrays their luxurious and indulgent lifestyle: lounging on ivory beds, feasting, and drinking heavily, while being indifferent to the nation's spiritual and moral crisis and the suffering of the poor.

questions.question: Because of their sin, how will God judge these complacent people?
options: He will make them lose all their wealth and become poor
He will make them the first to go into exile among the nations
He will bring famine and plague upon them, but no exile
He will bring them to repentance and bless them again
questions.explanation: God declares that those who are at ease will be the first to go into exile, and their revelry will cease.

questions.question: What warning does this passage offer for our lives today?
options: It's fine to enjoy life as long as you have money, without worrying about consequences
God's judgment was only for ancient Israelites and is irrelevant to us
We can fall into spiritual danger when we focus solely on our own pleasure and become indifferent to the suffering of others and social justice
We should avoid all pleasure and live an ascetic life
questions.explanation: Amos reminds us that true security is not found in material wealth but in walking with God and caring for what He cares about. Indifference to injustice and suffering can lead to spiritual peril.

en.reflection: Are there any 'comfortable' areas in your life that have made you dull to God's will or the needs of those around you?
reflectionOptions: My pursuit of material comfort has surpassed my pursuit of God
I have become indifferent to social injustices
I focus only on my own comfort, neglecting the needs of others
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, forgive me for sometimes falling into the sin of complacency and self-satisfaction. When I indulge in my own pleasures and become numb to Your justice and the suffering of those around me, please awaken my heart. Help me to live alertly, to see the world through Your eyes, and to live out love and justice. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, intentionally pray for someone you usually don't think about, or do a small act of care for another person.

en.theme: God's Eternal Plan and His Mercy
en.focus: Even in judgment, God remains merciful and has an eternal plan of salvation for His people.

questions.question: How many visions did the prophet Amos see in this book?
options: Three
Four
Five
Six
questions.explanation: Amos 7:1-9:15 records five visions seen by Amos: locusts, fire, a plumb line, a basket of summer fruit, and the Lord standing by the altar.

questions.question: In the first two visions, what was God's response when Amos interceded for Israel?
options: God immediately brought judgment
God said He had decided not to have mercy
God relented from the disaster He had threatened
God rebuked Amos for his intercession
questions.explanation: After Amos interceded for Israel, God relented and said, 'This will not happen.' This shows God's mercy.

questions.question: What important truth is emphasized in Amos 9:7-10?
options: Israel is the only nation chosen by God
God only cares about the welfare of Israel
God controls the destiny of all nations and judges righteously
God has abandoned Israel forever
questions.explanation: These verses highlight that God is not only the God of Israel but also controls the destiny of the Cushites, Philistines, and Arameans, judging and guiding all peoples righteously.

questions.question: Despite the judgment, what hope does the final section of Amos (9:11-15) give to the people of Israel?
options: They will no longer face any enemies
They will rebuild the walls of Jerusalem
God will restore the fallen tent of David, granting them renewed inheritance and blessings
They will rule over all other nations
questions.explanation: God promises to restore the fallen tent of David, rebuild and restore Israel, granting them renewed inheritance and abundant blessings.

en.reflection: In today's reading, how do you see God's justice and mercy coexisting? What insight does this bring to your life today?
reflectionOptions: Reminds me of God's power and sovereignty
Motivates me to trust in God's mercy more
Helps me understand God's attributes more deeply
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for being the sovereign God. Your justice is perfect, yet Your mercy is so vast. Please help me to trust in Your eternal plan and promises even when facing life's challenges. May my life glorify Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to meditate on God's justice and mercy, and thank Him for both.

en.focus: God will justly judge all pride and evil, and His people will be restored.

questions.question: Which nation is the primary subject of the vision Obadiah received?
options: Egypt
Assyria
Edom
Babylon
questions.explanation: The book of Obadiah clearly states from the beginning that this is a vision concerning Edom.

questions.question: What was Edom's primary sin?
options: Idolatry
Pride and malicious rejoicing over Jacob (Israel)
Greed and seizing neighbouring lands
Disregarding the Sabbath
questions.explanation: The text repeatedly mentions Edom's pride due to living in rocky strongholds, and their malicious inaction or even active participation against Jacob in his time of trouble.

questions.question: What will be the outcome of God's judgment on Edom?
options: Edom will become a great nation
Edom will gain more allies
Edom's wealth will increase
Edom will be utterly destroyed and left with nothing
questions.explanation: God declares that Edom will be 'despised,' 'cut off,' and 'utterly destroyed,' with all their treasures searched out.

questions.question: How does the message of Obadiah encourage us to trust God?
options: God only cares about powerful nations
God is indifferent to justice
God is a righteous judge who will punish evil and vindicate His people
Human pride ultimately leads to success
questions.explanation: This book reveals God's judgment against pride and evil, and His promise of restoration and salvation for Israel, demonstrating His justice and sovereignty.

en.reflection: Are there any injustices in your life today that you need to bring before our righteous God?
reflectionOptions: Pray for those who are suffering
Forgive someone who has wronged me
Ask God to help me overcome pride
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, thank You for being the sovereign God who will judge all evil and pride. Please help me to remove pride from my heart and walk humbly with You. When I face injustice in this world, strengthen my faith, knowing that You will ultimately bring justice. In Jesus' name, I pray, Amen.
en.action: Meditate for one minute on God's justice and sovereignty, and commit one matter of injustice to Him.

en.focus: God’s sovereignty extends over all things, and His will shall be accomplished even when humans try to flee.

questions.question: What was God's first command to Jonah?
options: Go preach in Jerusalem
Go to Nineveh and proclaim judgment
Go shepherd the people of Judah
Go declare the gospel to foreign nations
questions.explanation: The word of the LORD came to Jonah, commanding him to go to Nineveh and preach against it because its wickedness had come before God.

questions.question: What action did Jonah take in response to God's command?
options: Immediately obeyed and went to Nineveh
Asked God for more details
Arose to flee to Tarshish, away from the LORD
Gathered people to strategize
questions.explanation: Jonah rose, not to go to Nineveh, but to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

questions.question: How did God respond when Jonah was fleeing on the ship?
options: Allowed Jonah to go to Tarshish
Calmed the sea and protected the ship
Sent a great wind on the sea, threatening to break the ship apart
Appeared to Jonah and rebuked him personally
questions.explanation: The LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship was about to break up.

questions.question: How does the beginning of Jonah's story demonstrate God's sovereignty?
options: God only has sovereignty over Israelites
People can easily escape God's will
God's sovereignty transcends geographical boundaries and human choices
God only has sovereignty within the temple
questions.explanation: Even as Jonah fled to Tarshish, God was able to send a storm and control the sea, demonstrating that His sovereignty is absolute and no one can escape His will.

en.reflection: Is there a call or responsibility from God in your life that you are currently trying to avoid?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of a fleeing heart
Seek wisdom and courage to face it
en.prayer: Almighty Father, You are the Lord of heaven, earth, and sea. Please help me to turn back to You when I am tempted to flee from Your will. May I no longer act according to my own desires, but humbly obey Your call. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend 5 minutes in quiet reflection today: What is God's recent calling in my life? Am I willing to obey?

en.focus: Even in the darkest depths, God hears and saves those who genuinely cry out to Him in repentance.

questions.question: From where did Jonah pray to the LORD?
options: Inside the ship's hold
In the city of Nineveh
From inside the fish
On the seashore
questions.explanation: Jonah prayed to the LORD from inside the fish after he was swallowed.

questions.question: What did Jonah confess to God in his prayer?
options: That he was a good person
That he had been banished from God's sight
That he had never made mistakes
That he was more spiritual than others
questions.explanation: Jonah confessed that he had been cast out of God's sight and acknowledged his sin.

questions.question: What is the primary lesson from Jonah's experience in this chapter?
options: You can escape God's will by running away
God only saves obedient people
God can hear and save those who seek Him, no matter the circumstances
Human prayers have no effect on God
questions.explanation: Despite Jonah's disobedience and dire situation, God heard his cry and saved him, demonstrating His mercy and power.

questions.question: What was Jonah's ultimate action in Jonah chapter 2?
options: To continue running away
To complain about God's injustice
To give thanks and offer sacrifices of praise
To ask God for more time
questions.explanation: At the end of his prayer, Jonah declared his intention to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to God and fulfill his vows.

en.reflection: Are you facing any 'fish belly' situations today, needing to cry out to God with sincere repentance and honesty?
reflectionOptions: Ask God to reveal Himself in my struggle
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for being a God who hears our prayers even in desperate situations. When I feel trapped, hopeless, or far from You, remind me of Your vast and deep mercy. May I turn back to You and offer my life with a heart of gratitude. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment today to pour out your deepest struggles or fears to God, trusting that He hears you.

en.theme: The Power of Obedience and Repentance
en.focus: God's mercy is vast, and He is willing to forgive those who repent, but His people must obey His commands.

questions.question: Where did God command Jonah to go when He spoke to him a second time?
options: To Tarshish
To Joppa
To Nineveh
To Bethel
questions.explanation: God commanded Jonah a second time to go to Nineveh and proclaim the message He gave him.

questions.question: How did the people of Nineveh respond to Jonah's proclamation?
options: They mocked and drove Jonah away
They believed God and proclaimed a fast, putting on sackcloth
They immediately attacked Israel
They ignored Jonah and continued their wicked ways
questions.explanation: The people of Nineveh believed God. They proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least of them.

questions.question: How did the king of Nineveh respond to Jonah's message?
options: He ordered Jonah to be executed
He gathered his army to resist God
He rose from his throne, took off his royal robes, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in the dust
He issued a decree for everyone to offer sacrifices to idols
questions.explanation: When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he also responded with repentance: he rose from his throne, removed his royal robes, covered himself with sackcloth, sat in the dust, and issued a decree for a nationwide fast.

questions.question: What important lesson about God's character can we learn from this passage?
options: God only saves the people of Israel
God's anger is unchangeable, and He will always bring judgment
God is a God of great mercy and grace, willing to relent from disaster when people repent
People can manipulate God's decisions through their actions
questions.explanation: This passage clearly shows that God 'relented' from the disaster He had threatened because of the Ninevites' repentance, revealing Him as a God full of mercy.

en.reflection: Today, is there any 'Nineveh' in your life that requires you to bravely obey God's leading to deliver His message, or is there personal repentance you need to make to God?
reflectionOptions: Obey God to share the Gospel
Confess and repent of personal sins to God
en.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for being a God full of mercy and grace, slow to anger, and willing to forgive those who repent. Please help me, no matter the challenge, to obey Your commands like Jonah eventually did, and bravely proclaim Your truth. Please also illuminate my life; if there is anything I need to repent of, grant me a humble heart to turn back to You immediately. In Jesus' name, I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to pray for yourself or someone you know who needs to repent and turn to God, asking for His mercy.

en.focus: God's compassion for all creation far exceeds human understanding, and His desire for all people to repent and be saved challenges our narrow perspectives and self-righteousness.

questions.question: What was Jonah's reaction when God did not destroy Nineveh as he expected?
options: He was glad that the Ninevites repented.
He was greatly displeased and angry.
He was confused and didn't understand God's decision.
He immediately returned to Israel, no longer caring about Nineveh.
questions.explanation: Jonah was “greatly displeased and became angry” because God did not destroy Nineveh.

questions.question: What was Jonah's main complaint to God?
options: God did not listen to his prayer.
God withdrew His prophecy, making him look like a false prophet.
He knew God was a “gracious and compassionate God,” and thus expected God to forgive Nineveh.
He believed the Ninevites did not deserve God's forgiveness.
questions.explanation: Jonah complained that he knew God was “a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity,” which is why he initially did not want to go to Nineveh.

questions.question: How did God teach Jonah about the value of His compassion?
options: God taught him by letting Jonah experience hunger.
God taught Jonah by making a castor oil plant grow and then wither.
God taught him by letting Jonah see the misery of the Ninevites.
God taught him by directly rebuking Jonah's selfishness.
questions.explanation: God caused a castor oil plant to grow for shade and then caused a worm to destroy it, illustrating Jonah's concern for his own comfort over compassion for the people of Nineveh.

questions.question: What is the main message of Jonah chapter 4?
options: God loves only the Israelites, not foreigners.
The prophet Jonah is a flawless role model.
God’s compassion and love far exceed human narrowness; He cares for all creation.
God will immediately destroy sinful cities if the gospel is preached.
questions.explanation: This chapter contrasts Jonah's narrow perspective with God's vast compassion, emphasizing God's concern for the many people and animals in Nineveh.

en.reflection: Today, do you have any narrow perspectives like Jonah, lacking God's compassion for certain groups or individuals?
reflectionOptions: For someone who disagrees with me
en.prayer: Merciful and loving Heavenly Father, forgive me for sometimes being like Jonah, caring only for my own feelings and lacking compassion for those You love. Help me to broaden my heart, to see people through Your eyes, and to be willing to bring Your love to them. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, pray for someone around you whom you dislike or don't understand, asking God to give you a heart of compassion.

en.focus: God is a righteous judge, and His judgment on sin is real and inevitable, yet He also calls His people to return.

questions.question: Which two nations or cities are mentioned in Micah's vision?
options: Egypt and Assyria
Israel and Syria
Samaria and Jerusalem
Babylon and Persia
questions.explanation: Micah's vision concerned Samaria and Jerusalem, representing the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah.

questions.question: What happens to the natural world when God descends from His holy temple to judge?
options: The earth is filled with flowers and fruit
The mountains melt under Him, and the valleys split apart
The sky sends down refreshing rain
Animals gather and live together peacefully
questions.explanation: The passage describes mountains melting under Him and valleys splitting apart, like waters pouring down a slope, when God descends for judgment.

questions.question: Why did Samaria and Jerusalem face God's judgment?
options: Because they did not build magnificent temples
Because of their idolatry and various transgressions
Because they did not form alliances with other nations
Because they failed to participate in warfare
questions.explanation: Samaria's sin was idolatry and unfaithfulness to God, while Jerusalem's sin involved the transgressions and injustice of its leaders.

questions.question: What does the message of judgment in Micah chapter 1 remind us of in our lives today?
options: Outward religious rituals are sufficient
God is lenient with sin, so we don't need to worry
God is righteous and will judge our actions, so we must take sin seriously
Only people in ancient times needed to fear God's judgment
questions.explanation: Micah's message reminds us that God is holy and just, and He will judge sin. We too should take our sins seriously today and repent to God.

en.reflection: What aspects of your life, warned by Micah's message, might have drifted from God's heart and need to be brought back to Him?
reflectionOptions: Reflecting on any injustice in my words or actions
Taking God's teachings and commands more seriously
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, I acknowledge that You are holy and you hate sin. Please shine Your light on me, that I may see any hidden sins in my life, especially those areas where I have strayed from Your heart. Grant me a repentant heart, help me to turn back to You, and live a life that pleases You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time in prayer today, asking God to reveal any areas in your life that are not pleasing to Him, and honestly confess and repent.

en.theme: God's Judgment on Injustice and His Promise
en.focus: God hates injustice and oppression. His judgment is righteous, but He also preserves a remnant with a promise of restoration.

questions.question: What kind of sin is described in Micah 2:1–2?
options: Idolatry
Disregarding the Sabbath
Plotting evil, coveting and seizing property
Cowardice on the battlefield
questions.explanation: The text describes people who devise evil on their beds, rise early to carry it out, coveting fields and houses, and then seizing them.

questions.question: How will God respond to those who plot evil deeds?
options: Send abundant rain to make their fields fruitful
Make them even richer and more powerful
Decree disaster upon them, from which they cannot escape
Forgive all their sins without holding them accountable
questions.explanation: The LORD says, 'I am planning disaster against this people, an inescapable disaster for your necks.'

questions.question: In verses 6-7, how did the people react when the prophet Micah delivered God's message? What does this reveal about their mindset?
options: They welcomed God's words and immediately repented
They thought Micah was crazy and ignored him
They refused to listen, believing such messages of disaster should not be preached, showing their hard-heartedness and unwillingness to confront sin
They were merely curious but took no action
questions.explanation: The people told the prophet, 'Do not preach! Do not preach about these things; disgrace will not overtake us.' They refused to hear messages of judgment, revealing their insensitivity to sin and hard-heartedness.

questions.question: Despite the judgment, what ultimate promise does God give to His people (the remnant)?
options: To make them the most powerful empire
To gather them like sheep, breaking through barriers, with a king leading them
To allow them to continue doing evil unpunished
To scatter them forever, without hope
questions.explanation: God promises to surely gather all of Jacob, to bring together the remnant of Israel, like sheep in a pen, they will break through and their King will pass before them.

en.reflection: Today's scripture reminds us that God hates all injustice and oppression. In your life, have you ever treated others unjustly, or harbored thoughts of greed and seizing what is not yours?
reflectionOptions: Confess and repent of my sins
Seek reconciliation with someone I have wronged
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, thank You for reminding me through today's scripture that You are a God who hates sin. Please search my heart and remove all thoughts and actions of greed, injustice, and oppression. Help me to treat everyone around me with Your love and righteousness. May Your will be done in my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, think of someone you might have treated unjustly and pray to God about it, asking for an opportunity to make amends or restore the relationship.

en.theme: The Sins of Leaders and God's Judgment
en.focus: True justice comes from God, who will judge all leaders who deviate from His will.

questions.question: At the beginning of Micah chapter 3, whom does the prophet Micah rebuke?
options: The people of Israel
The priests of Israel
The rulers and leaders of Israel
The soldiers of Israel
questions.explanation: Micah 3:1 clearly states that the prophet is speaking to “the heads of Jacob and you rulers of the house of Israel.”

questions.question: How does the prophet Micah describe the way these leaders treat the people?
options: They care for the people like shepherds
They treat the people like tearing meat
They protect the people like building houses
They cultivate the people like gardeners
questions.explanation: The text describes the leaders' cruel oppression of the people by saying they “eat the flesh of my people and strip their skin from them, and break their bones.”

questions.question: Because of the evil deeds of these leaders, how will God respond to their prayers?
options: God will immediately forgive their sins
God will make them richer and more powerful
God will hide His face and not listen to their cries
God will send angels to help them
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that when they cry out to the LORD, He will not answer them but will hide His face from them.

questions.question: What is God's ultimate judgment on Jerusalem and the temple?
options: Jerusalem will become the capital of the world
The temple will become a center of worship
Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple hill a forest
Jerusalem will have strong walls
questions.explanation: Micah 3:12 prophesies that because of the leaders' sins, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple hill will be like a forest.

en.reflection: Have you ever felt disappointed or hurt by the actions of leaders? How do you view God's judgment on injustice?
reflectionOptions: Pray for the leaders around you
Reflect on whether you have acted unjustly
en.prayer: Righteous LORD, thank You that You are the God who judges all injustice. Help me to see Your integrity and righteousness, and enlighten me so that no matter my position, I may act justly and love my neighbor as myself. May my heart be solely devoted to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Pray for your church leaders or national leaders, asking God to grant them wisdom and a heart of justice to lead according to His will.

en.theme: The Glory and Hope of Mount Zion
en.focus: God promises that in the last days, His holy mountain will become the center where all nations seek truth and justice.

questions.question: Micah 4:1 describes what will happen to the mountain of the Lord's temple in the last days?
options: It will be utterly destroyed and uninhabited
It will become an ordinary mountain, losing its sacredness
It will be established as the highest of the mountains, exalted above the hills, and peoples will stream to it
It will be surrounded by high walls, isolated from the world
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that in the last days, the mountain of the Lord's temple will be established as the highest of the mountains, exalted above the hills, and all nations will stream to it.

questions.question: When all nations stream to the mountain of the Lord, how will they seek His instruction?
options: They will govern themselves, not obeying God's commands
They will say, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the temple of the God of Jacob.'
They will build their own temples and worship other gods
They will fight each other, leading to division
questions.explanation: The passage describes nations actively inviting one another, saying, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the temple of the God of Jacob. He will teach us his ways, so that we may walk in his paths.'

questions.question: What kind of future peace is depicted in Micah 4:3–4?
options: Nations will still fight each other, but with more advanced weapons
People will each own their land, but still live in fear
Nations will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks, and will no longer train for war
Everyone will live in cities, and there will be no rural life
questions.explanation: These verses paint a picture of complete peace: nations will transform weapons into farming tools, no longer train for war, and everyone will live securely without fear.

questions.question: What is the significance of the vision of peace and justice described in Micah 4:1–5 for our lives today?
options: Since the future is good, we don't need to strive for it today
It reminds us that God controls history and His promises will be fulfilled, inspiring us to live as witnesses of peace
It's merely a beautiful fantasy, unrelated to reality
We should strive to build a world without religious belief
questions.explanation: This passage shows us God's sovereignty over the future and His perfect plan, which should motivate us to live out peace, hope, and justice today.

en.reflection: How does the future vision of peace in Micah 4 strengthen your hope in God's sovereignty and ultimate redemption?
reflectionOptions: The future is full of hope, bringing comfort to my heart
God is in control, and I want to trust Him more
I see so much conflict in the world today, I need to pray more for peace
en.prayer: Almighty Father, thank You for revealing Your magnificent plan of redemption and Your promises for Mount Zion and all nations through the book of Micah. Strengthen my faith, enable me to live in Your hope, and be a witness of peace and justice in this world. May Your kingdom come, and Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute today thinking: If the world were as peaceful as Micah describes, who would you most want to share that joy with? Then pray for that person.

en.theme: The Shepherd King and the Remnant
en.focus: God will raise up a Shepherd King from Bethlehem who will gather and shepherd His remnant, ultimately bringing peace and victory.

questions.question: According to Micah 5:2, where will the ruler who is to rise come from?
options: Jerusalem
Bethlehem Ephrathah
The wilderness of Judah
Damascus
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that this ruler will come from 'Bethlehem Ephrathah'.

questions.question: What special action will this coming ruler perform?
options: Build mighty city walls
Shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD
Form alliances with other nations
Establish new laws
questions.explanation: The passage says this King 'will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD His God'.

questions.type: Understand the role of the remnant
questions.question: How does the passage describe God's 'remnant' among the nations?
options: Like hidden treasures
Like a lion and like dew
Like abandoned orphans
Like sleeping giants
questions.explanation: The remnant of Jacob will be like a lion among the beasts and like dew from the LORD, bringing refreshment and power.

questions.question: What is the main message conveyed in Micah 5:1–15?
options: Israel's army will defeat all its enemies.
God will save and shepherd His people through a King from Bethlehem, and purify them.
All foreign nations will ultimately be completely destroyed with no hope.
True peace can only be established through human effort.
questions.explanation: This passage prophesies the birth of Christ, His work of shepherding and salvation, God's purification of His people, and judgment on idols, leading to peace.

en.reflection: In what area of your life today do you most need Jesus, your Shepherd King, to guide and shepherd you?
reflectionOptions: Seeking His love and wisdom in relationships
en.prayer: Lord Jesus, my Shepherd King, thank You for coming from Bethlehem to shepherd and save me. Please guide me today with Your strength and majesty. Help me find true peace and direction in You. Enable me to trust Your leading and live a life pleasing to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Find a quiet moment to meditate on Jesus as your Good Shepherd and offer a specific prayer to Him.

en.focus: God calls His people to remember His grace and reminds them of what He truly desires.

questions.question: Who does God call to listen to His complaint in Micah 6:1–2?
options: The kings of the nations
The prophets of Israel
The mountains and the enduring foundations of the earth
The army of Assyria
questions.explanation: God calls the mountains and the enduring foundations of the earth to be witnesses to His complaint against His people.

questions.question: What actions does God remind His people of in Micah 6:4–5?
options: Giving them land and wealth
Bringing them out of Egypt, sending leaders, and frustrating enemy plans
Granting them victory over all enemies
Building strong walls for them
questions.explanation: God reminds them that He brought them out of Egypt, sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, and thwarted Balak's plan.

questions.question: What does Micah 6:6–8 clearly state that God truly requires of people?
options: Thousands of rams and ten thousands of rivers of oil
Offering their firstborn child
To act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God
To strictly follow all legal statutes
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that God requires people to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.

questions.question: How does this passage challenge our faith today?
options: It encourages us to increase the quantity of our sacrifices
It reminds us not to forget God's past grace and to live a life pleasing to Him
It tells us that faith alone is enough, without actions
It teaches us to focus only on personal spiritual growth, ignoring social justice
questions.explanation: Micah reminds us not to forget God's past grace towards us and to live out what pleases Him: justice, mercy, and humbly walking with Him.

en.reflection: Reflecting on God's grace in your life, in which area can you more specifically live out 'to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God' today?
reflectionOptions: Speaking out or acting against injustice
Showing mercy to someone in need around you
Humbly seeking God's will in daily decisions
en.prayer: Lord, thank You for being a faithful and covenant-keeping God who always deals with me in grace. Help me to always remember Your works in my life and not forget Your steadfast love. Guide me, I pray, that I may live a life of acting justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, intentionally find one specific action to show mercy to someone you might usually overlook.

en.focus: Even in the darkest times, we can find hope in God's compassion and His faithful promises.

questions.question: What feelings does the prophet Micah express at the beginning of Micah chapter 7?
options: Joy and gratitude
Anger and complaint
Despair and lament
Peace and contentment
questions.explanation: The prophet begins by expressing despair and lament over the moral decay of society, crying out, 'What misery is mine!'

questions.question: How is God described in Micah 7:18?
options: A God quick to anger
A God who delights in punishment
A God who delights in showing mercy
A God who stays far from evil
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that God 'delights to show mercy' and does not stay angry forever.

questions.question: How does Micah chapter 7 portray God's ultimate intention for His people?
options: To punish them eternally
To abandon them completely
To show mercy and restore them
To leave them to their own devices
questions.explanation: Despite acknowledging the people's sin, the chapter ultimately points to God's mercy, forgiveness, and restoration, as He will again have compassion.

questions.question: What hope does Micah chapter 7 offer to those facing difficult circumstances or societal corruption?
options: Everything can change if we try harder
Hope lies in waiting for the end of the world
Hope lies in God's forgiveness, mercy, and faithfulness
Hope lies in finding new leaders
questions.explanation: Even in despair, the prophet places his hope in God's forgiveness, mercy, and His promise to fulfill His covenant.

en.reflection: When you face your own weaknesses or the corruption around you, how does Micah 7 encourage you to place your hope in God?
en.prayer: Dear Lord, my heart sometimes feels heavy when I recognize my own sins and the brokenness of the world. Thank You that You are a God who delights in showing mercy and forgiving sin. Help me to place my hope completely in Your faithfulness and compassion. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Quietly reflect on Micah 7:18 and thank God that He is a God who delights in showing mercy.

en.theme: The LORD is a Good Refuge
en.focus: God is a faithful and just Judge who provides refuge for those who trust in Him.

questions.question: How is Nineveh described in Nahum 1:1?
options: A city of great wisdom
A city of bloodshed
A wealthy city
A city loved by God
questions.explanation: Nahum 1:1 refers to Nineveh as 'the bloody city,' foreshadowing God's judgment upon it.

questions.question: According to the passage, what attribute does the LORD display towards His adversaries?
options: Quick to anger
Slow to anger
Merciful and forgiving
Inactive
questions.explanation: The passage states that the LORD is 'slow to anger and great in power,' but 'will not leave the guilty unpunished.'

questions.question: How does the passage describe the LORD's treatment of those who take refuge in Him?
options: He will forget them
He is a stronghold in times of trouble
He will leave them to face difficulties alone
He will increase their wealth
questions.explanation: The text clearly states, 'The LORD is good, a refuge in times of trouble. He cares for those who trust in him.'

questions.question: What is the core message of Nahum chapter 1?
options: God only cares about Israel and not other nations
God executes righteous judgment on the wicked but offers loving protection to those who trust Him
Human destiny is entirely self-determined, without divine involvement
God unconditionally forgives all sin without the need for repentance
questions.explanation: This chapter emphasizes both God's judgment on wicked Nineveh and His goodness and protection for those who take refuge in Him.

en.reflection: When faced with anxieties or challenges in life, do you believe the LORD is your refuge? How do you take refuge in Him?
reflectionOptions: By casting my anxieties on Him in prayer
By seeking His Word more deeply
By sharing with trusted fellow believers and seeking support
en.prayer: Almighty Father, You are good, a refuge in times of trouble. Help me to fully take refuge in You, trusting in Your justice and love when I face anxieties and challenges. May my heart find peace in You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, when you feel worried, pause and silently say, 'The LORD is my refuge,' and offer a prayer to Him.

en.focus: God is just; He will punish evil and vindicate His people, but His judgment also carries a promise of deliverance.

questions.question: What declaration does God make against Nineveh at the beginning of Nahum 2:1?
options: A promise of peace
A call to repentance
A warning of judgment
An invitation to alliance
questions.explanation: The passage begins with a strong declaration of judgment and attack against Nineveh, describing an 'attacker coming up against you'.

questions.question: How is the fall of Nineveh described in the passage?
options: Walls collapsing and people fleeing
Chariots dashing and swords flashing
Storehouses burned and livestock killed
Kings captured and priests disgraced
questions.explanation: The text vividly portrays a scene of warfare with chariots dashing wildly and flashing swords and spears, signaling Nineveh's destruction.

questions.question: Why does the Lord bring such severe judgment upon Nineveh?
options: Because Nineveh was a city of wealth
Because Nineveh oppressed God's people and was full of bloodshed and lies
Because Nineveh worshipped false gods
Because Nineveh did not have a strong army
questions.explanation: The passage indicates that the Lord's judgment is due to Nineveh's oppression of His people, Israel, and its sins of lies and bloodshed.

questions.question: How does Nahum's prophecy against Nineveh reveal God's attributes?
options: God's love and mercy
God's patience and forgiveness
God's justice and power
God's silence and hiddenness
questions.explanation: This passage clearly demonstrates God's righteous judgment against evil and His immense power in executing that judgment, bringing justice to the oppressed.

en.reflection: How does Nahum's description of God strengthen your faith when you witness injustice and evil in the world?
reflectionOptions: Trust that God will ultimately bring justice
Grow in reverence for God's authority
Pray for those who are oppressed
en.prayer: Righteous Father, thank You that You are the sovereign Lord who does not tolerate evil and will judge all things according to Your justice. Strengthen my heart to trust in Your faithfulness and power amidst the injustices of this world. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a moment today to pray for a social injustice you are aware of, or for an oppressed group, asking God to bring His justice.

en.theme: The End of Wickedness and God's Justice
en.focus: God is a righteous judge; wickedness will ultimately face its consequences, and His people find refuge in Him.

questions.question: How is the city (Nineveh) described in Nahum 3:1?
options: Full of peace and prosperity
Full of lies, violence, and plunder
Full of wisdom and knowledge
Full of worship and sacrifice
questions.explanation: The passage immediately describes the city as 'Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without victims!'

questions.question: What kind of judgment did Nineveh's wickedness bring upon it?
options: Famine and plague
Burning by fire and disgrace before nations
Swallowed by the desert
Flooded by water
questions.explanation: God declares that Nineveh will be 'consumed by fire' and He will 'expose your nakedness to the nations, your shame to the kingdoms,' indicating judgment and disgrace.

questions.question: What attribute of God can we learn from this passage?
options: He is a God who always forgives evil
He is a God uninterested in human affairs
He is a righteous judge who will not overlook sin
He is a God who values outward rituals over inner heart
questions.explanation: The message of Nahum clearly demonstrates God's righteous judgment against Nineveh's wickedness, showing Him to be a just God who does not tolerate sin.

questions.question: How does this passage remind us to live before God?
options: We can do as we please, for God will ultimately forgive everything
We should live in constant fear, for God might punish at any moment
We should be watchful of our words and actions, knowing God is just, while also trusting in His mercy
We don't need to concern ourselves with worldly injustice, as God will handle it
questions.explanation: God's justice reminds us to revere Him and be careful in our actions. At the same time, knowing God is just assures us His judgments are not arbitrary, and He extends mercy to those who seek Him.
questions.evidence: Nahum 3:18-19 (implicitly points to the consequence of sin, thus prompting believers on how to live)

en.reflection: What tendency towards 'lies' or 'violence' (even subtle ones) in your daily life does this passage call you to be most vigilant about or repent of today?
reflectionOptions: Impatience or harshness towards others or self
Gaining advantage through dishonesty or unfair means
en.prayer: Righteous Lord, You are the God who searches hearts. Please shine Your light on me, that I may see any sinful tendencies in my life that are not pleasing to You, whether in words, thoughts, or actions of 'lies' or 'violence.' Forgive me, and grant me strength to live with honesty, gentleness, and justice. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, try to say a genuine word of encouragement or thanks to at least one person, instead of criticism or complaint.

en.focus: Even in confusion and perplexity, we can bring our honest questions to God and trust in His justice and sovereignty.

questions.question: What was Habakkuk's initial cry to God?
options: A request for more blessings
A question about why evil prevailed and God seemed silent
A plea for instructions on defeating enemies
A desire for Israel to be the greatest nation
questions.explanation: Habakkuk 1:2-4 shows the prophet's initial complaint to God about the rampant wickedness and God's apparent inaction.

questions.question: How did God respond to Habakkuk's initial complaint?
options: God promised to immediately destroy all sinners
God revealed He was raising up the Chaldeans to bring judgment
God assured Habakkuk not to worry about worldly affairs
God stated He would no longer intervene in human affairs
questions.explanation: God responded by stating He was raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians), a fierce nation, to bring judgment upon Judah.

questions.question: After God's response, what new perplexity did Habakkuk raise concerning God's justice?
options: Why God would use a nation more wicked than Judah to judge them
Why God would not immediately restore Judah
Why God did not grant Habakkuk supernatural powers
Why God did not directly reveal Himself to the world
questions.explanation: Habakkuk questioned why God would use the wicked Chaldeans, who were even more unrighteous than Judah, to punish His own people.

questions.question: What key truth does Habakkuk chapter 1 primarily demonstrate?
options: If we pray enough, God will always do what we want
We can honestly express our confusion to God when facing injustice
God only listens to the prayers of those who are perfectly holy
Humans cannot understand God's ways, so they should not ask questions
questions.explanation: Habakkuk chapter 1 shows that even when perplexed by injustice and God's response, the prophet could pour out his heart to God and ask honest questions.

en.reflection: Is there something in your life currently causing you confusion or perplexity, making you want to question God?
reflectionOptions: Concerned about the state of the church or nation
en.prayer: Almighty Father, You are righteous and sovereign over all. When I face confusion and perplexity, help me to open my heart to You and bring my questions before You. Strengthen my faith, so I can trust in Your wisdom and sovereignty, even when I do not understand. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take a quiet moment to express one of your confusions or questions to God in your own words.

en.focus: Even in times of trouble, God's promised vision will surely come to pass, and the righteous will live by faith.

questions.question: Where did the prophet Habakkuk wait for God's answer?
options: In the temple
On the city wall
In the wilderness
In his own home
questions.explanation: Habakkuk states that he will stand at his watchpost and station himself on the ramparts, to see what the LORD will say to him.

questions.question: What did God command Habakkuk to write the vision clearly on?
options: A scroll of parchment
Stone tablets
Clay tablets
Tablets (prepared boards)
questions.explanation: God commanded Habakkuk to write the vision clearly on tablets so that a runner may read it easily.

questions.question: What key message did God emphasize about the fulfillment of the vision?
options: The vision will be fulfilled immediately
The vision will be delayed indefinitely and never happen
Though it lingers, the vision will surely come, so wait for it
The fulfillment of the vision depends on human effort
questions.explanation: God said: “For still the vision awaits its appointed time; it hastens to the end—it will not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay.”

questions.question: How should one respond while waiting for God's promises?
options: Strive for it by one's own strength
Complain about God's injustice
Live by faith and wait patiently
Give up hope and go with the flow
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states, “but the righteous shall live by his faith,” emphasizing living by faith while waiting for God’s promises.

en.reflection: In your life, what promises or guidance from God are you currently waiting for Him to fulfill?
reflectionOptions: Waiting for improvement in family relationships
Waiting for guidance in work or ministry
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being a faithful God whose promises never fail. Please help me to maintain faith and patience in waiting, not losing heart or giving up. May my life be lived by faith, bringing glory to Your name. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some time today quietly reflecting on a promise you are waiting for, and offer a prayer of faith to God.

en.focus: Even in the toughest times, we can rejoice in God’s faithfulness and the strength He provides.

questions.question: In what form is the prophet Habakkuk's prayer presented?
options: A psalm of praise
A lament
A word of instruction
A contemplative song
questions.explanation: The text states that this is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, 'according to Shigionoth,' indicating a contemplative song meant to be sung with musical accompaniment.

questions.type: Observe the prophet's description of God
questions.question: How does the prophet describe God's appearance and power in his prayer?
options: He is like a gentle breeze, softly whispering
His splendor covers the heavens, and the earth is full of His praise
He is like a kind father, seated on a throne
He is like a solitary king, far removed from the world
questions.explanation: The prophet describes God's appearance with immense power and glory, stating, 'His splendor covers the heavens, and the earth is full of His praise.'

questions.type: Understand the core of the prophet's prayer
questions.question: Despite seeing future hardship and destruction, how does Habakkuk ultimately choose to respond?
options: Complain about God's injustice and seek human help
Feel hopeless and lose all expectation
Rejoice in the LORD and be joyful in God his Savior
Flee his home to escape the coming disaster
questions.explanation: At the end of the passage, Habakkuk expresses great faith, choosing to rejoice and be joyful in God even amidst dire circumstances.

questions.question: How does this chapter help us face difficulties and uncertainties in life?
options: It encourages us to focus on our own efforts and plans
It reminds us to trust and rejoice in God even in hardship
It teaches us to praise God only when everything is going well
It implies that God will prevent all difficulties before they happen
questions.explanation: The core message of Habakkuk chapter 3 is that even when circumstances are extremely difficult and material provisions are lacking, we can still rejoice in God's power and the strength He provides, firmly trusting in Him.

en.reflection: When the 'fig tree does not blossom and there is no fruit on the vines' in your life, how do you choose to respond?
reflectionOptions: Turn to God for His strength and joy
en.prayer: Lord, thank You that You are my strength and my Savior. When my circumstances are tough and fear grips my heart, help me, like Habakkuk, to choose to rejoice in You and be joyful in You. Enable my feet to walk steadily on the heights, and grant me strength to face all things. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, even when facing small disappointments, try to turn to God with a grateful heart and offer Him praise.

en.theme: The Day of the LORD Is Near
en.focus: God's righteous judgment is coming, but there is still an opportunity for His people to repent and seek Him.

questions.question: To whom did the word of the LORD come at the beginning of Zephaniah?
options: King Josiah
King Hezekiah
Zephaniah
King David
questions.explanation: The book of Zephaniah clearly states that the word of the LORD came to Zephaniah.

questions.question: Who will be judged on the Day of the LORD?
options: All foreign nations
Only the wicked in Judah
All inhabitants, idol worshipers, and leaders who turned away from God
Only the rich, not the poor
questions.explanation: The text indicates that the judgment will fall upon the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem, those who worship Baal and the starry host, and those leaders who have turned away from the LORD and do not seek Him.

questions.question: How thorough will God's judgment be on the Day of the LORD?
options: Only a few extremely wicked people will be judged
Judgment will cover the whole earth, destroying all evil
Only Jerusalem will be judged, not other places
Judgment will only involve lives, not possessions
questions.explanation: The passage describes the LORD's judgment as extremely thorough, destroying everything from the face of the earth, including man, beast, birds, and fish.

questions.question: What is the main message of Zephaniah chapter 1?
options: God is a tolerant God who never judges
Worshiping idols brings wealth
The Day of the LORD is a day of thorough judgment for sin
People can avoid God's judgment through their own efforts
questions.explanation: The core message of this chapter is the proclamation of the coming 'Day of the LORD,' which will be God's thorough judgment on all evil on earth and in Judah.

en.reflection: In light of the coming judgment, what do you most need to examine and repent of today?
en.prayer: Merciful and righteous God, I confess that my heart often harbors thoughts and actions that displease You. Help me to examine myself, repent of my sins, and turn away from anything that leads me astray from You. May I always live in Your truth and light, prepared for Your return. In Jesus' name, I pray. Amen.
en.action: Take some time today to list the things in your life you might value more than God, and ask Him to help you let them go.

en.theme: Seek the LORD and Escape His Judgment
en.focus: Before the day of the LORD arrives, humbly seeking His righteousness and gentleness is the only path to escape His judgment.

questions.question: Which group of people is called to gather and seek the LORD in Zephaniah 2:1?
options: All Israelites
Leaders of the nations
Shameless nation
Those who humbly seek the LORD
questions.explanation: The passage begins by calling for the “shameless nation” to gather, emphasizing their need to confront their sin and shame.

questions.question: Before the day of the LORD's wrath arrives, what does He call His people to do?
options: Build strong city walls
Form alliances with neighbouring countries
Seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility
Offer more sacrifices
questions.explanation: The text clearly states that before the LORD's fierce anger comes, the people should “seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, you who do what he commands. Seek righteousness, seek humility.”

questions.question: Zephaniah 2:4–15 predicts judgment against which regions?
options: Only the kingdom of Judah
Only Philistia and Moab
Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, Assyria
All nations hostile to Judah
questions.explanation: The passage specifically prophesies judgment against several Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, etc.), Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria (Nineveh).

questions.question: What is the primary message of this passage?
options: God’s judgment is only for Israel’s enemies
God unconditionally forgives all sins upon repentance
God’s judgment is near, and people must humbly seek Him to receive mercy
Salvation is assured by adhering to traditional religious rituals
questions.explanation: This passage emphasizes the coming day of the LORD's judgment, urging the “humble of the land” to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility, in order to possibly be sheltered on the day of His anger.

en.reflection: Considering any pride, injustice, or distance from God in your life, in what area do you most want to humbly seek God today?
reflectionOptions: Spend quiet time in prayer with God
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me through Zephaniah that You are a righteous Judge and a loving God. Please help me to humble myself and seek Your righteousness and gentleness before the day of Your wrath arrives. May my heart always turn back to You, so that I may receive Your mercy in judgment. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Take one minute today to reflect on God's emphasis on righteousness and humility, and ask Him to help you live out these qualities.

en.focus: Even amidst judgment, God shows mercy to His people, promising ultimate cleansing, gathering, and restoration.

questions.question: How is Jerusalem described in Zephaniah 3:1–2?
options: Full of joy and praise
Rebellious, defiled, and oppressive
Submissive to all nations, peaceful
Wealthy and prosperous
questions.explanation: The passage describes Jerusalem as 'rebellious, defiled, and oppressive,' refusing to listen or learn.

questions.type: Observe God's promise to the nations
questions.question: How does God promise to deal with the nations so they may ultimately turn to Him?
options: Destroy all nations immediately
Give them pure lips to call on His name with one accord
Make them fight each other forever
Allow them to worship only their own gods
questions.explanation: God promises to give the nations pure lips so that all of them may call on the name of the LORD and serve Him with one accord.

questions.type: Observe God's promise to His people
questions.question: What qualities will God's remnant possess after their restoration?
options: Full of pride and arrogance
They will do no wrong and tell no lies
Continue to oppress the poor
Only look out for their own interests
questions.explanation: God promises that His remnant 'will do no wrong; they will tell no lies, nor will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths.'

questions.question: What primary hope does this passage offer us?
options: God will bless us if we work hard and do good
God's love and salvation for His people are ultimate, even after judgment
Judgment is God's final purpose, with no possibility of restoration
Human sin can never be forgiven
questions.explanation: Although the passage begins with judgment, it concludes with God's promises of salvation for His people (including cleansing, gathering, joy, and restoration), demonstrating His love and faithfulness.

en.reflection: In what areas of your life today do you sense a need for God's cleansing and turning? How do you respond to God's promise of restoration?
reflectionOptions: Confess shortcomings and ask for God's cleansing
Pray for revival in my church or nation
Trust more deeply in God's promises
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being a God who judges yet is full of mercy and salvation. Please cleanse my heart and remove all rebellion and defilement. Help me to trust more deeply in Your promise of restoration each day and to live a life pleasing to You. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend some quiet time today praying for one area in your life that needs God’s cleansing and believe in His grace and restoration.

en.focus: When God's people prioritize their own affairs over God's, their efforts are in vain. God desires them to seek His kingdom and righteousness first.

questions.question: Which two leaders are mentioned at the beginning of the book of Haggai?
options: Joshua and Solomon
Zerubbabel and Joshua
David and Samuel
Ezra and Nehemiah
questions.explanation: The text explicitly mentions the word of the LORD coming through Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, son of Jehozadak.

questions.question: Why had the people not completed the rebuilding of the temple?
options: They lacked sufficient building materials
They were preoccupied with building their own houses
They were under attack from enemies
They lacked the skills for construction
questions.explanation: The word of the LORD points out that the people said, “The time has not yet come to rebuild the LORD’s house,” while they were busy building their own paneled houses.

questions.question: How did God respond to the people's misplaced priorities?
options: He made them wealthier so they could afford to build the temple
He caused them to labor without satisfaction or abundant harvest
He sent an army to protect them so they could build the temple safely
He commanded them to stop all work until the temple was built
questions.explanation: God reminded them through their life circumstances: they sowed much, but harvested little; they ate, but were not satisfied; they drank, but were not filled; they clothed themselves, but were not warm; and he who earned wages put them into a bag with holes.

questions.question: God commanded the people to “go up into the mountains and bring down timber and build the house.” What does this remind us of today?
options: We should donate all our money to church building funds
We should take care of our own lives first before considering giving
We should prioritize God's work and His glory
We should wait for God to directly command us to do ministry
questions.explanation: This command reminds us that when God's house is in ruins, we should not just focus on our own comfort, but prioritize God's glory and His work.

en.reflection: In what areas might you be prioritizing your own comfort or interests over God’s work today?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for reminding me through the book of Haggai to consider my ways. Please help me examine my heart, and forgive me if I have ever prioritized my own comfort or self-interest over Your kingdom. May I always place Your glory and Your work at the forefront of my life. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Today, take five minutes to reflect on one specific action you can take to prioritize God's work.

en.focus: God reminds His people that His presence and power will bring greater glory than before, and grant peace.

questions.question: To whom did God speak through the prophet Haggai?
options: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and all the people
The king, the generals, and the priests
All the young men, women, and children of Israel
The Babylonian rulers and the exiled Israelites
questions.explanation: Haggai 2:2 clearly specifies that God's word was to Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and all the people.

questions.question: What did God remind His people of to encourage them not to be discouraged?
options: Their past great achievements
His presence with them, not to fear
They would soon gain great wealth
Their enemies had been completely destroyed
questions.explanation: God, through Haggai, twice emphasized, 'I am with you,' and commanded them to be strong, work, and not to fear.

questions.question: What did God promise about the future glory of this temple?
options: It would be less glorious than the first temple
It would be the same as the first temple's glory
It would be greater than the first temple's glory
It would only be more magnificent in appearance
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that the glory of this present house will be greater than the former glory.

questions.question: How does this promise in Haggai encourage us not to be discouraged in serving God today?
options: Hard work guarantees immediate results
God's power and presence transcend our current visible circumstances
We should focus on pursuing worldly wealth and glory
Serving God is only for receiving recognition and praise from others
questions.explanation: God's promise of His presence and future glory reminds us that no matter how small our current vision, God's power and plans are far beyond what we can comprehend, so we should not be discouraged.

en.reflection: Is there an area in your life where, despite current unsatisfactory circumstances, you need to continue to be strong and work with hope, relying on God's promises?
en.prayer: Faithful God, thank You for reminding me that Your presence overcomes all difficulties. When I face seemingly small or discouraging situations, help me to fix my eyes on Your glorious promises, to be strong and courageous, and to work faithfully. May my heart be at peace because of the peace You give. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Spend one minute today meditating on 'I am with you' (Haggai 2:4) and ask God to strengthen your heart.

en.focus: God reminds His people that true cleansing and blessing come not from outward rituals, but from an obedient heart, and promises to bless them once they obey.

questions.question: In Haggai 2:10-14, what question does God pose to the people through the priests?
options: If someone carries holy meat and touches something else, will that something become holy?
If someone touches a dead body, will everything they touch become unclean?
Will those who build the temple receive extra rewards?
What regulations must those who offer sacrifices follow?
questions.explanation: The first question God poses through the priests is whether holy meat can make something it touches holy, and the answer is no.

questions.question: According to Haggai 2:10-14, what principle about clean and unclean is being emphasized?
options: Cleanness spreads easily, but uncleanness does not.
Uncleanness spreads easily, but cleanness does not.
Neither cleanness nor uncleanness spreads.
Only priests can make people clean.
questions.explanation: The passage indicates that holy meat cannot make something unclean holy, but an unclean person who touches a dead body makes everything they touch unclean. This emphasizes that uncleanness spreads more easily, while cleanness is harder to transmit.

questions.question: After the people began to build the temple, from what day did God promise to bless them?
options: From the day they offered their first sacrifice
From the day they resumed building the temple
From the day they completed the temple
From the day they called upon God
questions.explanation: God explicitly states that from the day they resumed building the temple (the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month), He would bless them.

questions.question: What is the most significant reminder this passage (Haggai 2:10-23) gives us today?
options: God only cares about our outward religious rituals.
God will give true blessings and power after we obey His will.
God will be pleased if we build magnificent church buildings.
God does not bless His people during difficult times.
questions.explanation: This passage first points out that an unclean attitude and actions can defile everything. God promises to bless His people from the day they obey His call and resume building the temple, and promises future glory and power. This shows that God values inward obedience and action, and will bestow true blessings and power after obedience.

en.reflection: In what area of your life today do you need God's cleansing and to respond to His call with an obedient heart?
en.prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for teaching me that cleansing comes not from outward rituals, but from my inward obedience to You. Please shine Your light upon me and cleanse every area of my life that displeases You. Help me to respond to Your call with an obedient heart, trusting that Your promised blessings and power will come. In Jesus' name I pray, Amen.
en.action: Think of a small act of obedience to God you can do today, and put it into practice immediately.

en.focus: God calls His people to return to Him and strengthens them with visions, preparing them to rebuild the temple and city.

questions.question: In the opening of Zechariah, in which year did the word of the LORD come to the prophet Zechariah?
options: In the second year of Darius
In the first year of Cyrus
In the seventh year of Artaxerxes
In the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar
